While Besiktas also covet another Newcastle midfielder in Joe Willock, Wilson appears close to securing a new goalkeeper. A £26m deal for the Braga and Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek is expected to be completed over the weekend.

Should that move for the 24-year-old progress as planned, Nick Pope, Newcastle’s current first-choice, will almost certainly prove to be yet another departure during a turbulent summer featuring a major changing of the guard on Tyneside.

Sports.title: Franco Baresi was not only the captain but the moral heart of great Milan team
Sports.content:
There are very few players who become bywords for their position, who enjoy universal acclaim. But for anybody who watched football in the late 80s or early 90s, Franco Baresi was the central defender. He was unsurpassed, obviously the best in his position in the world, the definition of the art of the defending. The oddity is, he really wasn’t like very many other defenders at all.

Baresi had just turned 19 when he won his first scudetto at Milan under Nils Liedholm. It was 1979 and Italian football was still dominated by the ideals of catenaccio. Most defences comprised a libero, two man-markers and, if you were lucky, an attacking left-back. But not Liedholm’s. The Swede was a pioneer in Serie A of zonal marking, and the idea that the game was not a series of physical battles but a question of space. Baresi was only 5ft 9in and a teenager. More traditional coaches may not have trusted him. But Liedholm saw an impeccable reader of the game, even at that age. Baresi was an ever-present, not only in the league but in the Coppa Italia and Uefa Cup as well.

That turned out to be a traumatic season for the club, with players arrested on the pitch after the final game of the season as part of the Totonero betting scandal, for which Milan were ultimately relegated. With the club in financial chaos, promotion was followed by another relegation and, although they were promoted again, the future seemed bleak before Silvio Berlusconi took over in 1986. Baresi remained loyal throughout. His parents died before he turned 16 and Milan became a sort of surrogate family.

He never played for any other club, amassing 719 appearances in all competitions over 20 years. And yet, he could easily have been an Inter player. Baresi’s brother Giuseppe, two years his elder, was already at Inter when Franco was offered a trial at the age of 14. Inter wondered if he was big enough to make it and asked him to come back the following year. So Franco went for a trial at Milan – which he insisted had always been his club – and was taken on.

Berlusconi was an outsider, determined to disrupt the establishment. In Arrigo Sacchi, who was appointed in 1987, he found a coach in the same vein: a radical who followed Liedholm’s tentative steps into the world of zonal marking with a giant leap into a full-blown flat back four and hard pressing. In the Serie A of the age it was almost unthinkably revolutionary. Conservatives were sceptical and, when Milan lost their second game of the season 2-0 at home to Fiorentina, and followed that up with defeat to Espanyol in the Uefa Cup and a disappointing draw against Cesena, the joke was that Berlusconi’s new messiah would not make All Saints’ Day, which is 1 November.

Form began to turn around, but Sacchi worried he had pushed the players too hard and eased back on training, at which point Baresi made a decisive intervention. He begged Sacchi to push the players even harder. It was vital, he said, that the players didn’t forget, that they came to learn the new way of playing, of working out their position not according to preset formulas but through constantly evolving reference to the opponent, their teammates, the ball and the space, to internalise the processes until they became instinctive.

View image in fullscreen Franco Baresi (kneeling, second left) and his Milan teammates celebrate beating Steaua Bucharest 4-0 to win the 1989 European Cup, for many the high point of their football under Arrigo Sacchi. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

For Sacchi, it was a huge moment. Baresi was not only the captain, but the moral heart of the team. If he was on board with the revolution, Sacchi realised, the squad would follow. Milan, with their ultra-modern style, won the scudetto in 1988 and backed it up with consecutive European Cup wins, playing some of the most memorable football ever witnessed. Baresi was central to it, not only snuffing out opposing forwards but constantly analysing and organising, and also beginning initiating counterattacks. The clipped forward pass became a trademark, but his greatest skill was his pass selection. He just didn’t give the ball away.

His icons were all creative players, plus Ruud Krol, but Baresi was also tough. Gianfranco Zola called him the best defender he ever played against but observed that afterwards “your feet need loads of ice and anti-inflammatories”. Baresi dished it out, as defenders in Serie A in those days had to, but he could also take it. He played more than an hour of a Milan derby in 1989 with a broken arm, helping keep a clean sheet, and, at the 1994 World Cup, managed to recover from knee surgery required after tearing his cartilage in the second group game in time to play in the final. Again, he oversaw a clean sheet but, cruelly, failed from the spot in the shootout as Italy lost to Brazil.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A Milan fan lays flowers next to a shirt of former captain Franco Baresi at Casa Milan. Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/Reuters

International football never quite gave Baresi the highs the club game did. He was part of the World Cup-winning squad in 1982 but didn’t play a minute, and was part of squads that got to the last four of Euro 88 and Italia ‘90, but he never achieved the same glory with Italy that he did with Milan.

And so the memory of him will always be in the red-and-black shirt, anticipating the game, stepping implacably in front of an opponent, shrugging him off and clipping a perfectly weighted ball in to a forward’s feet, the defining image of Italy’s new era of defending.

Sports.title: Jaissle heads for Newcastle after success in Saudi Arabia that has eluded so many
Sports.content:
Taking over a big, underachieving port city club with a loyal fanbase that is desperate for success should not faze Matthias Jaissle. Should he take the role vacated by Eddie Howe, the 38-year-old German will leave Jeddah as a hero and arrive in the north-east as one of the most successful coaches in the history of Asian football.

A decade younger than Howe, Jaissle has achieved plenty, not only surviving in a Saudi Pro League that chews through coaches at a rapid rate but emerging victorious. It also helps that Al-Ahli and Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) owners.

Newcastle fans may know little about the former centre-back, whose playing career was cut short by injury, but that was also the case in Saudi Arabia when he arrived three years ago. Austria’s Bundesliga is not followed much in Asia, so two titles won with Red Bull Salzburg did not mean a great deal: neither did Jaissle’s association with Ralf Rangnick.

Fans were more focused on Al-Ahli’s recent return to the top flight, after a first season in the second tier, and were contemplating an influx of big-name players. A little different to the situation at St James’ Park with stars such as Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon already gone and others seemingly about to follow.

In Jeddah, Riyad Mahrez, Roberto Firmino, Édouard Mendy, Franck Kessié and others arrived in a summer when the club was acquired by PIF. For a team that had been in the doldrums a year earlier, it was quite a turnaround.

Despite all that Al-Ahli may have been the perfect club for Jaissle. The fans are famously passionate but had only one domestic league win since 1984. In Asia there had been two comprehensive Champions League final defeats. Compared to Al-Hilal, Al-Nassr and Al-Ittihad – also in the PIF stable – the Green corner of Jeddah had been relatively starved of success and, for a while, challenging again was enough.

For the then 35-year-old, dealing with such names did not seem a problem. His straight-talking style, with the foreign stars treated the same as the locals, drew a positive response. With his wealth of attacking talent Jaissle tried to win possession as high as possible to give players such as Mahrez the chance to shine. His preferred attack-minded, high-intensity playing style may move up a gear by the North Sea compared to the heat and humidity of the Red Sea.

View image in fullscreen Galeno (right) was a key signing for Al-Ahli under Jaissle and brought the best out of Ivan Toney in attack. Photograph: Reuters

In his first season Al-Ahli finished third, 11 points ahead of their fierce local rivals Al-Ittihad and, crucially, qualified for the AFC Champions League Elite. The second season was more difficult, for a while at least. After the departure of Allan Saint-Maximin, Jaissle wanted a replacement winger but, instead, Ivan Toney was signed and the England striker started slowly. Results dipped but were improving by January 2025 when the axe threatened to fall. Max Allegri was ready to take over, the kind of eye-catching coach that fans often want. But not in this case – members of the Green Army supported Jaissle, who had always taken time out to praise and talk to fans. A group of them appeared at the training ground with banners telling club management they should be the ones to go.

And it worked. Al-Ahli said Jaissle was staying with their full support. In came a winger, Galeno from Porto, and with the Brazilian getting the best out of Toney, Al-Ahli moved up a gear. They finished fifth in Jaissle’s second season but got more points. It was all about the Champions League, however. In the semi-finals, they defeated Al-Hilal, 19-time Saudi and four-time Asian winners. Then, in May 2025, in front of 60,000 fans in Jeddah, Kawasaki Frontale of Japan were defeated.

Then Al-Ahli did it again, winning the Asian title for a second time last May to become the first team since their Jeddah rivals, Al-Ittihad (in 2004 and 2005), to clinch successive Champions League crowns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They also had a title challenge at home that only faded in the final weeks with Toney scoring 32 goals. In 34 games the team collected 81 points, 14 more than the previous season, and had Al-Nassr and Al-Hilal not been so consistent then it could have been a spectacular double.

The focus for the new season, due to start in August, was all about the Saudi Pro League title; but that should be someone else’s concern now.

Jaissle was recently linked with Al-Hilal and while that wouldn’t have gone down well with fans in Jeddah, he heads to Newcastle with the blessing of most. The German was always likely to return to Europe, and departs with success in Saudi Arabia, having won major titles. Many more experienced coaches have failed in that regard. Newcastle will be a different and tougher challenge.

He is not part of the elite any more but taking Newcastle closer to the Premier League’s top four would be a good start.

Sports.title: Who should win the men’s Ballon d’Or?
Sports.content:
Harry Kane

Seventy-three goals in 64 games for club and country – the second most prolific season by any player in history after Lionel Messi’s 82-goal campaign in 2011-12 – not bad for a man who once sat on the bench alongside Jamie Vardy in the Championship. Harry Kane was not a teenage prodigy like a few of the other players on this list but here he is crashing football’s top table at the age of 33.

It feels strange that a player who has scored at least 24 goals in each of the last 12 seasons, has won back-to-back Golden Boots in the Premier League, a World Cup Golden Boot and two European Golden Shoes, has never finished higher than 10th in Ballon d’Or voting.

The numbers were always there but now he is adding the silverware. Kane’s trophy drought ended when Bayern Munich won the Bundesliga last year and that triumph has opened the floodgates. Another Bundesliga title followed this season, alongside the DFB-Pokal and German Supercup.

England did not end their trophy drought at the World Cup but their captain scored six goals and overtook Gary Lineker as England’s top scorer at the tournament, ensuring he remained in contention for the Ballon d’Or.

Lamine Yamal

“It’s about being calm. When I’m in the area with the ball, I decide what happens,” said Lamine Yamal in February after he had scored the first hat-trick of his career in Barcelona’s 4-1 win against Villarreal. For most 19-year-olds this would sound like arrogance, but Yamal is not like most 19-year-olds.

He offered more proof of that this summer. The Spain forward became the first player to appear in a European Championship final and a World Cup final before turning 20 – and he won both. He only scored one goal at the World Cup, which was a modest return by his own lofty standards, but he was influential throughout. He won a gamechanging penalty in the semi-final against France, he made more successful take-ons than Messi across the tournament, and he had a hand in breaking down an Argentina side hellbent on baiting him into a physical duel in the final. He achieved all this after going into the tournament with a hamstring injury. Joe Hart captured the mood best after the final, saying: “Lamine Yamal is 19 years old. What a beautiful day for him. He’s 19 and has completed football.”

Add in the 24 goals and 18 assists he racked up in 45 appearances for Barcelona as they won La Liga and the Supercopa, and he has a strong case to go one better than his runners-up finish in last year’s Ballon d’Or.

Rodri

“We’ll see the real Rodri at the World Cup,” said Pep Guardiola last October, when the Manchester City captain returned to action after suffering an ACL injury. There were doubts that the 2023 Ballon d’Or winner would ever return to his best. But, as with most things in football, Guardiola was right.

Rodri was the heartbeat and the safety blanket in the Spain team, dictating every phase of the game, controlling possession and extinguishing almost every danger posed to his backline – Spain only conceded one goal in their eight matches at the tournament. Rodri completed 756 passes (more than anyone at the tournament) and he also topped the charts for touches, line-breaking passes and passes in the opposition third. In the final alone he completed 101 passes, completely strangling the life out of Argentina to the extent that they did not have a single shot on target.

He lifted the trophy as Spain’s captain, won the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player and earned a place in one of football’s most exclusive clubs as only the fourth man in history to have won the World Cup, European Championship, European Cup and Ballon d’Or, joining Gerd Müller, Franz Beckenbauer and Zinedine Zidane.

Kylian Mbappé

Kylian Mbappé went toe-to-toe with his old Paris Saint-Germain teammate Lionel Messi at the World Cup. They battled it out for the trophy, the Golden Boot, the Golden Ball and a place in the history books as the competition’s all-time leading scorer. He won two of the four. His two goals in the third-place playoff against England ensured he became the first man to win the Golden Boot twice. It also brought him to 22 goals in World Cups – one more than Messi – and made him the first man to reach double figures in a single edition since Müller in 1970.

And yet, it was not what Mbappé wanted. “I would have preferred not to be the top scorer and to have played in the final,” said the France captain. His domestic season was also prolific but disappointing, bringing goals and individual glory but no silverware. He scored 42 goals in 44 appearances, finishing the season as the top scorer in La Liga and the Champions League, but he did not win either trophy. The goals flowed but the medals did not follow. As Kane has discovered, goals alone are rarely enough to win the Ballon d’Or.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé has scored 22 goals in 22 matches at World Cups. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

Lionel Messi

Lionel Messi sat on the floor alone in a stadium of 80,000 people, boots off, staring into the distance as Spain’s substitutes streamed past him in celebration. It was not the fairytale image the Argentina captain had envisioned as he left the world stage. And, given his performances over the previous six weeks, it felt as if he deserved better even if his team did not.

Some expected Messi’s tournament to be a nostalgia act – a former great wheeled out for one last World Cup as he prepares for his 40th birthday. But then he went and scored a hat-trick in Argentina’s first game. He scored twice against Austria, then added another against Jordan. He stamped his authority on the tournament in the group stage and proceeded to drag Argentina through the knockouts: a goal against Cape Verde, a goal and an assist against Egypt, an assist against Switzerland, and two more assists to sink England in the semi-final. Had it not been for Mbappé’s brace in a bizarre third-place playoff, he would have collected the Golden Boot.

Could he win the Ballon d’Or having lost the World Cup final? In only four of the last 19 years has the award gone to a player who did not win the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa América in the same year. But three of them were won by Messi. A ninth Ballon d’Or is unlikely but the fact he is in this conversation at all – at 39 while playing in MLS having lost a final – is testament to his greatness.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches
Sports.content:
The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

Sports.title: Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubs
Sports.content:
The Premier League has agreed on a proposal to reset financial distribution within English football’s top four divisions, one that would lead to an extra £1.5bn being shared across the pyramid over the next decade.

Clubs voted unanimously to support the so-called “new deal for football” at a meeting on Thursday, after discussions with the EFL. The offer will now be presented to the EFL’s board for consideration.

According to details originally published by Sky News, the Premier League’s offer would run for 10 years and result in an additional £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs on top of the £1.6bn currently distributed to clubs and communities every three years. Some of the money would be put into discrete funds – a “lifeboat” fund for clubs in immediate crisis and one that is directed exclusively at infrastructure.

To cover the extra costs, Premier League clubs have reportedly agreed to raise the transfer levy applied to all top-flight deals from 4% to 6%. The Guardian reported this week that Manchester City were initially opposed to increasing the levy.

The Premier League said in a statement that its clubs had “unanimously voted to approve a funded proposal for a new strategic partnership with the EFL”. It said it would now “look forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal” and remain “committed to finding a football-led solution”.

The EFL has yet to officially receive the offer but acknowledged “constructive” discussions with the Premier League and said its board would “review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League”.

This is the first time that Premier League clubs have officially agreed a proposal that could be put to the EFL since they were first asked to give more money to the rest of the pyramid five years ago. The Covid pandemic had revealed the precarious nature of finances at many EFL clubs and in 2022 the then sports minister Nigel Huddleston said the British public were already “out of patience” over a failure to reach an improved settlement.

The belief that the Premier League’s riches could be shared more effectively across the game helped lead in part to the creation of the Independent Football Regulator, which came into being last year. The regulator has played no direct part in the negotiations, but has a “backstop” power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

While there is cautious optimism that a deal can now finally be agreed, it is not a guarantee that the EFL will accept the Premier League’s offer, with sources suggesting it sees the proposal as being very similar to one that was mooted in 2023 but ultimately never approved by Premier League clubs. Both sides say they remain committed to ongoing dialogue.

Sports.title: Manchester United keeping tabs on Newcastle defender Lewis Hall ahead of potential summer move - plus latest on Marcus Rashford's Old Trafford future
Sports.content:
Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle United left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position.

Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only recognised senior option in that position.

Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United admire Newcastle and England left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80million, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Sports.title: Inter Milan continue pursuit of £30m-rated Liverpool star, Bournemouth agree deal for Benfica defender - and West Ham step up chase for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Inter Milan continue pursuit of £30m-rated Liverpool star, Bournemouth agree deal for Benfica defender - and West Ham step up chase for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

United keeping tabs on Hall

Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position. Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only senior option in that position. Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United are keen on Newcastle left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80m, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Hamer heading back to Coventry

Coventry are closing on a deal to bring back midfielder Gustavo Hamer from Sheffield United. The 29-year-old Brazilian has one year left on his deal.

He spent three years at Coventry after joining from PEC Zwolle, before moving to Sheffield United in August 2023.

Inter continue Jones pursuit

Inter Milan are continuing to pursue Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones but have still to hit the Anfield club's valuation.

The 25-year-old has cut a frustrated figure in recent months and has wanted more regular game time.

He has one year left on contract and Liverpool say they are relaxed about his situation.

Liverpool value the academy graduate around £30million but Inter's last offer was just under £22m.

The Italian club were interested in January and proposed a loan with a view to a permanent move but that was also turned down by Liverpool.

Inter Milan are continuing to chase Curtis Jones but are yet to meet Liverpool's valuation

Piero Ausilio, Inter's sporting director, confirmed he was still on their radar earlier this summer, saying: 'Curtis Jones - we are paying attention to him. We didn't hide. We understand what the developments will be.'

Teammate Federico Chiesa, another who could depart, also told Italian media that Jones asked him what it is like to live in Italy.

The midfielder has been with Liverpool since he was nine and signed his first professional contract with them in 2018.

Inter yesterday confirmed the signing of England defender John Stones on a free transfer.

Cherries swoop for Silva

Bournemouth have agreed their £25m deal with Benfica to sign defender Antonio Silva.

The 22-year-old centre back captained and played 90 minutes for Benfica in their emphatic 5-0 Europa League qualifying win against St Gallen last night.

The transfer is worth £21.4million plus £4.3m in add-ons.

The Portugal international is due to travel over this weekend to have a medical and complete his move.

Antonio Silva is set to move to Bournemouth from Benfica

Leicester bring in Championship forward

Leicester City have signed Swansea City forward Liam Cullen for an undisclosed fee.

The Wales international, who has agreed a three year deal, can play as a centre-forward, attacking midfielder or right winger.

He previously worked under manager Russell Martin at Swansea.

Cullen, 27, said: 'When this opportunity came about and with the size of the club and the project they’re getting started with now, I thought it was the perfect fit for me.'

Welsh forward Liam Cullen has signed for Leicester, who will play in League One this season

Hammers trying to nail down Engels

West Ham are moving ahead on talks for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels.

The 22-year-old was the subject of bids up to £25million from Nottingham Forest in January which Celtic rejected.

West Ham have a long-held interest in the Belgium international and, after sounding out figures over a couple of conversations with the Scottish champions, are pressing to see if agreement can be reached on bringing Engels to London and making him the midfield replacement for Mateus Fernandes.

Forest, Sunderland and Fulham had also shown interest.

Sports.title: Andy Burnham calls for Gianni Infantino to RESIGN: Prime Minister tells under-fire FIFA president he is 'the wrong man' to lead football in wake of World Cup backlash
Sports.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has joined the growing contingent calling for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign over his plans to introduce private investment into the World Cup.

Burnham, an Everton fan, has said Infantino - who wants to generate £3.1billion in private investment in the World Cup - is no longer fit to govern world football.

It comes after UEFA announced a boycott of FIFA competitions over the plans while Concacaf and the AFC also opposed the proposals.

The AFC went as far to urge FIFA to undertake an urgent review of their leadership.

Speaking to reporters in Sheffield, Burnham said: 'This was an outrageous suggestion.

'The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.'

Chancellor John Healey added: 'I think FIFA's plans are falling apart, and I'm dead proud that the FA and UEFA have led the charge against the idea that the World Cup is for sale.

'The prime minister is right when he says football is for the fans. I want to see these plans put to one side and let's concentrate on the football.'

Concacaf nations are understood to be losing faith - or have already lost confidence - in the FIFA president.

Andy Burnham has joined the growing calls for FIFA president Gianni Infantino to resign

FIFA have 211 member nations, meaning 106 signatories are required to block or approve any changes to their statutes. 135 nations have voiced opposition to Infantino’s plans - he does not have the votes.

Should Infantino press ahead or abandon the plans but try to remain FIFA’s kingpin, discontented nations could convene an emergency FIFA congress to initiate a vote of no confidence.

Only 20 per cent of FIFA members are required to trigger a vote, meaning support from all of UEFA’s members or CONCACAF’s 46 FIFA-registered nations would be sufficient.

Sources have suggested that Norway have floated an emergency congress while all options remain on the table for UEFA nations.

Burnham is the latest high-profile British politician to oppose Infantino after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage urged the Swiss football administrator to step down on Thursday night. 'Football is for the people,' Farage posted on X. 'UEFA are right to take a stand and Gianni Infantino must resign.'

In support of UEFA's boycott, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: 'This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It's time to take a stand to protect our game.'

Sports.title: Shocking moment Team England cyclist Matt Richardson is brutally wiped out by rival - with crash ending star's Commonwealth Games dream
Sports.content:
Team England's Matt Richardson was sensationally knocked out of contention while racing in Japan - ending his dream of competing for his country at this month's Commonwealth Games.

The cyclist had switched his nationality from Australian to English two years ago and hoped to compete in Glasgow at the ongoing games.

But Richardson received a brutal injury while taking part in the Keirin World Series, with footage emerging of the Kent-born rider being caught up in a collision with opponent Kento Suzuki.

Suzuki appeared to be speeding up heading towards the racing line, but a mistake saw him fall into Richardson to prematurely call time on both of their races.

Richardson later left the outdoor velodrome in an ambulance.

Suzuki was later disqualified from the event, and took to social media in the aftermath to public his sincere apologies.

Matt Richardson's hopes of competing at the Commonwealth Games were ended in Japan

'There's no excuses, it's simply down to my own lack of skill,' he wrote.

'From this point onwards, I've changed my mindset. If it doesn't work vertically, I'll try horizontally – I just couldn't help but move. I'm sorry.'

Richardson had been due to compete in the team sprint, keirin, and the sprint in Scotland.

The 27-year-old won two silver medals for Australia at the Paris Games in 2024, but controversially switched his allegiance to Team GB just days later.

Sports.title: Real Madrid hand Vinicius Jr contract ultimatum: Spanish giants 'table take it or leave it offer' to Arsenal target amid contract stand-off
Sports.content:
Real Madrid have reportedly tabled a final 'take it or leave it' contract offer to Vinicius Jr as the Spanish giants look to find a resolution to the Arsenal target's future.

The Brazilian, 26, has been locked in talks with the LaLiga club over fresh terms, with his existing deal expiring in two years, but senior figures have baulked at his demands to be put on an even footing with the team's top earner, Kylian Mbappe.

Marca now report that Madrid have put forward one final offer to Vinicius and his camp and there will be no further increases or another round of negotiations.

If the player rejects the deal, the report claims, the Spaniards will look to sell the star this summer.

Real Madrid have reportedly tabled a final take it or leave it offer to Vinicius Junior

Madrid want to keep the Brazilian but will not disrupt their wage structure - which could pave the way for a swoop from Arsenal

Vinicius' uncertain future at Madrid has alerted Premier League champions Arsenal, who are looking to strengthen the left side of their attack.

Some Arsenal insiders fear their efforts are futile but others want to continue to press in case Madrid fail to reach an agreement.

Madrid still view Vinicius as a key figure in the team and their desire is for him to extend his contract, but will not risk the squad's salary structure - and therefore the harmony of the playing group - in order to accommodate the Brazilian.

The imminent arrival of RB Leipzig star Ousmane Diomande could also pave the way for Vinicius' exit, with the Ivorian expected to join Jose Mourinho's team imminently.

Mourinho has telephoned Vini Jr and is understood to have told him he wants him to stay.

The footballer has stayed away from pre-season training while his representatives remain in talks with the club.

Daily Mail Sport understands Roc Nation’s talks with Real Madrid have centred on Vinicius’s huge commercial worth to the club.

The player’s current contract means he gives around 50 per cent of publicity-deal revenue to them, during the World Cup he had lucrative deals with 15 multinational sponsors – a number topped only by his international team-mate Neymar.

The 26-year-old has the same representatives as Diomande, who was also on Arsenal's radar, and there has been interest from Saudi Arabi over the past 12 months.

Vinicius is one of a number of forward targets Arsenal are exploring, with Julian Alvarez, Yan Diomande and Bradley Barcola also of interest.

Sports.title: Revealed: Chelsea's secret talks to get SIX-POINT deduction overturned as Blues are hit with £10MILLION fine for 'illegal' signings under Roman Abramovich
Sports.content:
Revealed: Chelsea's secret talks to get SIX-POINT deduction overturned as Blues are hit with £10MILLION fine for 'illegal' signings under Roman Abramovich

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Chelsea have avoided a potential points deduction from the FA after an appeal, it has been revealed, but will now pay a £10million fine and serve a suspended two-window transfer ban.

The Stamford Bridge side were hit with 74 charges by the FA and admitted to their chargesheet. The charges related to the use of and the making of payments to unregistered agents between 2011 and 2018.

It has now been revealed that Chelsea were initially hit with a six-point deduction suspended until June 2027 and a £10m fine from an independent regulatory commission.

However, after appealing, the club will now only pay for their financial penalty with a suspended transfer ban added in.

Earlier this year, the Blues were fined £10m and handed a suspended transfer ban by the Premier League after admitting to making £47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third parties between 2011 and 2018.

Chelsea’s owners BlueCo voluntarily reported themselves to several footballing regulators previously upon taking over from Roman Abramovich in 2022, as they were understood to notice their financial irregularities while doing their due diligence amid that takeover.

Now that they have reached settlement agreements with UEFA and the Premier League, and concluded their charges with the FA, it finally brings an end to Chelsea’s issues from their old ownership.

Chelsea have overturned a six-point deduction following 74 breaches of financial rules under former owner Roman Abramovich

In a statement, Chelsea said: ‘In 2022, the club self-reported potential historical rule breaches to all applicable regulators. Following that report, it has worked openly and transparently with all regulators, including voluntarily and proactively disclosing many thousands of documents.

‘As previously announced, settlement agreements have been entered into with UEFA and the Premier League concerning the same self-reported regulatory matters and topics that have been addressed before. The club is pleased to confirm that, now the FA process has concluded, this brings all regulatory proceedings against the club to a close. We are grateful to UEFA, the Premier League and the FA for their engagement with the club throughout these processes.’

A statement from the FA read: ‘A financial sanction of £10m and a suspended two-window registration ban have been imposed on Chelsea FC for breaches of the Football Association Football Agent Regulations, Regulations on Working with Intermediaries and Third Party Investment in Players Regulations. The FA charged Chelsea FC with 74 breaches of FA Rule E1.2 after its current ownership self-reported misconduct upon its purchase of the club. The FA is continuing to investigate individual misconduct arising out of this case.

‘Chelsea FC admitted to the 74 breaches of FA Rule E1.2 prior to a hearing and an independent Regulatory Commission imposed a six-point deduction, which was to be suspended until June 30, 2027, and a £10m fine.

‘The club appealed against the suspended points deduction and an independent Appeal Board allowed the appeal and set aside this sanction following a further hearing.

The Blues were hit with a £10million fine for making seven 'illegal' signings including David Luiz (left) and Ramires (right)

Eden Hazard joined in 2012 and became one of the best players in the world while at Chelsea. He was also one of the seven players signed by the club under illegal circumstances

‘In its place, the Appeal Board imposed a registration ban for two complete and consecutive transfer windows which is suspended until 30 June 2027.’ The £10m fine was not subject to appeal and the full amount will be invested into grassroots football.

The punishment relates to activity under Chelsea’s old ownership prior to BlueCo.

With the Premier League in March, Chelsea were previously fined £10m and handed a suspended transfer ban after admitting to making secret payments to unofficial agents between 2011 and 2018. That related to several transfers such as Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic, though it should be noted that there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of those players. The £10m fine topped the £5.5m fine given to West Ham in 2007 over their signings of Javier Mascherano and Carlos Tevez.

Chelsea also received a nine-month academy transfer ban and a £750,000 fine over the registration of academy players between 2019 and 2022.

The Premier League did say at the time that the £10m fine would have been £20m, but was reduced by 50 per cent after Chelsea proactively self-reported and co-operated.

It was also concluded that Chelsea would not have breached the Premier League’s Profitability and Sustainability rules during the applicable seasons in which they were investigated – even if the payments had been registered properly.

Sports.title: 'He's a delusional dictator who's lost touch with reality': Insiders reveal how FIFA boss Gianni Infantino went from 'pleasant and unassuming' to a 'greedy narcissist' with 'zero empathy' so drunk on power he is trying to sell the World Cup
Sports.content:
'He's a delusional dictator who's lost touch with reality': Insiders reveal how FIFA boss Gianni Infantino went from 'pleasant and unassuming' to a 'greedy narcissist' with 'zero empathy' so drunk on power he is trying to sell the World Cup

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

The date was March 20, 2025, and a gilded ensemble had convened at a beautiful spot in southern Greece. Against the backdrop of the Ionian Sea, one of the many mysteries of Gianni Infantino was about to play out.

His reason for being at the Costa Navarino resort was a task of some importance. Same went for the rest of the group – an assortment of royals, heads of state and sporting powerbrokers known collectively as the membership of the International Olympic Committee.

As president of football’s global governing body, Infantino was part of their gang. And that was a big deal on this particular Thursday, because they were in town to elect the movement’s next leader. Seven candidates were in the running, 97 votes would be cast, and the finer detail of who ticked which box is usually lost to secrecy.

But whispers can carry on a sea breeze.

According to three prominent sources contacted by Daily Mail Sport, the shared wisdom was that FIFA’s supreme ruler sided with the Spanish candidate Juan Antonio Samaranch Jr. Evidently, Samaranch Jr’s team felt pretty sure of it.

But therein lies the intrigue, because we have also been told that figures close to a rival candidate, Lord Sebastian Coe, heard a different song in Greece. Apparently, they were given reason to believe Infantino’s vote would be his.

Gianni Infantino has been FIFA president since 2016 and will stand for re-election next year

The Swiss has been instrumental in the bloating of the World Cup from 32 nations to 48

As it transpired, neither man won, but here’s the thing: 15 months on, the two parties are still said to trust that Infantino went their way.

FIFA did not respond to Daily Mail Sport’s request for a little clarity, so what are we to do with this vignette? Is it par for the famously opaque course of sporting politics, or indicative of the confusion that forever surrounds Infantino? It’s just one thought to consider after the strangest, most politicised World Cup in recent memory and find ourselves studying the many faces of the man behind it.

Because who and what is Gianni Infantino, the man who tried to sell the World Cup?

Four years have passed since he took to a stage at the Qatar tournament and offered his own answer. Addressing his audience that day, he said: ‘Today, I feel Qatari. Today, I feel gay. Today, I feel disabled. Today, I feel like a migrant worker...’

Prior to this World Cup, the portrait is somehow more surreal.

Today, it can be tempting to wonder if there is a world leader Infantino wouldn’t feel for a buck.

Today, it can feel as though Infantino has bucked football senseless.

Today, it feels prudent to query if football is safe in his hands.

It was February 26, 2016, when Infantino was elected to clean the wreckage left by the institutional corruption found beneath his predecessor, Sepp Blatter

Infantino has hungered for the limelight unlike any sporting administrator in recent memory

From presidents and sheikhs to Salt Bae, carver of steaks – the cast of individuals embraced by Infantino and presented to his four million Instagram followers is broad. But he wasn’t always so ostentatious.

It was February 26, 2016, when Infantino was elected to clean the wreckage left by the institutional corruption found beneath his predecessor, Sepp Blatter. Back then, the new guy he was largely anonymous to the outside world.

The Swiss-born son of working-class Italians and a lawyer by trade, Infantino had been the accidental candidate. He had risen across the course of 16 years to the rank of UEFA’s general secretary, but FIFA’s top job was seemingly ordained for his boss, Michel Platini.

It was only after Platini was sucked into the same investigations as Blatter that a door opened for Infantino. ‘I had dinner with Platini the week before the whole thing blew up, and he genuinely thought he was there,’ says Greg Dyke, who was the FA chairman during the Blatter demise and for the first few months of Infantino.

‘I don't quite know where the idea came from for Infantino to run, but my first impressions were that I liked him. He was a guy you could sit down with and have a chat. I never thought he was particularly political and thought he would bring a positive change.’

Dyke’s FA were among those to vote for him.

Patrick Nally’s instincts were similar to Dyke’s and date back further. Renowned as the founding father of modern sports marketing, the Englishman, 79, was one of the foremost king-makers behind Blatter’s rise at FIFA in the 1990s and he remains connected to the lever-pullers of elite sport. He first met Infantino in 2010 and found him ‘pleasant and unassuming’. He adds: ‘He didn't strike me as an incredibly political or ambitious individual, which clearly he seems to have become.’

That understatement only skims over the changes we have witnessed across Infantino’s decade on the throne. Neither his personality nor his alterations to the very fabric of football point to a leader who dwells long on where to impose his limits.

The FIFA president drew criticism for posing for selfies close to Pele’s coffin in 2023

Infantino sends birthday messages to Cristiano Ronaldo which hint at his obsession with celebrity

The question is: how closely are the two factors linked? And from there, how worried should we be? We’ll stick with the personality traits for now, because Infantino has hungered for the limelight unlike any sporting administrator in recent memory. To look at one of his most contentious creations, the Club World Cup, is to see his name engraved into trophy. Twice.

Then there's his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, with each of the 211 member nations getting a (very small) slice and private investors invited to hoover up a chunk more. This giant overreach may be his Icarus moment, after Europe called his bluff and said they will boycott any future World Cups if this plan goes through. Asia and North America are also against the plan.

Birthday messages to Cristiano Ronaldo sit at a trivial end of this discussion about celebrity obsession but posing for selfies close to Pele’s coffin in 2023 drew greater flak. Caught somewhere between pragmatism and fawning, Infantino’s relationships with autocratic rulers is where the chat becomes more germane to what football has become on his watch.

It hasn’t gone unnoticed that the ongoing grins of fealty to Donald Trump are an echo of what has gone before with Vladimir Putin and the ruling family of Qatar, but, like so much else, it has grown more extreme with each World Cup cycle.

To the riposte of whether such endorsements matter, some would suggest the migrant workers who built Qatari stadiums are best qualified to answer; or those elements of the Iranian football delegation denied visas to the United States.

When Infantino wore a red Trump hat at the US President’s Board of Peace meeting in February, the optics were so jarring the IOC investigated a potential breach of their principles around political neutrality. As a member of the IOC, he might have been expected to play closer attention to their sensitivities – the Winter Olympics were in progress at that very moment. Infantino was cleared, but IOC president Kirsty Coventry was unimpressed. A seasoned Olympics source tells us their relationship is ‘not close’.

A kind interpretation would argue occasional clumsiness on Infantino’s part. But is it something else? Has it morphed closer to grandiosity and delusion?

Let’s review what played out at FIFA’s congress in Vancouver in April. Having already requested – and been denied – a motorcade beyond the privileges of the Canadian prime minister, Infantino attempted to coax a handshake on stage between senior executives of the Israeli and Palestinian football associations. Predictably, they refused and Palestinian FA president Jibril Rajoub walked away in audible displeasure from an excruciating scene.

When Infantino wore a red Trump hat at the US President’s Board of Peace meeting in February, the optics were so jarring the IOC investigated a potential breach of their principles around political neutrality

Infantino cosied up to the ruling family of Qatar ahead of the 2022 World Cup

‘To me, it looks like a muppet show,’ says the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, who initially campaigned for the FIFA post after Blatter’s demise. ‘What we saw in Vancouver and that embarrassing situation around Israel and Palestine, showed me a man with zero empathy and a superiority complex that degraded the position of FIFA president.’

It might be academic to ponder why Infantino craves the spotlight. But it would also be naive to assume power has no impact on those who wield it, especially if we rewind to the environment Infantino entered in 2016. Having inherited the political gold dust of a disgraced predecessor, Infantino was almost lionised as the reformist football needed. From there, the scope to become intoxicated is self-evident.

In Nally’s mind, a key transition point will have been the World Cup in Russia in 2018, which Infantino inherited from the previous regime and placed him in proximity to Putin. What follows is a compelling theory.

‘All I can say is that power goes to one's head,’ Nally says. ‘I think Russia showed him just how powerful a position that he was in. The fact he was given one of the highest awards he could be given by Russia (the Order of Friendship Medal, patted onto his chest by Putin in 2019), and the realisation of what he had become, the penny dropped quite quickly.

‘Look at Qatar. This brought Infantino into complete contact with the most powerful families in Qatar. And then through Qatar into Saudi Arabia. He's allowed his personality and ego to suddenly think he is another leader of the world. He will see himself as being equal to a Trump. He will see himself as being equal to a Putin. In other words, it's difficult when you're being feted by these individuals for it to not have an influence. Some individuals forget the reality.’

Two things to note on the conversation with Nally. One is to declare is he remains in contact with Blatter, whose distaste for his successor was made clear by other sources used in this report.

The other is that he was speaking to Daily Mail Sport before that botched handshake in Vancouver – an episode that might lend some prescience to his speculation.

‘There is no humility there at all,’ Nally adds.

The peace prize conceived and handed to Trump is a natural bookend to this chapter. Infantino could not have forecast the invasion of Iran three months later, pitting his World Cup host against a participant, but the very belief that such a prize was his to gift will surely feature in his final legacy at FIFA.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin awards an Order of Friendship to Infantino during a ceremony to present state decorations at the Moscow Kremlin in 2019

Donald Trump is presented with the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize by Infantino late last year

There is a relevance to the conversation about ego, mainly for the way in which one explosion has been mirrored by others more fundamental to football. So much of the game has swelled on Infantino’s watch – a bigger World Cup, a bigger Club World Cup, bigger ticket prices, bigger demands on tired players, bigger takings.

We can talk at length about the other sliding-door moments of Infantino’s election win – for one, Dyke reaffirmed to us Platini was opposed to VAR – but the adaptations and the World Cup expansion from 32 nations to 48, and potentially 64 in 2030, have manifestly altered a crown jewel of sport. The qualification process and group-stages of the tournament are plainly diminished for it.

‘The expansion will dilute the quality of play,’ says Vega, capped 23 times by Switzerland. ‘This could cause massive player burnout and concerns over the welfare of the athletes.’

Few beyond those 48 nations, or entities that stand to profit from 40 extra games, have spoken in favour. Ditto the Club World Cup, which prompted the threat of strikes from players. And yet the sprawl will continue. The 2030 World Cup - should the threat of a boycott be headed off - will be spread around Africa, Europe and South America, with guaranteed qualification for no fewer than six host nations.

A saving grace is that FIFA officials insist it is highly unlikely the tournament will swell to 64 nations, despite Infantino saying ‘every idea is a good idea’ when the thought was floated in 2025. It remains to be seen if he realises his wish of jamming in a Club World Cup every two years.

Time will tell on the wisdom of 2030 and possibly the motivation behind it. As a manoeuvre, this messy concoction opened a convenient path for an Asia host to jump a queue of continents in 2034. That being Saudi Arabia, of course. Accusations of sportswashing and profit before sense have already recommenced on that front, but multi-faceted issues in the US are the matter at hand.

The immense backlash against FIFA’s ticket prices this summer stands as the preeminent challenge to Infantino’s view of every idea being a good one.

‘He (Infantino) has changed the game for the worse,’ says Vega. ‘He completely lost touch with reality, prioritising financial revenue. Real fans cannot afford to go to the World Cup.’

'He (Infantino) has changed the game for the worse,’ says Ramon Vega, the former Spurs player who initially campaigned for the FIFA post after Blatter’s demise. ‘He completely lost touch with reality'

Infantino with Colombian singer-songwriter Shakira at a World Cup event

Other major issues sit not far beneath the surface of the approaching jamboree, and as ever will be largely forgotten once balls are kicked.

‘As the World Cup looms, it wouldn't pass any human rights smell test,’ says Minky Worden, the director of global initiatives at Human Rights Watch. ‘FIFA have been unable to secure a guarantee that armed ICE enforcement officials aren't greeting the millions of fans here.’

Worden has offered scathing views previously in these pages about what happened in Qatar and, now, she fears for US-based Haitian supporters attending the June 13 match against Scotland. Her worry is that ICE agents might scoop them up. FIFA did not respond to a request for comment on that one.

Worden is among the many to have noticed a change in Infantino. On June 20, 2016, she visited him at FIFA HQ in Zurich. ‘He kept a promise to meet in his first 100 days,’ she says. ‘But the evolution in 10 years shows there’s clearly no value system that says he has to do that anymore.’

Human Rights Watch lost patience two years ago when Saudi Arabia emerged unopposed from a curiously truncated bidding process to land the World Cup. They cut ties.

Worden’s assessment of Infantino’s tenure concludes with a reference to what played out in Vancouver. ‘The Pope isn't asking for treatment like this so where would he have gotten the idea that he deserves it?’ she asks. ‘This is delusional dictator behaviour.’

Vega used the very same description before adding: ‘He is only serving his own ego.’

As criticisms, they are withering. But those with voting rights show no sign of joining a chorus – Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023 and has been cleared to stand again in 2027 because his first term fell short of the full four years. He will almost certainly win.

Infantino is front and centre again as a bisht is put on Lionel Messi by Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, in 2022

Other than the Norwegian FA, who called out the peace prize saga and his rescinding of Folarin Balogun's red card at Trump's request, there are no vocal dissidents among FIFA’s 211 member nations. The development allowances handed their way have grown eight-fold in Infantino’s tenure and whatever private discontent exists, it has never spread to the ballot papers.

Because whatever else has been observed during Infantino’s time, there has not been a corruption scandal. And financially, the game is thriving – FIFA’s accounts a decade ago showed an annual revenue of $502million and in 2025 that was up to $2.66billion.

In this World Cup year, the projections suggest $9bn. Everything has bloated in tandem.

Today, Infantino will feel good about that. Today, we might be entitled to feel the worst of the ‘good ideas’ was to think he was ever the solution.

Sports.title: 'He'll be a handful': Why Alexander Isak is ready to fire in second Liverpool season - LEWIS STEELE reveals his new role under Andoni Iraola, new intensity in training and mentoring Reds' young stars
Sports.content:
One of many phrases to tick off during the weekly Friday morning game of Arne Slot Press Conference Bingo was ‘Alexander Isak has signed for six years, not six months’. The now-departed Liverpool boss would use it as a quip to those questioning why the £125million man had not even got close to repaying his British-record price tag, with just two goals in his first 15 games for the club as he struggled to gain fitness. Six years, remember, not six months. The problem was that one of those years has already been and gone. Given the mammoth outlay, that’s £20.8m of the fee gone already with just four goals to show for it. Just when he looked like he had finally cracked it, away at Tottenham in December with a first-half goal, he was crocked in the process of scoring by defender Micky van de Ven and broke his leg. That was pretty much that for the season and he was nowhere near full fitness until the World Cup. But 12 months on from his acrimonious exit from Newcastle, Isak is finally ready to put that nightmare year behind him and be the player Liverpool thought they were signing. On Sunday, he is expected to play his first pre-season match against Leeds United here in Chicago and Andoni Iraola, the man now sitting in Slot's chair, could do with Isak more than anyone. Alexander Isak, the £125million man had not even got close to repaying his British-record price tag, with just two goals in his first 15 games for the club as he struggled to gain fitness Just when he looked like he had finally cracked it, away at Tottenham in December with a first-half goal, he was crocked while scoring by defender Micky van de Ven and broke his leg

Your browser does not support iframes.

There were many reasons Slot failed – but one was the failure of his two big-money buys last summer, Isak and £116m Florian Wirtz, to step up. Isak was barely fit and Wirtz looked like a fish out of water at times. In both cases, one bad season can be forgiven and forgotten but serious questions will be asked if it continues into their sophomore years at Anfield. I understand that both have been enjoying the intensity of Iraola’s new regime and are ready to step up. Isak, it is easy to forget, is one of the best strikers in the Premier League. Since he joined Newcastle ahead of the 2022-23 season, only three forwards have more than his 57 goals: Erling Haaland, Mohamed Salah and Ollie Watkins. Iraola needs him to rediscover that form more than ever. With fellow No 9 Hugo Ekitike a long-term absentee with a ruptured achilles, Mohamed Salah gone and no new top winger yet signed, Liverpool need a goalscorer. Isak needs to show why he was worth £125m just a year ago, and rediscover the form that saw him score 62 goals in 109 games for Newcastle. ‘Alex is exciting,’ said Iraola when asked about Isak this week in Chicago. ‘He has come to pre-season in a good place, had a good World Cup, feeling comfortable. First training here, still early but I hope he can play against Leeds and have a proper pre-season. It is not long, but three or four weeks of quality training I hope and he is in a good place because he is going to be massive for us.’ There was emphasis on the word ‘massive’ and he is not wrong. Robbie Fowler, who proved 183 times he knows how to score goals for this club, sat down with Daily Mail Sport earlier this week in New York City and told us why he is such a big fan of Isak – backing him to pay back the club’s huge investment. ‘I am a massive fan,’ Fowler tells us. ‘He is proven in the Premier League. For whatever reason, he turned up not fit or whether it was that he struggled to step up to a big club. Robbie Fowler, who proved 183 times he knows how to score goals for this club, told us why he is such a big fan of Isak I understand that both Isak and Florian Wirtz have been enjoying the intensity of Andoni Iraola’s new regime and are ready to step up ‘But I have no qualms with him. He is exciting. He will score goals. He will be a handful. Hopefully this is the season he kicks on. He got injured at the wrong time but I want him to come back fit and firing. He did OK in the World Cup but I want him to be ready at the start of the season rather than waiting months and months like last season. ‘If it was me, the price tag would not bother me. The players are focused on doing well, it is left to others to talk about money. Price tags are only one thing the clubs put on a player. For me, it would not bother me, whether that’s my mentality, I don’t know… some players don’t have that. ‘Alexander is world-class and the price tag won’t bother him either. He has everything in the locker, exciting when he drives with the ball, he makes things happen. He excites the fans which is imperative for a club like Liverpool. ‘Not only can he beat players, he can bring others into the game and he can score goals which is massive. He has other areas in his game which are impressive.’ Isak has been working hard on bulking up after a positive World Cup, in which he enjoyed playing in tandem with Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres for Sweden, and scored an impressive solo goal against Tunisia in the group stage. Isak has rubbed shoulders with one of the best strikers of this generation, Robert Lewandowski, here in Chicago. The former Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Bayern Munich striker, now 37, recently moved to MLS club Chicago Fire having won eight Bundesligas, three La Ligas and a Champions League. He, like Isak, has been working hard in their gym here, which has personalised dumbbells. The Swede has also been helpful to young strikers out here, such as teenagers Will Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie. Isak has been working hard on bulking up after a positive World Cup, in which he enjoyed playing in tandem with Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres (left) for Sweden The Swede has also been helpful to young strikers out here, such as teenagers Will Wright (pictured) and Josh Sonni-Lambie Six years, not six months – but now more than ever, it is time for Isak to step up Iraola is keen for Isak to play as an out-and-out No 9, with Florian Wirtz playing as a traditional No 10 – close to the striker, unlike last season when he would often be instructed to drift out to the left. At £241m, the duo – and Liverpool’s bank balance – cannot afford another year of adaptation. Neither can Iraola, who will be relying on the pair that ultimately let Slot down. The Basque has been impressive in his opening weeks but cannot deliver success if the big-money duo do not start to look like the mega-money players they are. Six years, not six months – but now more than ever, it is time for Isak to step up.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury winner offered world title shot
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury winner offered world title shot

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will clash later this year with Murat Gassiev willing to offer the winner a shot at his newly-minted world title

View Image Tyson Fury challenges Anthony Joshua (Image: Getty)

Murat Gassiev is willing to offer Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury a shot at his world title.

‌



Gassiev was upgraded to full WBA heavyweight world champion last month when Oleksandr Usyk gave up his three belts ahead of the final fight of his career. Gasiev, who made a successful first defence against Peter Kadiru two weeks ago, now sits alongside Daniel Dubois and Agit Kabayel as rulers of the division.

‌



And he is willing to face Fury or Joshua next year, once they settle their rivalry in November. "They are two great fighters, great people, and good guys," he told Mirror Fighting. "I have a lot of respect for both guys and if I could fight them in England then I would say yes, because I have never been before.

‌



Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury READ MORE :

"Tyson and Anthony are still great fighters, great champions and are still at the top level. Either of these two guys is a very hard opponent for any fighter. Anthony showed in his last fight that with just one uppercut he went down. But he woke up, recovered and won the the fight; that is heavyweight boxing. They are both at a top level and for sure can still fight for world titles.

"But maybe Tyson never fights Anthony. You never know, maybe tomorrow Tyson say, 'No more. I'm retired.' After two weeks or two years, he comes back, or Anthony fights some other names. But I am ready for anyone."

Article continues below

Gassiev lost to Usyk when the pair were cruiserweights but insists he has no regrets over never facing the Ukrainian again in boxing's premier division. "After my loss, to be honest, it's not my goal to get a rematch, because I know this is sport, this is boxing. I'm don't wake up and think, 'I want rematch, I want rematch, I want rematch'," he added.

Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr lined up for fight 'bigger than Rumble in the Jungle'
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr lined up for fight 'bigger than Rumble in the Jungle'

Chris Eubank Jr is in talks over a return to the ring which is being billed as the biggest in African boxing history

View Image Chris Eubank Jr in Nigeria

Chris Eubank Jr is being lined up for a return to the ring in Africa.

‌



The son of a legend has not fought since he lost his rematch with Conor Benn last November and has since undergone treatment for medical issues he believed affected him in the build-up to the sequel and in the fight itself. Eubank Jr has also become a dad to twins.

‌



He recently travelled to Nigeria to hold talks over a return to the ring and Balmoral Promotions chief Dr Ezekiel Adamu expects to announce a groundbreaking fight. "We are having a good conversation with Chris," he told Mirror Fighting . "Chris loves legacy, and he understands him fighting in Africa is going to be a huge legacy for Africa.

‌



"The fight we have for him is actually going to be the biggest fight in the history of African pay-per-view. I mean, it's going to be way bigger than the Rumble in the Jungle was 50 years ago.

Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury READ MORE :

"Chris is excited about that; when he came to Nigeria, he met the President of Nigeria and he met top sponsors who assured him that they're fully behind this happening. We've spoken with DAZN who are excited to jump on it and we are having similar conversations with Netflix as well. It's still in the works but we should have a date and an announcement coming soon."

Article continues below

Meanwhile, Dr Adamu is confident his outfit can finally help realise the potential Africa has in combat sports. "Africa has always produced the talent over the years, but we've never had our own proper platform where world-class talent and African talent can actually converge," he added.

"So what we're building here is not just another fight night; what we're building is a proper ecosystem when it comes to boxing, so it's a game-changer for us. We have like another 1,000 Anthony Joshuas walking the streets of Lagos and Johannesburg.

"Africa is a population of about 1.4 billion people, and out of that 1.4 billion, about 75 to 80 per cent are between the ages of 15 to 30. So, it's the youngest demographic of youth in the world. Africa is genetically built for sports generally, but we've never had a proper platform, and what Balmoral Group is doing is providing that platform for Africa and for Africans."

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua told exactly how he can beat Tyson Fury

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are finally set to fight later this year to settle their decade-long heavyweight feud

View Image Anthony Joshua knocked out Kristian Prenga (Image: Getty Images)

Anthony Joshua has been told the only way he can beat Tyson Fury is to knock him clean out.

Joshua returned to the ring last weekend with a second-round stoppage of Kristian Prenga, but only after twice being knocked down himself in the opening session. Twenty four hours earlier, Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in his own warm-up fight to set up a clash with Joshua later this year.

And former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew believes Joshua will have to flatten Fury to to win. "There’s never been a better time to beat Tyson Fury," Bellew told Fight Your Corner, in partnership with Midnite. "Eighteen months ago, Fury is an overwhelming favourite. He is the one who doesn't want to have a straight up fight with you, he's the one who wants to box you.

"And the best way to beat a boxer is, well, it is to just get rid of them, and I think that's Anthony Joshua 's best chance. If this fight goes to points, Anthony Joshua loses. Anthony Joshua has to win by knockout to win this fight, in my opinion. Let's be brutally honest, he's not going to out-box Tyson Fury."

Anthony Joshua opponent finally addresses fight 'fix' claim READ MORE :

Fury's clash with Joshua as yet has no venue or date and could head to New York to satisfy Netflix's demand for a prime-time US audience. Bellew has been outspoken about the prospect of the showdown being moved from London, and added: "Listen, the top and bottom of it is, is I'd understand it if it was going to Saudi because they're paying for the fight.

Article continues below

"What I don't like and don't understand is why it's going to the US. Why take a British fight and put it in America because no one cares in America? And I know I went a bit far when I said American boxing's been dead since Evander Holyfield. I was talking about the heavyweight division.

"Terence Crawford's amazing. I'm a fan of Terence Crawford, a brilliant fella, an amazing fighter, but let's just be brutally honest here, you've had the WBC heavyweight champion of the world for nearly a decade. He could walk down the street and be unrecognised, no one cared. After the Klitschkos took rein and dominated an era, American heavyweight boxing is just forgotten about, and it is right now.

"Now the people who are bringing it to life is Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. American boxing public don't care about Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. This is me now putting in layman's terms for everyone to understand, they don't care. So why should the fight go there? No one's going to be paying to want to come and see Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. The American public aren't doing it."

Sports.title: Rio Ferdinand's son signs for Premier League club as Man Utd icon sends four-word message
Sports.content:
Rio Ferdinand's son signs for Premier League club as Man Utd icon sends four-word message

Rio Ferdinand was one of the greatest England defenders of all time and now Manchester United great's name looks set to live on in the Premier League

View 2 Images Another one of Rio Ferdinand's son has signed a pro contract with a Premier League club (Image: Lev Radin/Shutterstock)

The son of Manchester United legend Rio Ferdinand has signed a professional contract - with Brighton and Hove Albion. Tate Ferdinand, 17, has been playing with the Seagulls' U21s side, having first joined the club in 2024.

‌



He made a huge contribution to the South Coast team last season, playing a key role on their way to reaching the Sussex Transport Senior Cup final. Tate is not the first son of the former England captain to sign a pro deal at the Amex Stadium.

‌



Lorenz Ferdinand, who is a goalkeeper, also put pen to paper on a pro deal in Sussex, having spent some time on loan with non-league side Havant and Waterlooville in the past.

‌

Man Utd transfer talks confirmed as agent says deal is close READ MORE :

Over a fortnight since Lorenz committed his future to the club, Tate has followed suit to the delight of a beaming Ferdinand and his ex-team-mate Edwin van der Sar, who left a kind four-word message for the teen prodigy.

Confirming the news on Instagram, the ex-United central defender wrote: "Proud moment with the family, my boy Tate Ferdinand signing his first pro contract. Keep up the hard work.”

‌



Van der Sar was one of the first of Ferdinand’s United team-mates to say congratulations, commenting: “All the best Tate," while Darren Fletcher also wrote: "Love it" alongside some clapping emojis.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Last season, then Brighton U18s coach Bjorn Hamberg did his best to urge fans and other figures in football to not let the fact Tate is the son of Ferdinand put more pressure on his young shoulders.

‌



Hamberg said: "Tate Ferdinand is Tate Ferdinand and he needs to be play his game and have his pathway and career. For us as a team, for the under-18s as a captain, he is a big voice in our dressing room. He is obviously a leader in the back line and playing very well for the moment. I am really pleased for him as well.”

The fact Tate is playing against players who are four years his senior suggests he is progressing at a quick rate. Last season, he made 24 appearances with Brighton's U18s side and even contributed two goals. Considering the trajectory of their careers, it's not impossible that Lorenz and Tate may feature together on the same team, just like Ferdinand did with his brother Anton.

View 2 Images Lorenz Ferdinand is also at Brighton (Image: Dave Haines / SWNS)

‌



Interestingly, when speaking about their development in 2025, Ferdinand revealed his football prodigy sons often ignored his advice, preferring to listen to the views and opinions of their coaches. He said: "Even though I played, when I told them about football when they were 12, 13, 14 years old, they were like ‘What do you know?'

"They were listening to their football coach – who’d never played a league game in his life or been a professional – and coming in and saying 'But so-and-so said this dad’.”
