World.title: De la vivienda a la amenaza climática: así ha cambiado la forma de proteger las cosas que nos importan
World.content:
En los últimos 50 años, las prioridades aseguradoras de los españoles han evolucionado y compañías como Allianz se han amoldado dando un paso más: adaptarse al gran reto de anticipar los riesgos derivados de las nuevas amenazas digitales y el cambio climático.

En 1976, año en que EL PAÍS llegó a los quioscos, el gran sueño y prioridad de las familias españolas era la consolidación del hogar: el piso en propiedad, el patrimonio familiar construido con décadas de esfuerzo. En aquel momento, el sector seguros ya recaudaba 132.000 millones de pesetas (unos 793 millones de euros), y llegó un punto en el que ya no sólo se trataba de proteger cuatro paredes, sino toda una nueva forma de vida, con aventurados proyectos empresariales, con comodidades inéditas, con inmuebles y bienes materiales en abundancia, que se abría camino y requería ser asegurada. El estado de bienestar.

Esta relación entre progreso y riesgo viene de mucho antes. Hace casi cuatro mil años, un mercader babilonio que preparaba una travesía comercial ya sabía que un imprevisto podía arruinar de un plumazo su empresa. Para protegerse, los antiguos recurrían a un mecanismo recogido en el Código de Hammurabi, el llamado préstamo a la gruesa ventura, un contrato en el que un prestamista costeaba el viaje del comerciante y asumía el riesgo financiero de la misión. Si la expedición llegaba a buen puerto, el prestamista recibía de vuelta el dinero con intereses añadidos; en cambio, si la expedición fracasaba, el prestamista perdía el capital adelantado. Aquel sistema fue una de las primeras formas documentadas de transferencia (o reparto o división) del riesgo.

Desde Babilonia hasta hoy: el concepto de seguro a lo largo del tiempo Compartir el riesgo como cuestión de supervivencia En la Antigüedad, babilonios, griegos, romanos o comerciantes chinos ya idearon fórmulas para repartir las pérdidas entre varias personas. Préstamos marítimos, fondos comunes, diversificación y protección de las mercancías (con mecanismos como el que se recoge en el Código de Hammurabi, en la imagen) sentaron las bases de los tres principios que sigue definiendo el seguro: compartir el riesgo, dividirlo entre el máximo número de entidades posibles y compensar así las pérdidas. El comercio inventa el seguro moderno El auge del comercio marítimo hizo del riesgo en un elemento que podía calcularse. Entre los siglos XIV y XVIII, en ciudades como Génova, Venecia o Barcelona, nacieron las primeras pólizas, mientras que en Londres, Lloyd's (en la imagen) impulsó un sistema de corredores que revolucionó la forma de asegurar barcos y mercancías marítimas. Los avances en matemáticas y estadística permitieron, además, calcular las primas con criterios científicos. La Revolución Industrial multiplica los riesgos Ferrocarriles, fábricas y grandes ciudades trajeron nuevas oportunidades en el siglo XIX, pero también nuevos peligros. Se popularizaron los seguros para accidentes laborales, catástrofes (en la imagen, un perito de Allianz evalúa los daños del terremoto de San Francisco de 1906), responsabilidad civil o transporte. En este contexto, en 1890 nació Allianz como aseguradora especializada en transporte y accidentes, un reflejo de las necesidades de una economía cada vez más industrializada. Del patrimonio a la protección social Ya en el siglo XX, el seguro dejó de ser una herramienta exclusiva del comercio para convertirse en una pieza esencial de la vida cotidiana. Los sistemas públicos de salud y pensiones, junto con la expansión internacional de las aseguradoras, ampliaron la protección frente a los principales riesgos implícitos en la sociedad de masas y el estado de bienestar: el trabajo (como muestra la campaña de Allianz de 1958 que recoge la imagen), la vivienda, el automóvil o la jubilación. El reto de la anticipación En la actualidad, el sector afronta desafíos globales como los ciberataques o el cambio climática, con la inteligencia artificial, el análisis de datos o los seguros conectados como herramientas esenciales para anticipar problemas y personalizar coberturas. El seguro evoluciona y pasa de una lógica reactiva —indemnizar después del daño— a una cada vez más preventiva.

Es decir: la historia del seguro es la historia de lo que hemos necesitado proteger según el momento. El comercio marítimo, la industrialización, la expansión del automóvil, el estado de bienestar o la revolución digital, entre otros hitos históricos, han ido ampliando el mapa de riesgos y dirigiendo la brújula de los seguros. Allianz, una compañía alemana nacida en 1890 para cubrir los riesgos del transporte y los accidentes que se multiplicaron en plena revolución industrial, hoy opera en un escenario marcado por la conectividad, la inteligencia artificial y las amenazas climáticas. Lo hace en 70 países, entre los que se cuenta España, donde la compañía tomó su forma actual en 1999, fruto de la integración de varias aseguradoras nacionales. La filosofía, en un mundo acelerado e hiperconectado, es clara: servirse de la innovación para mejorar el servicio y anticiparse al riesgo antes de que suceda.

Una de las primeras agencias de Allianz en Bonn (Alemania), en 1907.

Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz Seguros, entiende que esta transformación de los riesgos empuja a los seguros a repensarse y abrazar los últimos avances como la inteligencia artificial. Esta evolución de las empresas del sector, sin embargo, no depende únicamente de adoptar la tecnología de turno, sino que descansa en la sana combinación del avance con el conocimiento humano: “La inteligencia artificial no sustituye el talento comercial, lo acelera. Nuestro objetivo es que cada cliente reciba un asesoramiento de mayor calidad y que nuestros mediadores dispongan de las mejores herramientas para conseguirlo”.

La IA es una de las apuestas principales de Allianz, que ha desarrollado en España un modelo de entrenamiento en el que sus agentes se forman mediante avatares basados en el algoritmo, capaces de personificar diferentes roles para reproducir situaciones reales de asesoramiento y venta. Tal ha sido el éxito del programa que varios directivos de distintos países han viajado a Madrid para tratar de replicar este sistema en sus mercados: “Que esta iniciativa nacida en España se haya convertido en referencia para el Allianz demuestra nuestra capacidad de innovar y generar valor desde aquí”, explica Stutz.

1890 De asegurar transportes y accidentes… Allianz nació en Berlín el 5 de febrero de 1890 de la mano del actuario Carl Von Thieme (en la imagen) y el banquero Wilhelm Finck. Con un capital inicial de cuatro millones de marcos, comenzó ofreciendo seguros de transporte y accidentes en plena revolución industrial, cuando el crecimiento económico propició riesgos inéditos que requerían nuevas formas de protección. La empresa alemana se expandió con velocidad: en 1929 ya operaba en 30 países y, en 1956, se convirtió en la primera empresa privada europea en incorporar un ordenador IBM650, un hito que anticipaba la transformación tecnológica que estaba por llegar. 2026 …a asegurar un mundo conectado y en peligro climático Hoy, 136 años después, Allianz se ha convertido en uno de los principales grupos aseguradores y gestores de activos del mundo: está presente en cerca de 70 países, cuenta con alrededor de 97 millones de clientes particulares y empresas y supera los 156.000 empleados, además de patrocinar a múltiples entidades (como el estadio del FC Bayern de Múnich, club de fútbol alemán, en la imagen). El objetivo es repensar la protección del ciudadano frente a las dos amenazas más acuciantes de nuestro tiempo: los ciberataques (2.000 millones de dólares en primas en todo el mundo) y el impacto del cambio climático (con unas pérdidas aseguradas por catástrofes naturales que rondan los 130.000 millones de dólares anuales desde 2020.

Otro ejemplo muy gráfico de aplicación de la IA en Allianz es el que explica Victoria Medina, CTDO (jefa de tecnología) de la empresa: “Tenemos un proyecto al que coloquialmente llamamos Minority Report [como aquella película de ciencia ficción en la que Tom Cruise tenía el poder de anticiparse a los crímenes] que nos permite solventar la insatisfacción de los clientes antes de que se produzca”. ¿Cómo? “Gracias a la IA, podemos detectar cuando un cliente no está contento por cómo se está gestionando un siniestro, o recibir una alerta cuando la resolución de un siniestro se está demorando. Así, nos anticipamos antes de que el cliente nos llame enfadado, lo que propicia una gestión más rápida y ágil”, detalla Medina.

De la reacción a la anticipación: el nuevo paradigma de los seguros

Los riesgos a asegurar han ido cambiando a raíz del desarrollo tecnológico y los nuevos hábitos de consumo. Fenómenos como la exposición a los ciberataques, la vulnerabilidad de la identidad digital o el incremento de catástrofes meteorológicas extremas exigen hoy un paradigma distinto en el que ya no basta con indemnizar el daño: se busca prevenirlo antes de que se produzca.

Para abordar esta nueva realidad, Allianz está desarrollando y recurriendo a sistemas de vanguardia, con más de 600 aplicaciones de IA escalables que se sirven de la gran masa de información que generan los dispositivos conectados para fijar precios, evaluar riesgos o agilizar la gestión de los siniestros. El resultado: una protección en tiempo real, inteligente y a medida de cada persona. Un capítulo en el que la compañía aseguradora ha invertido cerca de 6.500 millones de euros en 2025.

El cliente tiene que poder acceder como y cuando quiera a nosotros. Si tiene que contratar una póliza a las once de la noche, debe ser posible hacerlo de forma rápida y sencilla” Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz

Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz, incide en cómo la IA está redefiniendo el mundo de los seguros a pasos agigantados: “Estamos pasando de compensar daños a anticipar riesgos, de cubrir problemas a prevenirlos. Queremos acompañar a las personas en momentos de incertidumbre”. En esta misma línea, Victoria Medina enfatiza la noción de tecnología al servicio del cliente: “Nos enfrentamos a un contexto marcado por la aceleración tecnológica y a clientes cada vez más exigentes. La esencia del trabajo no ha cambiado, pero podemos ser más eficaces apoyándonos en la innovación y las nuevas tecnologías”.

Así, Allianz ha desarrollado con éxito una solución que monitoriza en tiempo real más de 50 millones de hectáreas de terreno en España para prevenir incendios mediante el uso de IA, observación satelital avanzada y modelos predictivos. Esta solución, creada en colaboración con la empresa Satellites on Fire, es capaz de reducir el tiempo de detección en una media de 35 minutos e identificar hasta un 30% más incendios. Además, los datos que acumula esta herramienta sirven para avisar al cliente cuando sus bienes asegurados se encuentren próximos a focos de potencial propagación.

El objeto de nuestras preocupaciones, aquello que queremos proteger, ha mutado de forma constante al ritmo de la propia sociedad. Si hace cuatro mil años el reto era salvaguardar una mercancía babilónica en alta mar y hace medio siglo salvaguardar la vivienda, hoy la prioridad es la seguridad digital o la resiliencia climática. Dentro de esta gran transformación, la tecnología no altera el fin último del seguro, pero sí le proporciona un nuevo poder: la capacidad de otorgar una protección previsora, proactiva e inteligente que vaya por delante del siniestro.

World.title: Cuatro detenidos y siete armas de fuego intervenidas por un tiroteo sin heridos en La Mina
World.content:
El fuego cruzado del 12 de mayo, provocado por un enfrentamiento entre bandas, no dejó heridos pero puso en peligro a los vecinos del barrio

Un agente de los Mossos d'Esquadra, durante el operativo del pasado 14 de julio. Mossos d'Esquadra (MOSSOS D'ESQUADRA)

No hubo heridos, pero el fuego cruzado puso en peligro las vidas de los vecinos. El tiroteo ocurrió el 12 de mayo en el barrio de La Mina, en Sant Adrià de Besòs (Barcelona), donde los enfrentamientos armados asociados al tráfico de drogas se han convertido casi en parte del paisaje cotidiano. Dos meses y medio después, los Mossos d’Esquadra han detenido a cuatro personas (tres hombres y una mujer) como presuntos responsables del tiroteo. La policía ha intervenido además siete armas de fuego: cuatro pistolas, un revólver, un subfusil y una escopeta.

Los detenidos forman parte, presuntamente, de dos grupos enfrentados entre sí por el control del tráfico de drogas en este barrio históricamente lastrado por la pobreza donde viven cerca de 11.000 personas. Los tiroteos asociados a esas peleas son cada vez más frecuentes por el acceso de los grupos a las armas de fuego, que preocupa especialmente a los Mossos d’Esquadra. En 2025, según datos de la policía catalana, hubo 93 tiroteos, lo que supuso un aumento del 45% en relación con el año anterior. Estos episodios suponen un problema de seguridad pública y los Mossos han llevado a cabo operativos específicos para tratar de contener el acceso a las armas.

El tiroteo del 12 de mayo dejó, en las calles de La Mina, una treintena de casquillos de bala. Tras una investigación minuciosa, los Mossos lograron identificar a los presuntos autores y, con autorización judicial, irrumpieron hace dos semanas en domicilios de Sant Adrià, Badalona, Barcelona o Terrassa, pero también en Maçanet de la Selva (Girona). En el operativo participaron 150 efectivos, además de la unidad canina y la de drones.

Los detenidos son una mujer de 48 años y tres hombres de 64, 40 y 46 (este último se entregó en comisaría días después del suceso). La mayoría de armas de fuego encontradas estaban en los dormitorios, preparadas para ser utilizadas y sin ninguna medida de seguridad. Los Mossos intervinieron, además, munición de diferente calibre, un chaleco antibalas, defensas extensibles, armas blancas y unos 40.000 euros en efectivo.

World.title: Mi casero quiere recuperar la vivienda para uso propio tras 17 años, pero en el contrato no figura esta cláusula, ¿puede hacerlo?
World.content:
Pregunta. He estado viviendo en una casa en un pueblo de la provincia de Toledo durante 17 años sin deber ningún alquiler y ahora el propietario me ha enviado un burofax pidiéndome que deje la vivienda porque la necesita para su uso personal. Esta cláusula no está en el contrato de arrendamiento de vivienda firmado en 2009. ¿Cuáles son mis derechos como inquilino? Goyo.

Respuesta. Si en su contrato de alquiler no está prevista la posibilidad de que se le pueda poner fin al mismo por causa de necesidad del arrendador para que sea habitada por él, el propietario no puede poner fin al contrato por este motivo. Sin embargo, teniendo en cuenta que su contrato es del año 2009, a no ser que la duración pactada hubiera sido por más de los 17 años que ya lleva vigente, el contrato se encuentra actualmente en situación de prórroga legal.

En esta fase, la duración de la prórroga depende de la forma en que se haya establecido la renta en el contrato: el contrato se prórroga por meses, si la renta pactada en el contrato es mensual; o se prórroga anualmente, si en el contrato se pactó una renta anual (aunque se pague mensualmente).

De modo que cada vez que se produzca el vencimiento del periodo de prórroga correspondiente, mensual, en el primer caso, o anual, en el segundo caso, el propietario podría poner fin al contrato. Para ello, bastaría con que comunique la decisión dejando constancia de su recepción con una antelación mínima de un mes respecto de la fecha en que vaya a producirse la siguiente renovación, mensual o anual, en función de lo anteriormente comentado.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Entrecanales considera vender el 100% de Acciona Energía tras recibir las primeras ofertas
World.content:
La venta del 100% de Acciona Energía es “definitivamente una posibilidad que se considerará dentro de las opciones”, ha asegurado esta mañana el presidente del grupo, José Manuel Entrecanales, en la presentación ante analistas de los resultados del primer semestre. Esta semana, la matriz recibió las muestras de interés por su filial de energía, entre las que figuraban propuestas de Brookfield, KKR, EQT y GIP (propiedad de BlackRock), con Ardian y Qualitas Energy en la retaguardia, como publicó CincoDías el pasado martes. El mercado espera alianzas si la operación para comprar toda la compañía llega a materializarse. También existe la posibilidad de que entre un socio o de una división por países.

La revisión estratégica de Acciona sobre su filial de renovables continúa sin prisa pero sin pausa. Citi y Goldman Sachs son los bancos encargados de pilotar la eventual operación, que puede quedarse en nada si los precios no alcanzan las expectativas, según explican fuentes financieras. El pasado lunes, concluyó el periodo para hacerles llegar las pujas, por el 100%, por un porcentaje minoritario o por activos. Entrecanales ha confirmado que “hay apetito, hay un buen conjunto de oportunidades de diferentes tipos y diferentes alternativas”.

El directivo aseguró en junio, en la junta de accionistas del grupo, que el escenario de la venta del 100% era “extremadamente improbable”, pero ahora eleva las posibilidades. Tras ser preguntado por los analistas si ese veredicto continúa vigente, después de recibir las ofertas no vinculantes, ha abierto más la puerta: “Permítame decir que es improbable. Pero es definitivamente una posibilidad que se considerará dentro de las opciones”.

Respecto al escenario de que se tome una decisión en el tercer trimestre, ha advertido de que aún no han comenzado las negociaciones, pero que “estarán en curso en los próximos meses”. “Me sentiría muy incómodo haciendo declaraciones sobre cuáles pueden ser las potenciales oportunidades”, ha señalado.

En todo caso, la clave será el precio. El mercado descuenta que el precio mínimo para que los Entrecanales tomen en consideración la posibilidad de deshacerse de su negocio de energía ha de superar los 26,7 euros por acción, el precio al que la compañía debutó en Bolsa hace cinco años. Hace cuatro años, en pleno bum de las renovables, el precio por acción llegó al entorno de los 44 euros, con una valoración de más de 14.000 millones de euros. Ahora, vale aproximadamente la mitad. La familia Entrecanales, que controla el 56% de la matriz, tendrá la última palabra.

Acciona Energía aportó el año pasado un resultado bruto de explotación (ebitda) superior a los 1.500 millones de euros, casi la mitad del obtenido por todo el grupo. El precio de renunciar a esa notable porción del resultado debe ser necesariamente elevado, según los analistas del sector. La contrapartida de centrarse en las infraestructuras y en las concesiones, que conforman el ADN del grupo, está en una reducción inmediata de la inversión que requieren los negocios de renovables. Destinó a ellos más de 1.400 millones de euros el año pasado, lo que supone una cifra elevada a pesar de haberla recortado cerca de un 7%.

La venta por partes también está sobre la mesa, con la posibilidad de deshacerse de los negocios por países a través de una segmentación limpia y sencilla. A cierre del año pasado, Acciona Energía contaba con unos 15.000 megavatios de potencia instalada, repartidos en 16 países, si bien los cuatro primeros sumaban el 77%. España representaba el 32,7%; Estados Unidos, el 20,5%; Australia, el 13,7%; y México, el 10,1%. Las fuentes financieras consultadas destacan que estas ofertas por segmentos geográficos corren a cargo de industriales.

World.title: El mar de Iroise, donde los faros desafían algunas de las aguas más peligrosas del mundo
World.content:
El faro de Créac'h, en la isla bretona de Ouessant, es el más potente de Europa y alcanza hasta 60 kilómetros de distancia.

Del Créac’h al mítico La Jument, un recorrido por la costa bretona donde estas torres han guiado la navegación y moldeado la vida de los marineros durante siglos

Nos encontramos en el mar de Iroise. Situado en el extremo occidental de la Bretaña francesa, es uno de los más peligrosos para navegar del mundo, debido a sus arrecifes, profundidades variables y fuertes corrientes. De ahí que sea el lugar de Europa con mayor concentración de faros y balizas. El extremo sur de este mar está en la Punta de Raz, y aquí espera nuestro primer faro, el de la Vieille (faro de la Vieja), que comenzó a construirse en 1882 y no fue hasta 1887 cuando se pudo encender por primera vez. Este faro señala a los barcos el peligroso paso del Raz de Sein, entre la isla de Sein y la Punta de Raz.

Más al norte está el de Tévennec, un faro que enloqueció a más de un farero al escuchar, decían, las voces agonizantes de los náufragos que habían perdido la vida en el mar. Así, 23 guardianes se sucedieron en la roca durante 35 años, hasta su automatización en 1910. En 2016, Marc Pointud, presidente de la Sociedad Nacional para el Patrimonio de los Faros y Balizas de Francia, lo habitó durante 69 días, lo que dio lugar al libro Tévennec: Las puertas del infierno.

Dejamos Brest atrás y vamos más allá, hasta la punta y el faro de Saint-Mathieu, cuyo nombre en bretón, Penn-ar-Bed, significa “fin del mundo”. El faro, construido en 1835, tiene a sus pies las ruinas de una antigua abadía del siglo XI, la capilla Notre-Dame-de-Grâce y un semáforo naval. El conjunto es espectacular a cualquier hora del día, pero sobre todo cuando el sol se apaga en el mar y se enciende el faro. Paseando por la costa, en menos de cuatro kilómetros se llega a Le Conquet (Konk Leon, en bretón), una pequeña y agradable ciudad de cara a la ría y a sus grandes mareas, con un puerto muy vivo desde el que parten cada día los barcos de pesca y los que conectan el continente con las islas de Molène y Ouessant. Atravesando la pasarela de Croaë sobre la ría se alcanza la península de Kermorvan y, tomando cualquier sendero, se llega al extremo de la misma y al faro homónimo, que se puede visitar. Seguimos rodeando la península y nos topamos con el fuerte de La Latte, al que se accede durante la marea baja. A continuación, la playa de Blancs Sablons, de 2,5 kilómetros de longitud, recorrible por un pequeño sendero que discurre por encima del arenal.

El faro de Kermorvan, en la península del mismo nombre, frente a Le Conquet. Está considerado el faro más occidental de la Francia continental. Cristina Candel

En lancha por el archipiélago de Molène

La compañía Archipel Excursions ofrece salidas en embarcaciones semirrígidas de diferente duración por el mar de Iroise. La más extrema dura nueve horas y llega a los seis infiernos, que es como llamaban los fareros a los faros en alta mar de Le Four, La Jument, Kéréon, Les Pierres Noires, Ar-Men y La Vieille, por su aislamiento extremo, unas condiciones meteorológicas brutales y la peligrosidad de la vida de quienes residían en ellos. Pero esa excursión, debido a las corrientes y la climatología, solo se consigue hacer unos cinco días al año, así que nos embarcamos para ver las focas grises zambullirse y secarse al sol en el islote de Kervourok, pasar por la isla de Beniguet y, finalmente, llegar al faro de Les Pierres Noires. Esta torre, que emerge 30 metros del mar, es el primer “infierno” que se construyó y el primero en automatizarse, en 1992.

El faro de Stiff, en la isla de Ouessant, fue diseñado por Vauban y está en funcionamiento desde 1700. Cristina Candel

La travesía a la isla de Ouessant, a tan solo 20 kilómetros del continente, pero tan aislada en el pasado, hoy dura tan solo hora y media, parando en la isla de Molène. Entre las dos divisamos el faro de Kéréon, que fue patrocinado por la señora Jules Le Baudry en 1910 y fue apodado el Palacio del Mar por las maderas nobles que visten su interior. En bretón, Ouessant es Enez Eusa, la más lejana, pero era también llamada la isla de las mujeres porque los hombres pasaban largas temporadas en alta mar y eran ellas las que realmente la habitaban. Hoy es una isla con mucha vida y merece la pena echarle un vistazo a su agenda antes de visitarla para no perderse nada (ot-ouessant.fr/agenda). También podemos leer Los crímenes de la isla de Ouessant (2025), de Jean-Luc Bannalec, que transcurre en este escenario y sirve como guía.

La escalera de caracol del faro de Isla Virgen, situado frente a la costa de Plouguerneau, en Bretaña.

Aquí conocemos a Ondine Morin, guía y pescadora de la isla que, como dice el comisario George Dupin en el libro, “es el alma de la isla”. Uno lo comprueba dejándose guiar por ella para descubrir este peculiar territorio repleto de faros en su excursión nocturna (kalon-eusa.com). En Ouessant está el faro más potente de Europa, con 60 kilómetros de alcance: Créac’h, enclavado en un increíble paisaje de agujas de piedra y que en unos años albergará el Museo de los Faros y Balizas, actualmente en construcción. También el faro de Stiff, obra del famoso ingeniero Vauban y en funcionamiento desde 1700, al cual se puede acceder para ver la isla desde lo alto.

Merece la pena ver la película El extraño (2004), de Philippe Lioret, rodada en la isla y en el faro de La Jument, para hacerse una idea de cómo era el día a día de los fareros y cómo lograban hacer los cambios de guardia. Las rotaciones, que eran de 15 días, no siempre se podían llevar a cabo, como fue el caso de Ar-Men, cuyos fareros permanecieron sin relevo 102 días, y 97 los de La Vieille.

El faro de Les Pierres Noires, frente a la costa de Le Conquet, fue el primero de los llamados "faros del infierno". Cristina Candel

La Jument, situado frente a la costa suroeste, se hizo famoso por la fotografía que tomó el 21 de diciembre de 1989 desde un helicóptero Jean Guichard al faro y a su farero en pleno temporal. Con ella ganó el segundo premio de naturaleza del World Press Photo. La historia que llevó a su construcción es bien curiosa: al morir en 1904, Eugène Potron, miembro de la Sociedad de Geografía de París, dejó al Estado francés dinero suficiente para su construcción, pero con la condición de que se levantase en siete años. Se retrasaron siete meses, pero a nadie pareció importarle.

También merece una visita el faro de Isla Virgen, a tan solo 1,5 kilómetros de la costa. Tiene 82,5 metros de altura, 383 escalones y paredes revestidas de opalina azul celeste. Se puede llegar en barco y en otro tipo de embarcación, como un kayak.

El faro de Créac'h, pintado sobre una piedra en la isla de Ouessant. Cristina Candel

Se dice que la primera leyenda bretona fue la de la barca de los muertos conducida por Ankou, en la que los marineros llevaban un pendiente de oro para poder pagar al barquero en caso de morir en el mar. Las bellas Morgans, con su ciudad sumergida, o las Cygnes, mujeres aladas con cara de cisne, son otros mitos que han llegado hasta nuestros días contados de manera oral, generación tras generación.

A Jean-Luc Bannalec se le atribuye la frase: “En la Bretaña hay más luz que en ningún otro rincón del mundo”. Después de recorrerla viendo sus faros iluminarla, añadimos: “Tanto de día como de noche”.

World.title: Dutch unions call 24-hour public transport strike on September 9
World.content:
Public transport workers across the Netherlands are to stage a one-day strike on Wednesday, September 9, bringing buses, trains, trams and metro services almost to a standstill.

The FNV union has called the strike in the latest escalation of its campaign against the government’s social welfare reforms, which it says will lead to lower living standards for millions of working people.

The three major unions FNV, CNV and VCP have vowed to fight the cabinet’s social welfare reforms, which are designed to secure €6.5 billion in cost savings during the goverment’s four-year term.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief scrapped a plan to increase the statutory retirement age faster by raising it in step with life expectancy, but the unions want the cabinet to go further by abandoning cuts to unemployment pay and long-term disability benefits.

Staff working for NS, ProRail, urban and regional transport sevices and DB cargo will down tools for 24 hours on September 9, making it impossible to run timetables.

Delays inevitable

“We are aware that a 24-hour strike will cause disruption,” said FNV official Edwim Kuiper. “We regret that deeply. But the consequences of the dismantling of our social security are much greater for everyone and will last much longer.”

National train operator NS said it could not say exactly what the impact of the stoppage would be because it had not been officially notified by the union.

Lobby organisation OV-NL, which represents nine smaller public transport companies such as Arriva, QBuzz and the major city network operators GVB, RET and HTM, said it “understood up to a point” the reason to call a strike.

But it said it was “very unfortunate that passengers are being disadvantaged by a social and political debate”.

Union leader Henri Janssen said that the strike was being called on behalf of commuters. “Every working person has to deal with sickness, work incapacity or involuntary unemployment. They should be able to count on a decent social safety net,“ he said.

World.title: Amsterdam steps up Pride security in wake of attack in Berlin
World.content:
Amsterdam has stepped up security around this weekend’s WorldPride street parties and the annual canal parade in the wake of last week’s attack in Berlin.

A total of 250 concrete blocks have been placed along the canals and nightclubs are carrying out extra bag searches during the two-week event, which runs until August 8.

Richard Keldoulis of Club Church, one of Amsterdam’s best known gay clubs, told NOS: “I’ve never known anything like this.”

Venue owners are in constant contact with the police and intelligence services about appropriate security measures, although they conceded that it is almost impossible to prevent a so-called “lone wolf” attack by one person using a knife or a vehicle.

Last Sunday a woman was killed and 29 people were injured when a man drove a car into a crowd near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where the annual Christopher Street Day parade, Germany’s main Pride event, was taking place.

The suspect, Abdul B., was later shot dead by police, who have said they are treating the incident as an Islamist terrorist attack.

Lone wolf attacks

“I come from Berlin and I was at the scene of the attack last week. I left the party few minutes before it all went wrong, but my friends were still there,” Keldoulis said.

“It’s always nice to feel safe, but ultimately you can never rule it out altogether. There were barriers and security measures in Berlin as well, but it still went wrong.”

Michel Peters, chair of the gay police association Roze in Blauw (“pink in blue”), said police would maintain a high-visibility presence during the weekend.

“We are there mainly to maintain contact with the [LGBTQI+] community,” he said. “We want to do more to show that we are there in the coming dys, so that people know they can approach us when something is going on.”

On Tuesday evening thousands of people in Amsterdam gathered at the Homomonument, the national memorial to victims of homophobic persecution, to commemorate the victims of Berlin.

City mayor Femke Halsema addressed the crowd, calling for courage and resilience. “We will win if we keep spreading hope loud and clear,” she said.

World.title: Dutch inflation rises to 3.1% in July as fuel costs soar
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Inflation rose slightly to 3.1% in July, sustaining the above-target trend of the last two and a half years, according to statistics agency CBS’s latest flash forecast.

A 9.7% spike in energy prices, including motor fuels, was the main driver of the increase as overall inflation ticked up from 2.9% in June.

Services inflation was measured at 4.1%, the same level as in June, while purchases abroad were 4.8% more expensive, down from 5.7% a month ago.

The harmonised European rate, which does not include the costs associated with owning or renting a home, was measured at 2.9%, up from 2.5% in June.

Since January 2024 inflation in the Netherlands has been persistently above the European Central Bank’s target level of 2%, peaking at 4.1% in December 2024 and April 2025. Its highest level so far this year was 3.5% in May.

The Dutch government has so far resisted calls to cut prices at the pumps, even though the Netherlands has the most expensive fuel in Europe, at €2.35 for a litre of petrol and €2.39 for diesel.

The CBS will publish the confirmed results with a more detailed breakdown on August 11.

World.title: Woman finds dinner-plate sized tarantula in her garden
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A woman in Twente was enjoying the sunshine in her garden on Wednesday when she came face to face with a tarantula the size of a dinner plate.

Dierenambulance Enschede posted photos of the poisonous spider on social media after they were called to the town of Oldenzaal to retrieve the arachnid.

The woman spotted the creature in her yard and informed the regional animal ambulance, who were able to capture it by placing a container over the creature and slowly sliding the lid underneath.

Tarantulas do not live in the wild in the Netherlands and it is suspected the spider escaped from a neighbour’s house.

According to the Dierenambulance Enschede, tarantulas are largely harmless. Their bites are akin to a wasp sting.

A number of people admitted they would not have had the woman’s composure. “If I had found the spider, this spider would now be the new owner of my former house,” one commenter wrote on the animal organisation Facebook post.

World.title: Arne Slot rules himself out as next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Former Liverpool and Feyenoord coach Arne Slot has ruled himself out as the next manager of the Dutch men’s national team, saying he wants to keep working in club football.

The 47-year-old was one of the names put forward to succeed Ronald Koeman, who resigned after the Netherlands were knocked out of the World Cup by Morocco in the round of 32.

Slot has also been courted by AC Milan and English Premier League side Fulham since he was sacked by Liverpool at the end of May after two seasons in charge.

The Dutchman, who arrived after steering Feyenoord to only their second Eredivisie title since the turn of the century, won the Premier League in his first season but could only manage fifth place last term.

The Dutch football association KNVB wants to appoint a manager well ahead of the next UEFA Nations League match against Germany on September 24.

Two other potential successors have also dropped out of the running. PSV manager Peter Bosz has extended his contract at the Eindhoven club, while former Ajax head coach Erik ten Hag recently joined his home town club Twente Enschede as director of football and has said he wants to continue in that role.

World.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
World.content:
Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?

I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?

Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?

Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Ask Me How It Works is available for sale at the American Book Center. You can follow Deepa on Substack and Instagram.

World.title: Drugs baron Bolle Jos convicted in absentia in Belgium
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

World.title: More sluice gates close but no national drought measures yet
World.content:
No national drought restrictions will be imposed immediately despite coastal water boards taking steps to keep sea water out of river mouths and the Rhine dropping to its lowest ever level.

At a weekly meeting to discuss the ongoing water shortage, regional authorities agreed to work together to ensure the “most efficient distribution possible” of water and announced local measures to protect drinking water.

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, the point where the river crosses the Dutch border, has dropped to less than 700 m3 per second, one-third of its normal level for July and an unprecedentedly low rate.

River cruise operators have had to cancel or shorten their excursions on the Rhine, while water authorities are considering introducing restrictions such as one-way traffic to prevent ships becoming stuck in the shallow water. Such measures would extend delivery times or force freight companies to transport cargo by road.

The Netherlands is currently at level two on a three-stage scale of water shortages, which authorises officials in the ministry to hold crisis talks. An actual crisis is level three.

The canal locks at Eefde, which gives access to the Twentekanaal, closed for the first time because of drought on Friday. Local businesses say the closure of the sluice gates, which carry 15,000 to 20,000 ships a year, will have an impact on the economy around Almelo, Enschede and Hengelo.

Harsh measures

“We understand this is necessary for security, but it’s a harsh measure,” said Frank van Zomeren. manager of the Port of Twente Bornebroek.

Deventer is closing its harbour to shipping this weekend for the first time in eight years because the IJssel has dropped below safe levels.

In the west, Delfland water authority has restricted the opening of the Parksluizen gates between the Nieuw Maas and the Schie to prevent sea water encroaching on the river mouth.

Sluice gates at Maassluis, Schiedam and Vlaardingen were closed last week. Other authorities are also imposing restrictions to prevent drinking water becoming contaminated.

Recreational swimmers have been warned to look out for blue-green algae, technically known as cyanobacteria, which grows faster in warm water and can cause skin irritation or sicknesses such as diarrhoea if swallowed.

World.title: Poland bans use of smartphones by children in primary schools and kindergartens

Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. World.title: Russian missile that crashed in Poland carried “significant amount” of explosive material

Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership

Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. A newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has said he will refuse to sit on the court until four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year, but blocked by the president, are allowed to take their seats. It is the latest development in a months-long dispute between the opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki and the government, which considers the TK to be improperly staffed and therefore illegitimate. Although Nawrocki swore in Sławomir Patyra, who was appointed by the ruling majority in parliament in June, as a TK judge on Tuesday, he continues to refuse to swear in four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year. Po złożeniu przysięgi Patyra ogłosił, że zamierza odmówić orzekania. To gest solidarności z czwórką sędziów, od których prezydent nie chce przyjąć przysięgi https://t.co/jdbKusQ3H9 — OKO.press (@oko_press) July 28, 2026 Shortly after his swearing-in ceremony at the presidential palace on Tuesday, Patyra arrived at the TK headquarters in Warsaw, where he was accompanied by four other judges appointed by parliament this year, including two whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. There, he announced that his decision not to sit on the court was a matter of loyalty to the constitution and his belief in judicial ethos. “I cannot imagine taking an oath today to uphold the constitution, only to start breaking that constitution tomorrow,” he said. Patyra told journalists that he would “submit a declaration of refusal to adjudicate” due to his solidarity with judges who are “unlawfully deprived of the chance to participate in the work of the tribunal”. He added that, along with the other judges chosen this year, he is “fully mobilised to restore the Constitutional Tribunal to its proper, constitutional, systemic form”. Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK, the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, TK’s chief justice Bogdan Święczkowski has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again later in the month, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. After repeated requests, Nawrocki finally decided last week to invite Patyra to the presidential palace. The president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, noted that “there were some doubts” but “the president dispelled them” and added that Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”. Nowo wybrany przez Sejm Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej uchwałą z dnia 11 czerwca 2026 r. sędzia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Sławomir Patyra złożył wobec Prezydenta RP ślubowanie. pic.twitter.com/VLMRAIg1Yj — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the group was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years.
