World.title: Iraq denies launching strikes from its territory against neighboring nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The military spokesperson for the Iraqi commander-in-chief, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed on Thursday that neither a foreign nor local body has presented proof that recent regional drone attacks were launched from Iraqi territory.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), al-Numan urged accusing parties to submit reliable proof, saying that Baghdad has yet to receive such data.

The development comes following statements made by the Saudi Ministry of Defense, alleging that drone attacks targeting key oil infrastructure in the past few days originated in Iraq.

The Iraqi official indicated that the government will neither tolerate unilateral military acts from within its borders nor accept foreign violations of its territorial sovereignty.

Al-Numan’s remarks come a day after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes targeting several bases of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing and injuring many fighters.

The joint operation targeted several logistical and weapons storage locations in different provinces in Iraq, escalating the current regional battle.

The PMF described the joint US-Saudi strike as a dangerous escalation and a clear breach of Iraqi sovereignty.

World.title: Iraqi oil flows to continue via Turkey’s Ceyhan as renewal deal is discussed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish sources told Reuters that crude oil shipments from northern Iraq to the Turkish port of Ceyhan will continue while the two countries seek an arrangement to extend the pipeline’s operation for another 12 months.

On July 27, a bilateral agreement that had been in place for decades ended. Despite expectations, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi did not sign a 12-month renewal deal during his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Tuesday.

According to a Turkish official, oil flows via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, which is Baghdad’s only operational export pipeline, will continue while negotiations for a renewal deal are still in progress.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently announced a 12-month extension agreement between the two countries.

During a joint press conference in Ankara, Erdogan stated on Tuesday that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible.

An extension is intended to provide additional time for discussions on a complete accord. Turkey aims to fully utilize the 1.5 million barrels per day pipeline and consider expanding it to oil fields in southern Iraq.

Turkish data suggests that the pipeline currently transports approximately 170,000 barrels per day.

World.title: Turkey seeks comprehensive energy cooperation deal with Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement with Iraq following discussions with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in Ankara.

Erdogan said that Turkey’s state-owned oil and gas company, TPAO, will operate at Iraq’s Kirkuk oilfield, which is now being developed by British Petroleum (BP), during a joint press conference following a signing ceremony that had been expected to extend the Kirkuk-Ceyhan oil pipeline deal for another year, according to Reuters.

The agreement to renew the decades-old pipeline contract, which regulates shipments along the strategic route, expired on Monday.

After signing three agreements, Erdogan noted that additional deals were anticipated. However, his ministers promptly briefed him on stage, and the two leaders continued with their statements without announcing any further agreements.

The agreement between Iraq and Turkey regarding the crude oil pipeline expired on July 27.

“Our goal is to complete an energy cooperation deal that benefits both parties as quickly as possible,” Erdogan said.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said in a statement on X that TPAO has bought a 15 percent stake in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited (BPECKL), enabling the Turkish business to operate in the sector.

Bayraktar explained the TPAO will cooperate with BPECKL to raise oil production at the Kirkuk field, which has reserves estimated at three million barrels.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports to India fall as New Delhi diversifies import sources
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi oil exports to India fell in the first half of 2026, as Indian refineries diversified their crude import sources to minimize the geopolitical risks associated with shipping via the Straits of Hormuz.

According to officials at Indian refining companies and the Indian Ministry of Petroleum, the goal of this measure is to improve supply security.

The drop in Iraqi supplies to India comes at a time when the global oil market is under increased pressure due to security worries along critical maritime routes. This pressure is causing consumers in Asia to split their purchases among many producing countries.

Iraqi oil remains a vital resource for India due to supply security and the high quality of Basra crude.

Indian refiners confirmed they have secured their crude oil requirements until the end of September and have begun arranging purchases for the fourth quarter of the year, despite persistent concerns about the impact of any interruptions to shipping routes on global supply chains.

Meanwhile, Russia remained India’s top crude oil supplier in the first half of the year, while imports from the UAE and Brazil increased.

India’s purchases from Iraq and the United States fell as New Delhi attempted to diversify its supply sources and reduce the risks associated with reliance on a single source.

Indian refiners have warned that increased shipping risks and higher insurance costs, along with declining discounts on Russian oil, are affecting profit margins.

Experts anticipate that continuing instability in the Middle East will raise oil prices and pose new hurdles for Asian oil-importing countries.

World.title: Six Iranian advisors killed in US-Saudi attack on Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A joint US-Saudi attack on targets in Iraq killed six Iranian advisors on Wednesday, according to two Iraqi officials who spoke to the Associated Press (AP).

A meeting that was set for Thursday in Saudi Arabia between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was called off due to recent attacks by armed groups targeting Saudi Arabia.

Al-Zaidi ordered an emergency meeting of Iraq’s National Security Council following the coordinated attacks on the country.

The Iraqi Security Media Cell said in a statement that the meeting was ordered in response to the evolving security situation and the airstrikes that targeted several Iraqi provinces early on Wednesday.

The US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Wednesday that US forces, in cooperation with Saudi armed forces, carried out precision airstrikes targeting sites linked to Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

The coordinated airstrikes were in retaliation for a series of drone attacks targeting US interests and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

CENTCOM said in a statement that the strikes, carried out on July 28, targeted logistics sites and weapons depots allegedly used by Iranian-backed groups. It added that these groups were directed by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to attack US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

US and Saudi fighter jets carried out the strikes, an operation described by CENTCOM as a strong response to more than 30 drone attacks that the IRGC had conducted in the past few days.

Headquarters and sites belonging to the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in several Iraqi provinces were targeted by the US-Saudi airstrikes in the country.

World.title: US-Saudi strikes test Iraq’s fragile security balance
World.content:
Baghdad – US-Saudi strikes on Iraq killed at least 20 militants, including several Iranians, on Wednesday, according to the Hashed al-Shaabi, an armed Iraqi alliance that includes pro-Iran groups.

The United States and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed armed militants in Iraq in response to attacks on US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

Washington and Tehran are Iraq’s main allies, but their enmity has long turned the country into a proxy battleground and left successive governments struggling to maintain a delicate balance between the foes.

The Hashed al-Shaabi, also known as the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), said that at least 20 fighters “were martyred and another 32 wounded according to a preliminary toll”.

Two Hashed officials told AFP that five Iranian advisors were among those killed in a strike in the central province of Diyala.

AFP correspondents saw coffins wrapped in Iranian flags during a funeral organised by the Hashed al-Shaabi in Baghdad for those killed.

The Hashed alliance was created in 2014 to fight jihadists before it was formally integrated into the Iraqi armed forces.

It now includes brigades belonging to Iran-backed groups reputed for acting unilaterally.

US President Donald Trump said the strikes were coordinated with the Iraqi government, according to Fox News.

They follow growing US pressure on Baghdad to disarm pro-Iran armed groups, which have frequently targeted US facilities in the country and have long called for the withdrawal of US troops.

Iraq’s new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who came to power this year with Washington’s blessing, vowed to ensure those groups would hand over their weapons, but has faced pushback from some powerful factions.

Earlier this month, Zaidi visited both the United States and Iran.

– ‘Inevitable response’ –

The strikes came after Riyadh said its forces had intercepted drones targeting oil facilities, blaming the Iran-backed groups in Iraq.

The most active pro-Iran armed groups are united under an alliance known as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, which has acted in support of Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks against US bases in Iraq and across the region.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq said “our response to the American enemy is inevitable, and may target its tools in Saudi Arabia”.

But the group added that it would only retaliate after the Arbaeen day of pilgrimage, which falls on Tuesday.

The Arbaeen marks one of the most significant events in the Shia Muslim calendar, during which pilgrims, many from Iran, flock to Iraq to visit the holy shrines.

The pro-Iran groups denied attacking Saudi Arabia and they haven’t claimed any attacks since the US-Iran war resumed earlier this month.

– Violation –

Iraq denounced the US-Saudi strikes and said it rejects “all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented.”

The Ministerial Council for National Security said it would “confront any violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, and prevent any source from using Iraqi territory to threaten neighbouring states”.

It reaffirmed its commitment to ensure the state’s monopoly over weapons.

Zaidi’s government has given those groups that Washington designates as terrorist organisations until September 30 to disarm.

Oil-rich Iraq has been trying to move past decades of war and unrest, but it remains vulnerable to regional and internal flare-ups.

World.title: Iraq condemns US-Saudi strikes, vows tighter control over armed groups
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq condemned U.S.-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday that targeted Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) sites, calling the attacks a violation of its sovereignty, and announced new measures to tighten state control over security and prevent Iraqi territory from being used to threaten neighboring countries.

Following the attacks, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, which the government said killed and injured many Iraqis.

As regional tensions rose, Al-Zaidi cancelled a planned visit to Saudi Arabia on Thursday.

In a statement published after the meeting, the council said that the strikes happened when Baghdad was already in talks with US and Saudi authorities over suspicions that Iran-aligned armed organizations operating from Iraq committed drone assaults on Saudi land.

“The government was actively engaging with the relevant parties to verify and address the concerns raised by both the Saudi and US sides,” the statement stated, adding that the military action hampered such efforts.

The council authorized a comprehensive security strategy aimed at strengthening state authority across Iraq, combating breaches of Iraqi sovereignty, and prohibiting any party from exploiting Iraqi territory to threaten neighboring nations.

The steps reflect Baghdad’s efforts to guarantee that no armed organization may launch assaults from Iraqi soil that could pull the nation into larger regional wars, while also confirming the government’s goal of bringing all security actions under state control.

The council also directed the Foreign Ministry to take legal and diplomatic measures under international law and the United Nations Charter to record the attacks and protect Iraq’s legal rights.

The government condemned the attacks but emphasized that responding to security threats and enforcing the law is solely the responsibility of Iraq’s constitutional institutions.

“The government rejects all acts of aggression, regardless of the party responsible or the justifications presented,” the statement read.

The council underlined Baghdad’s commitment to addressing regional conflicts via diplomacy while maintaining efforts to keep all armaments under state control.

It also restated Iraq’s commitment to carrying out the security agreement guiding the departure of the US-led international coalition by the end of September 2026.

The emergency conference occurred hours after US President Donald Trump claimed that the midnight attacks were coordinated with the Iraqi government, something Baghdad has not officially verified.

Iraqi authorities have openly opposed the operation, emphasizing the political sensitivity of the attacks.

The events highlight Al-Zaidi’s increasingly precarious situation, as he seeks to boost Iraq’s connections with the US and Gulf Arab governments while retaining relations with Iran.

His decision to cancel the Saudi visit underlines the gravity of the problem, as Baghdad seeks to temper regional tensions while preventing Iraqi land from becoming a battlefield for opposing forces.

The government’s current security strategy also suggests a renewed desire to prevent armed groups from operating outside official control, as Baghdad wants to reassure neighboring nations that Iraq will not be used as a springboard for assaults that endanger regional peace.

World.title: Uptime Institute partners with T964 to expand Iraq’s digital infrastructure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Uptime Institute, based in the United States, and Iraqi digital infrastructure company Tech964 Holding Limited (T964) have formed a strategic partnership to help develop Iraq’s digital infrastructure, marking the latest technology agreement to result from Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s investment-focused visit to Washington.

The agreement, signed earlier this month at the U.S.-Iraq Business Summit hosted by the US Chamber of Commerce, names T964 as Uptime Institute’s business partner in Iraq to promote international data center standards, professional training, and the development of resilient digital infrastructure.

The agreement is part of Baghdad’s larger effort to diversify its economy beyond oil by increasing digital infrastructure, attracting technological investment, and bolstering industries including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, financial technology, and cybersecurity.

T964, one of Iraq’s major private digital infrastructure businesses, has announced that it would collaborate with the Uptime Institute to implement internationally recognized standards for the country’s expanding network of data centers, as well as increase technical competence and operational best practices.

The partnership is anticipated to help establish carrier-neutral data centers, telecommunications infrastructure, cloud services, and AI-ready digital platforms, all of which the government believes are important to modernizing public services and stimulating private-sector investment.

The pact follows a series of technological ties announced during Al-Zaidi’s tour to the United States, during which Iraq inked more than 50 agreements totaling more than $60 billion in the energy, banking, infrastructure, industrial, and technology sectors.

Improving digital infrastructure has become a key component of Iraq’s long-term economic plan, as the country strives to lessen reliance on oil earnings and establish a knowledge-based economy capable of attracting foreign technology businesses while also encouraging homegrown innovation.

The alliance also underscores increased US private-sector interest in Iraq’s digital economy, especially as demand for secure data centers, cloud computing capacity, and AI infrastructure in the Middle East grows.

Iraq has increasingly prioritized digital infrastructure for foreign investment alongside energy and transportation, with officials claiming that internationally certified data centers and modern telecommunications networks will be critical to supporting e-government services, digital banking, e-commerce, and artificial intelligence, as well as strengthening Iraq’s role as an emerging regional technology hub.

World.title: Explained: India's first urban ropeway is almost here. Can Varanasi's sky-high commute change how Indian cities travel?
World.content:
For centuries, getting around Varanasi has been part of the city's experience.

Its narrow lanes, bustling bazaars, temples and ghats are integral to the spiritual capital's identity.

But as one of India's oldest continuously inhabited cities welcomed millions of pilgrims and tourists every year, those same streets also became one of its biggest infrastructure challenges.

The stretch between Varanasi Cantonment railway station and Godowlia, the gateway to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Dashashwamedh Ghat, often witnessed bumper-to-bumper traffic.

During festivals or the peak pilgrimage season, a journey of less than four kilometres could easily take 40 minutes or more.

Building wider roads was never a practical solution. Much of the corridor passes through densely populated neighbourhoods and heritage areas, where large-scale demolition would not only be expensive but also risk altering the city's centuries-old character.

Instead, policymakers looked upwards.

Later this year, Varanasi is expected to become home to India's first urban public transport ropewayâa project that promises to ferry commuters and pilgrims above the city's congested streets in gondola cabins suspended nearly 45-50 metres above the ground.





Unlike the ropeways familiar to tourists in hill stations, this one is being built as part of the city's everyday mass transit network.

Officials say it will cut travel time between Cantt and Godowlia from around 40-45 minutes by road to roughly 15 minutes, while reducing pressure on one of the city's busiest traffic corridors.

The project is also a global rarity. Urban ropeways are still uncommon worldwide, with only a handful of cities integrating them into their public transport networks.

Indian officials have frequently described the Varanasi project as among the first of its kind globally to use ropeway technology for mass urban commuting rather than tourism.

Beyond offering a faster ride for pilgrims heading to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, the project is being viewed as a test case for whether aerial mobility can solve transport problems in India's densely populated and heritage-rich cities, where conventional infrastructure often faces severe space constraints.

If successful, it could influence similar projects planned in cities ranging from Guwahati and Shimla to Dehradun and beyond under the Centre's broader ropeway expansion programme.

That makes Varanasi more than just another infrastructure project, as it could become the template for a new model of urban transport in India.

So, what exactly is India's first urban ropeway? Why has the government chosen cable cars over roads or metro lines? And can this technology genuinely become part of India's future public transport network?

What exactly is the Varanasi Urban Ropeway?

The Varanasi Urban Ropeway is India's first ropeway designed primarily as an urban mass transit system rather than a tourist attraction.

The project is being implemented by the National Highways Logistics Management Limited (NHLML), a wholly owned company of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Swiss ropeway manufacturer Bartholet Maschinenbau AG has supplied the cable transport technology for the project.

Once operational, the ropeway will connect Varanasi Cantonment railway station with Godowlia Chowk, one of the busiest intersections in the city and the main access point for pilgrims visiting the Kashi Vishwanath Temple.

Stretching approximately 3.75-3.85 kilometres, the corridor will include stations at Cantt, Vidyapeeth, Rath Yatra and Godowlia, linking the railway station with major commercial, residential and religious hubs.

The project was conceived after authorities concluded that expanding roads through Varanasi's congested core would be extremely difficult because of the city's dense urban fabric and heritage structures.

Instead of competing for road space, the ropeway will operate entirely above existing traffic, offering commuters a predictable travel time regardless of congestion below.

According to the government, the system will use 148 modern gondola cabins, each capable of carrying 10 passengers. Gondolas are expected to arrive every one-and-a-half to two minutes, allowing the system to transport nearly 3,000 passengers per hour in each direction, or about 6,000 passengers every hour in total.

Official estimates suggest the network could eventually handle close to 96,000-1 lakh passengers daily, depending on operational schedules and demand.

Passengers boarding at Cantt Railway Station will be able to reach Godowlia in about 15-16 minutes, less than half the time the journey often takes by road during busy hours.

The Uttar Pradesh government has also finalised passenger fares. The minimum ticket has been fixed at Rs 10, while travelling the entire stretch from Cantt to Godowlia will cost Rs 50.

Holders of the Kashi Smart Pass will receive a 20% discount, reducing the end-to-end fare to Rs 40. Premium gondolas have also been planned for tourists and group bookings.

Modern passenger facilities, including lifts, escalators, CCTV surveillance, digital ticketing, fire safety systems and dedicated infrastructure for senior citizens and persons with disabilities, have been incorporated at stations to position the ropeway as a full-fledged public transport system rather than simply another tourist attraction.

The project, estimated to cost over Rs 800 crore including long-term operation and maintenance, has already completed trial runs and is expected to begin commercial operations after receiving the necessary regulatory clearances.

Why is the government betting on ropeways?

The Varanasi project is not an isolated experiment. It is part of the Centre's much larger strategy to introduce ropeways as an alternative mode of transport in places where building conventional roads, metro lines or rail corridors is either too expensive, technically difficult or environmentally disruptive.

This vision took shape in 2022 with the launch of the Parvatmala Pariyojana, the National Ropeways Development Programme announced in the Union Budget. The scheme aims to develop ropeways in hilly regions as well as congested urban areas through public-private partnerships.

Traditionally, ropeways in India have been associated with tourist destinations such as Gulmarg, Auli, Mussoorie or pilgrimage centres.

Under the new policy, however, the government wants them to become part of mainstream public transport.

Officials argue that ropeways offer several advantages over conventional infrastructure. They require significantly less land acquisition than roads or metro systems because towers occupy relatively small footprints.

Construction is also faster since there is little need for tunnelling, large flyovers or extensive utility shifting.

Since the cabins are electrically operated, ropeways also produce lower emissions than conventional road traffic, making them an attractive option for cities trying to reduce congestion and pollution.

The Varanasi project perfectly fits this philosophy.

The city's historic core leaves almost no room for widening roads without affecting heritage structures and densely populated neighbourhoods. A metro line would have involved far greater costs and engineering challenges.

An aerial ropeway, planners argue, offers a way to increase mobility while preserving the city's cultural fabric.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi had also highlighted this balance between tradition and technology when the project was announced.

Sharing details of the ropeway on social media in 2023, he described it as an "adbhut sangam" (remarkable confluence) of faith and technology and said it would not only make travel more convenient for devotees but also improve access to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple.

The government now sees ropeways as a solution that can complementânot replaceâexisting transport systems.

Can ropeways really work as urban public transport?

The idea may appear futuristic in India, but urban ropeways have been operating successfully in several parts of the world for years.

Perhaps the best-known example is La Paz, Bolivia, where the Mi TelefÃ©rico network has evolved into one of the world's largest urban cable car systems. With multiple interconnected lines stretching across the city and neighbouring El Alto, it carries hundreds of thousands of passengers every day while navigating mountainous terrain that makes conventional transport difficult.

Another frequently cited example is Mexico City, whose CablebÃºs system has transformed commuting for residents living in densely populated hillside settlements.

What once took well over an hour by road can now be completed in a fraction of the time using aerial cabins integrated with the city's wider public transport network.

These examples have demonstrated that ropeways need not remain tourist attractions.

They can function as reliable mass transit systems when integrated with buses, railways and pedestrian infrastructure.

Varanasi is now attempting to replicate those successes

Unlike metro systems that require passengers to travel underground or elevated through fixed corridors, ropeways can fly directly over existing development, reducing construction challenges and avoiding traffic altogether.

Continuous movement of gondolas also means passengers spend less time waiting compared to conventional bus services.

However, experts caution that ropeways are not a universal solution.

Their passenger capacity is considerably lower than metro rail systems, making them suitable only for specific corridors rather than citywide transport. Weather conditions, periodic maintenance and evacuation protocols also require careful planning. Unlike buses, expanding routes later is neither simple nor inexpensive.

Consequently, transport planners view ropeways as a niche solutionâbest suited for heritage cities, mountainous terrain or highly congested corridors where traditional transport networks are difficult to expand.

Could Varanasi become a model for other Indian cities?

That is perhaps the biggest question surrounding the project.

If the ropeway succeeds in reducing congestion, attracting regular commuters and integrating smoothly with the city's existing transport network, it could become a blueprint for similar projects elsewhere.

The Centre has already identified several ropeway proposals across the country under the Parvatmala programme, particularly in Himalayan states and pilgrimage destinations.

Cities facing severe geographical or heritage constraints are also studying whether aerial mobility could complement existing infrastructure.

But the success of the Varanasi ropeway will ultimately depend on far more than engineering.

Passengers must find it affordable enough to use regularly. The stations need seamless connections with railway stations, buses, auto-rickshaws and pedestrian routes. Safety standards, maintenance schedules and operational reliability will determine whether commuters choose the ropeway over conventional road transport.

Ridership will also be critical.

Unlike tourist ropeways that witness seasonal demand, an urban transport system must attract consistent daily commutersâoffice-goers, students, residents and pilgrimsâto remain financially viable over the long term.

There is also the question of whether ropeways can genuinely ease congestion or merely shift it from roads to stations if passenger management is inadequate.

These are precisely the issues transport planners and policymakers across India will be watching once commercial operations begin.

The bigger picture

India's urban transport story has traditionally revolved around roads, flyovers, suburban railways and metro systems. Ropeways are rarely featured in discussions about everyday commuting.

Varanasi could change that.

By carrying passengers above one of the country's oldest and most congested cities, the project represents an attempt to rethink how mobility solutions are designed for places where conventional infrastructure has reached its limits.

Its significance therefore extends beyond the four-kilometre journey between Cantt and Godowlia.

If successful, it could demonstrate that innovative transport systems can coexist with heritage conservation, allowing cities to modernise without fundamentally altering their historic character.

At the same time, the project is also a reminder that no single technology can solve every urban mobility challenge.

Ropeways are unlikely to replace metros or buses in India's largest cities. Instead, they could become another tool in the transport planner's toolkitâone best deployed where geography, density or heritage leave few alternatives.

For Varanasi, the benefits could be immediate. Faster journeys for pilgrims, easier access to one of India's holiest temples, reduced traffic on chronically congested roads and a cleaner mode of transport for residents and visitors alike.

For India, however, the stakes are much larger.

The country's first urban public transport ropeway is not merely about moving people from one station to another.

It is a test of whether the next generation of urban infrastructure can think beyond roads and rails and whether its oldest cities can embrace modern mobility without sacrificing the heritage that defines them.

World.title: IMD flags below-normal rainfall in August; heavy rain alerts for Kerala, Assam, Northeast
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Friday forecast below-normal rainfall in August across India, at 94 per cent of the long-period average. It also issued weather alerts across several parts of the country, including Kerala, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and other northeastern states, warning of heavy to very heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, flash floods and landslides over the next few days.

The latest warnings come as several states continue to grapple with flood and landslide risks during the monsoon season. The IMD said monthly average rainfall over India as a whole is most likely to be below normal in August after the country recorded near-average rainfall in July, raising concerns about crop yields and broader economic activity.

"Rainfall in August is likely to be below 94% of the long-period average," Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, director-general of the India Meteorological Department, told a press conference.

August outlook raises concerns for crops and economy

The IMDâs latest forecast of below-normal August rainfall comes after a season marked by intense regional downpours despite broadly average rainfall across the country in July. The weather officeâs assessment suggests that while parts of southern and northeastern India may continue to experience heavy rain in the immediate term, rainfall across India as a whole is expected to remain below the long-term average during August.





Kerala under orange alert, schools shut in several districts

In Kerala, the IMD issued an orange alert for 11 districts on Friday, including Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod. An orange alert indicates the likelihood of very heavy rainfall ranging between 115.6 mm and 204.4 mm within 24 hours at isolated places.

For August 1, orange alerts remain in place for Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod, while yellow alerts have been issued for several southern districts through August 2.

Following the warnings, educational institutions in several Kerala districts were declared closed on Friday. The Kerala State Disaster Management Authority advised residents in areas vulnerable to landslides, mudslides and flash floods to move to safer locations if directed by authorities. People living near riverbanks, downstream of dams and in houses with weak roofs were also urged to remain vigilant.

Flash flood warning issued for Arunachal Pradesh

In Arunachal Pradesh, the IMD forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning from July 31 and issued a flash flood alert for nine districts, including Tawang, West Kameng, East Kameng, Kurung Kumey, Upper Subansiri, Anjaw, Dibang Valley, Tirap and Changlang.

Very heavy rainfall of 12 cm to 20 cm in 24 hours is expected at isolated places in Papum Pare district through Saturday, while Lower Subansiri is likely to receive heavy rainfall of 6 cm to 11 cm. The weather office warned that heavy rain could trigger surface runoff and inundation in saturated and low-lying areas and advised district administrations to remain on high alert.

The ongoing spell of floods and landslides has already claimed seven lives and affected 1,53,553 people across Arunachal Pradesh.

The monsoon has affected 373 circles and 668 villages in 27 districts so far.

Assam and northeast brace for another spell of heavy rain

A fresh spell of heavy to very heavy rainfall has also been forecast across Assam and several northeastern states over the next three to four days. An orange alert has been issued for Tinsukia district in Assam, while similar alerts are in place for Mon, Mokokchung and Wokha districts of Nagaland.

The IMD said widespread rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms is likely between July 30 and August 1 across parts of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

Runoff from districts in Arunachal Pradesh, including East Siang, Lohit, Namsai, Longding, Papumpare, Lower Subansiri and Lower Dibang Valley, could affect Tinsukia, Dhemaji and Lakhimpur districts in Assam.

The Assam State Disaster Management Authority warned that the fresh spell of rain could worsen flooding, trigger urban waterlogging and flash floods, and cause localised landslides, particularly in hilly and vulnerable areas. UK highlights AI cooperation and vision 2035



Leaders discuss AI and emerging technologies

World.title: CBI arrests 2 in Suvendu Adhikari aide murder case, probes political links
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Friday arrested two brothers, Sagar Sonkar and Sahib Sonkar, in connection with the murder of Chandranath Rath, a close aide of West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, in Kolkata.

The arrests were made as part of the agency's probe into the alleged assassination plot, which investigators now believe may have links to a functionary of a rival political party.

The two accused, who had worked with Rath, are expected to be produced before a special court in Kolkata later on Friday, officials said.

Investigators alleged that Sagar Sonkar maintained regular contact with the office of a rival political party through landline calls while working with Rath.

The agency is now examining those communications to identify the individual with whom he was allegedly in touch.

According to officials, analysis of Sagar's call detail records revealed numerous calls made to the local office of the rival party. The CBI has also learnt that until 2020, Sagar had worked with an MLA of that party before later switching to the BJP.

Officials said the agency had gathered sufficient material linking Sagar to the shooters allegedly hired to kill Rath.





He is accused of arranging the contract and providing money for the execution of the murder.

The CBI believes the conspiracy to eliminate Rath had been in motion since December 2025 and that the plan was repeatedly delayed before it was finally carried out.

Rath, who served as Adhikari's personal assistant and was considered a key figure behind his election campaign in Kolkata's Bhabanipur ahead of the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections, was shot dead on Jessore Road near Madhyamgram in North 24 Parganas district on May 6.

He was travelling in a car when motorcycle-borne assailants opened fire.

The killing took place two days after the declaration of results in the fiercely contested Bengal Assembly election, which saw the BJP defeat the Trinamool Congress and come to power in the state.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The CBI has so far arrested six alleged shooters identified as Monu Singh, Raj Singh, Golu Singh, Mayank Raj Mishra, Vickey Maurya and Naveen Kumar Singh, along with middlemen Vinay Rai, Sanjay Rai and Vikas Mishra, who are alleged to have facilitated the contract.

One accused remains absconding.

The central agency took over the investigation from the West Bengal Police after a request from the state government. A seven-member special investigation team headed by a Deputy Inspector General from the CBI's Special Crime unit in Delhi has been constituted to investigate the case.

World.title: Govt summons Meta's global team over PM Modi post restriction, to question algorithmic bias
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Centre has summoned Meta's global team to explain the temporary restriction of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Facebook post, with government officials set to question the social media giant on alleged algorithmic bias, the functioning of its content moderation systems and its role in maintaining public order, PTI reported citing sources.

According to the sources, Meta's global team is expected to arrive in India sometime in the middle of next week. Besides appearing before government officials, the executives will also depose before a parliamentary panel.

The move comes days after the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) summoned a senior Meta executive following the temporary restriction of

's Facebook post addressing India's youth and promising stringent action against paper leaks.

Government to seek answers on algorithmic bias



Sources told PTI that the government's interaction with Meta's global team would focus on whether the platform's algorithms exhibit bias, how those algorithms function and the company's broader responsibility in matters affecting public order.

The officials are expected to "categorically" seek clarification on issues surrounding algorithmic bias and the manner in which Meta's content moderation systems operate, the sources said.





Meta apologised, government found explanation inadequate



Meta had earlier attributed the restriction of the Prime Minister's post to a technical glitch and issued an apology. However, according to PTI, MeitY considered the company's explanation "inadequate".

Following the incident, Meta informed the ministry that content posted by Prime Minister Modi and certain other prominent accounts would be subjected to additional oversight on its platforms.

The company also wrote to the government outlining enhanced safeguards, including multiple levels of review involving senior company officials before action is taken on posts published by the Prime Minister and other high-profile accounts.

Parliamentary panel to examine issue



Apart from appearing before government officials, Meta's global representatives are also expected to testify before a parliamentary panel as scrutiny over the company's content moderation practices intensifies.

Government sources told PTI that when platform rules or Indian laws are violated, liabilities would arise.

The sources also pointed to studies highlighting the wider impact of social media on society, including concerns over cognitive health and mental well-being among both children and adults due to excessive digital media consumption.

"Keeping all these aspects in mind, steps that are needed will be taken," a government source told PTI, adding that the government was treating the matter seriously.

Hyderabad Police also register cases



The government's scrutiny comes amid parallel legal action in Telangana.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Earlier this week, Hyderabad Cyber Crime Police registered cases against Meta India head Arun Srinivas and operators of several Facebook and Instagram accounts over allegedly morphed and AI-generated content targeting Prime Minister Modi during protests over the NEET paper leak issue.

According to police, the cases were filed following complaints by BJP supporters alleging that manipulated videos and images of the Prime Minister were circulated on social media. Investigators have issued notices to Meta and are tracing the operators behind the accounts named in the complaints.

The latest developments mark an escalation in the government's scrutiny of Meta, with the company now facing regulatory, parliamentary and law enforcement action over its content moderation practices and handling of politically sensitive content.

World.title: Tahir Hussain gives first public reaction after being sentenced to life in prison
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former AAP councillor

on Friday said he would challenge his conviction and life sentence in the Delhi High Court after a Delhi court sentenced him and four others to life imprisonment for the murder of Intelligence Bureau (IB) officer

during the 2020 northeast Delhi riots.

"I will get justice from the High Court," Hussain told reporters after the Karkardooma Court pronounced the sentence.

Additional sessions Judge Praveen Singh sentenced Hussain along with co-convicts Shah Alam, Mehtab, Gul Firoz and Mohammad Riyan after hearing arguments on the quantum of punishment. While the Delhi Police had sought the death penalty, calling the murder a "rarest of rare" case, the court held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the convicts were beyond the possibility of reform and instead awarded life imprisonment.

The court had convicted all five accused earlier this month. The judgment was delivered amid tight security in a packed courtroom attended by senior Delhi Police officials, including officers from the Crime Branch.

During sentencing, Special public prosecutor Madhukar Pandey argued that Sharma's murder was premeditated and exceptionally brutal. He told the court that the IB officer suffered 51 injuries, seven of which were individually sufficient to cause death.





The prosecution alleged Sharma, who was unarmed, was surrounded by a mob, repeatedly assaulted, dragged with a cloth tied around his neck and his body dumped in a nearby drain.

The prosecution further argued that Hussain, who was serving as an AAP councillor at the time of the riots, had a public duty to protect citizens but instead participated in the conspiracy that led to Sharma's killing. It urged the court to impose capital punishment, describing the crime as one that shocked the collective conscience of society.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Hussain's counsel Rajiv Mohan opposed the death penalty, arguing that capital punishment could not be imposed in every murder case. The defence maintained that the prosecution had failed to establish any conspiracy or assign Hussain a specific role in the killing and urged the court to consider mitigating circumstances while determining the sentence.

The case relates to the killing of 26-year-old IB staffer Ankit Sharma during the communal violence that erupted in northeast Delhi in February 2020, leaving more than 50 people dead and hundreds injured. Sharma's body was recovered from a drain near Hussain's residence after he went missing during the riots. Hussain has consistently denied the allegations against him and is expected to challenge the verdict before the Delhi High Court.

World.title: 139 Indians released from Russian Army, 2 dozen remain: MEA warns against shady job offers
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India is continuing to engage with Russia to secure the release of the remaining Indian nationals serving in the Russian military, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said on Friday, adding that 139 Indians have been brought back so far.

Addressing a weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the government has been consistently taking up the matter with the Russian authorities.

"We have been following up with the Russian side for the release of the remaining Indian nationals in the Russian army. So far, our efforts have led to the release of 139 Indian nationals. We continue to pursue the release of the remaining two dozen Indian nationals who are reportedly in the Russian army," Jaiswal said.

He also cautioned Indian citizens against falling prey to fraudulent overseas job offers, saying many such recruitment drives are carried out by unscrupulous individuals and agencies.

"We would like to caution our people against job offers that are fraught with risk and made by unscrupulous individuals and agencies," he said.

MEA to appoint nodal officer to coordinate

The Supreme Court on Friday directed the ministry of external affairs (MEA) to appoint a nodal officer to coordinate with the families of Indians who died, were injured or went missing after joining the Russian military during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.





A bench also asked the MEA to facilitate DNA matching of family members with the mortal remains of those killed in the conflict and assist them in filing compensation claims with the Russian Embassy in New Delhi. The court further directed that all relevant information be provided to the affected families in their respective vernacular languages.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The issue came to light after several Indian nationals were allegedly recruited by agents on the promise of lucrative jobs in Russia but were later sent to serve in the Russian military amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine.

India has repeatedly urged Moscow to facilitate the early discharge and repatriation of its citizens.

The Centre had earlier informed the Supreme Court that Russian authorities had lured foreign recruits with attractive financial packages, including a signing bonus of around USD 5,000, a monthly salary of $2,500, promises of Russian citizenship, social benefits and compensation of around USD 168,000 in the event of death.

World.title: The new public life of bats
World.content:
Nobody grows up wanting to be a

person. Unless your parents fell in love over dead ones. For Aditya Srinivasulu, bats were never mysterious creatures of the night. They were family lore.

Long before he became a bat biologist himself, the UK-trained researcher grew up with the now-famous story of how his parents â renowned zoologists at Osmania University, Chelmala and Bhargavi Srinivasulu â fell in love over dead bats.

As college classmates, Bhargavi gifted Chelmala a dead bat instead of roses; years later, Chelmala returned the gesture with another dead bat on their wedding day. Fortunately, Aditya jokes, there is no pressure on him to replicate the romantic gesture.

Today, when Aditya is not doing his academic heavy-lifting, he conducts evening bat walks across the sprawling green campus of Osmania University.

The setting is a biodiverse, wooded stretch where evening descends over a shrinking summer lake and the sky begins to flicker with movement. "If you stand there and look up, the sky is littered with a swirling mass of bats," Aditya says. "Think of a swarm of mosquitoes over your head near a lake â that kind of density.





Except these are bats." Most of the tiny, fluttering shapes overhead are pipistrelles, among the smallest bats in South Asia.

Then there are the crowd favourites: the flying foxes. "Big leathery boys," Aditya calls them affectionately. These large fruit bats emerge in dramatic numbers at dusk, soaring overhead while participants stand along the bund walkway. Sometimes they come within ten feet of the group. "As long as people don't make sudden movements or do flash photography, there's no issue," he says.

The myth-busting happens organically. Bats are not blind, not aggressive, not waiting to fly into human hair. Fruit bats actually possess excellent eyesight and an extraordinary sense of smell. Families, retirees, students and curious residents from across Hyderabad show up. "Honestly, the children are always the highlight," Aditya says. The team hands out tiny stuffed bat plushies, and he watches reluctant children transform from "my parents dragged me here" to suddenly being completely fascinated.

"Children ask the smartest questions. One child once asked if bats use sound to figure out where they're going, how do they think so quickly?" Srinivasulu remembers pausing, momentarily stumped by the question. "Anything that goes bump in the night immediately gets associated with witchcraft, bad omens or danger. Animals like bats, owls and snakes are burdened by stigma and misinformation," says the 28-year-old scion of the OG bat family of Hyderabad; he is now developing booklets and brochures on the city's bat diversity aimed at everyone from four-year-olds to researchers.

Rajesh Puttaswamaiah founded Bat Conservation India Trust in 2014

Aditya is not alone. Bat researchers across Indian cities are beginning to trade the lab coat for the headlamp, leading groups of curious oglers through darkening parks and ruins, passing around ultrasound detectors like prized telescopes to catch bat calls and translate them into a crackling chorus of clicks and static bursts. For most participants, it's the first time they've not just seen a bat, but actually heard one "think" with echolocation.

These researchers will tell you bats are the unacknowledged night-shift workers. When birds clock out at dusk, bats take over pollinating flowers, scattering seeds and hoovering up the kinds of insects that would otherwise devastate crops. Yet for a country that hosts around 135 bat species â roughly 10 percent of the world's total â India has remarkably few people who actually study them. That imbalance is precisely why many researchers now say that getting the public on board matters as much as any fieldwork.

"One of the biggest challenges is the lack of data or public participation when it comes to bats. Scientists alone cannot monitor every colony or every park. But ordinary citizens can," says Nikhil John, a naturalist with WWF India's Nature Connect outreach programme. That idea drove WWF India's recent bat walks in Delhi, organised around International Bat Appreciation Day in April, which also marked the launch of a first-of-its-kind fold-out guide to the bats of Delhi-NCR.

It documents 12 of the 15 species recorded in the region, complete with identification tips, habitats and where people might actually spot them across the city. The first walk at Sunder Nursery last month drew around 65 people. A second walk to Tughlaqabad Fort the next day merged natural history with architecture and storytelling.

Kolar Leaf-Nosed Bat by Rajesh Puttaswamaiah

While birds have long dominated India's citizen-science culture, bats have mostly remained invisible.

There are birders everywhere. WhatsApp groups swap photographs from dawn trails, hobbyists upload sightings onto eBird, entire communities are built around identifying warblers and raptors. Bats instead are heard but not recorded, feared more than followed, thanks to haunted house and vampire movie mythologies.

Conversationalists hope these walks become the springboard for a broader base of bat-watchers.

John compares it to the rise of dragonfly festivals which transformed a largely ignored insect into a community-led conservation movement. "We now have volunteers and young people who are not from biodiversity or zoological backgrounds, but they can now talk about dragonflies and conduct walks." The hope is to replicate that energy for bats. "This year we are also trying to do a three-day Bat Festival in Delhi," John says.

Beyond viruses and villainy

Back in the pandemic era, when early evidence linked bats to the SARS-CoV-2 virus, they became global villains overnight. Alarming viral spillover theories prompted a wave of widespreadâand often misguidedâpublic fear, with calls for culling and roost destruction. And suddenly, bats needed a PR team. âWith the unnecessary villainization of bats, we had to step up and be more vocal online in those days,â says Rohit Chakravarty, who has become one of the most visible public voices for bat conservation in India.

The 34-year-old speaks at lit fests and schools, gives lectures in bars and cafÃ©s through Bengaluruâs 'Pint of View series, and leads twilight bat walks through lakes, gardens and medieval ruins in Delhi and Bengaluru. He is also one of the editors of a hefty, 200-page 'State of India's Bats (2024â2025)' report, the first-ever national assessment of bat species in India, compiled by 36 experts from 27 institutions, released by the Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF) and Bat Conservation International (BCI) in collaboration with WWF India .

Although released last month, the report's genesis really was the pandemic years, when researchers across India began collaborating on public statements against the killing of bats. "I think the Covid-era was a great turning point because we managed to convert the crisis into a more positive outcome," says Chakravarty. One of the report's central concerns is bats living in monuments. In Delhi, many protected monuments still shelter bat colonies because cities have lost most natural roosting spaces, yet bats are often treated as pests during restoration work.

"This has been a cause of friction between the ASI and bat researchers for a long time. We're trying to understand why bats are disliked in these spaces, how we can conserve them in monuments when there are no natural roosts left around cities, and how these spaces can become opportunities for public awareness," he says. But he is careful not to romanticise bats as harmless mascots. "Any wild animal is dangerous. If you are in the same room with a tiger, the tiger will eat you.

But if you are in the same room with a bat, the bat will not kill and eat you but the risk of disease is there from any wild animal." During enclosed monument walks, participants wear masks and maintain distance from roosting colonies. "Let's not single out bats. This applies to every animal."

Rajkumar Patel, another researcher who leads guided bat walks through Mumbai's ancient rock-cut Buddhist caves at Mahakali in Jogeshwari and Kanheri inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, gets particularly irritated about bat-blaming when it comes to zoonotic viruses from Covid to Nipah.

"Bats carry pathogens but spillover happens when viruses jump species barriers through habitat destruction, wildlife trade, unsanitary conditions in wet markets and contamination like uncovered toddy sap collection sites.

People should be more scared of mosquitoes and pigeons. They're far more likely to transmit disease to you. How many times in your day do you actually come face-to-face with a bat?" Patel asks.

His walks have participants hunting for clues in the dark: urine stains on cave ceilings, bat shit (guano) on stone floors, discarded insect wings and, if they're lucky, spotting insectivorous species like Schneider's leaf-nosed bat or the black-bearded tomb bat hanging upside down in the shadows. His favourite conversational detour is the false vampire bat, a carnivorous hunter that preys on amphibians, birds and even smaller bats.

"False" only because the actual blood-drinkers live in the Americas. "But mosquitoes also suck blood. Leeches too. But as soon as we mention bats, people get really scared. That kind of partiality should be eliminated completely." He also translates bats into a language everyone understands:F&B. "Mahua flowers, central to local liquor economies in central India, depend on fruit bats for pollination. Bananas, too.

Tequila, one of the most trending drinks today, owes its existence to bats who are the primary natural pollinators of the blue agave plant. You won't get chocolates too without bats. They act as natural pest controllers in cocoa plantations, eating insects that would otherwise damage cocoa pods."

When hobby became conservation

Not all of India's bat advocates came through the academic route. Some simply fell into it and never climbed back out.

For Bengaluru-based Rajesh Puttaswamaiah, it started with a stack of forgotten film slides. A corporate lawyer and entrepreneur, he spent the 1990s as a birder and wildlife enthusiast before stumbling, while digitising old slides in 2011, upon bat photographs nobody around him could identify. "Wildlife conservationists back then would talk tiger, elephants, birds, leopards, but how come no one ever talked about bats? The existing public photos online didn't help either.

These images showed bats stretched out with their wings in awkward positions. Not really attractive. There are already so many negative myths about bats, and when you show them in an ugly manner, it doesn't help." So he decided to fix both problems. First through better photography, then by founding the Bat Conservation India Trust in 2014. Today his focus is the critically endangered Kolar leaf-nosed bat, rediscovered in 2013 near Hanumanahalli village in Karnataka's Kolar district by a team led by Bhargavi Srinivasulu, one of the few female bat researchers in India.

The bat exists nowhere else on earth. When Puttaswamaiah arrived in 2019, the mood was hostile: quarrying on the granite hillock housing the bats had just been stopped and locals were furious. "They used to come and shout at us, saying, 'Because of you people, we lost our livelihood.'" Slowly, trust followed. "We tried to instil a sense of pride in them by saying that this is a rare bat found nowhere else in the world except their village," he says.

Hunting dropped, children stopped disturbing roosts, farmers cut back on pesticides and locals were persuaded to protect the tamarind and Pongamia trees the bats feed on. It has since grown into a 10-year management action plan with the forest department.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Rajkumar Patel, who leads guided walks through Mumbai's rock-cut Buddhist caves, explains bat echolation using ultrasound detectors

But not every conservation story soars. An attempt to work with the Bomrr clan in Nagaland â who traditionally hunted bats â had to be abandoned after running into financial and cultural barriers.

Members of the Bomrr clan in Nagaland traditionally hunt fulvous fruit bat colonies every year after the monsoon."They sometimes smoke out entire caves, killing not just fulvous fruit bats but also other cave-dwelling species," says Puttaswamaiah.

He says his team spent two years and a lot of money trying to negotiate a compromise. "But they were not inclined toward that. For them, it is an annual ritual, and their belief was that unless they hunted and ate these bats, their ancestors would not accept them. So ultimately, the project had to be shelved," he says. "Without involving local communities, we can't do any conservation," says Puttaswamaiah. Bat conservation, he has learned, is as much about navigating culture, livelihoods and identity as it is about science.

World.title: Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, passed in Lok Sabha amid protests over police crackdown
World.content:
The Lok Sabha on Friday (July 31, 2026) passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, without debate amid loud protests by the Opposition against the police crackdown on student protesters at Jantar Mantar on July 20.

Opposition protests began as soon as the House convened at 11 a.m. forcing Speaker Om Birla to adjourn it till noon.

Also read: Parliament Monsoon Session Day 10 highlights on July 31, 2026

Similar scenes were witnessed when the House reassembled. BJP MP Dilip Saikia, who was in the chair, asked for listed papers to be laid on the table. These included grant of deadline extension – till the first day of the last week of the Winter Session – to BJP MP Aparajita Sarangi-led Joint Parliamentary Committee examining the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025, for submission of the report. The Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025, proposes the automatic removal of any Union or State Minister, Chief Minister, or Prime Minister who is arrested and detained in custody for 30 consecutive days on serious criminal charges carrying a jail term of five years or more.

Following this, Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai put up the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill for discussion.

The Opposition MPs, meanwhile, trooped into the well of the House demanding the presence of Home Minister Amit Shah in the House even as Mr. Saikia called out the names of MPs listed to speak during the debate.

The Bill was passed by a voice vote amid sloganeering by Opposition members. The proposed legislation seeks to make delayed registration of births and deaths more stringent by requiring an order from a judicial magistrate (first class) for registrations done after two years.

Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said the passage of the Bill in this manner was unfortunate. “Please do not repeat this in the future. People who sent you to Parliament will seek answers from you,” he said.

The House was adjourned for the day after the Bill’s passage.

World.title: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar lauds Tamil Nadu's record voter turnout
World.content:
Chief Election Commissioner of India Gyanesh Kumar on Friday congratulated the people of Tamil Nadu for recording 4.93 crore votes in the recent Assembly elections, describing it as the highest number of votes polled in the State since Independence. He also lauded voters for achieving nearly 86% voter turnout, calling it the highest polling percentage in Tamil Nadu since Independence.

Speaking to reporters at Coimbatore International Airport, Mr. Kumar said he was in the city with his wife, Anuradha, to attend the convocation at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham.

He described Coimbatore as one of South India's fastest-growing cities, highlighting its world-class education system, textile industry and engineering excellence. He added that the people of Tamil Nadu, particularly Coimbatore, could take pride in the serene Western Ghats and the region's rich spiritual and cultural heritage.

World.title: Bihar BJP MLC resigns, unelected RLM leader Deepak Prakash may be elected in his place to remain Minister
World.content:
A day after the Supreme Court rapped the Bihar government for keeping an unelected Minister, Deepak Prakash, beyond six months, the ruling party BJP’S MLC Devesh Kumar on Friday (July 31, 2026) resigned from his position. Mr. Prakash might be elected in his place to remain a Minister in the ruling NDA cabinet. Mr. Prakash was the State’s Panchayati Raj Minister since November 20, 2025, without being a member of either house of the State Legislature.

Earlier, on May 30, 2026, a petition in the Supreme Court was filed by Rakesh Kumar Singh seeking Mr. Prakash’s appointment as Minister be declared “invalid”. The petition further alleged Mr. Prakash’s appointment as “fraud upon the constitution”.

Hearing the petition, the apex court on July 30, had rapped the State government, asking how could an unelected member be a Minister in the government even after six months.

Experts said that Article 164 (4) of the Constitution grants Ministers a grace period of six months to get elected to either house after being appointed as a Minister. “A Minister who, for any period of six consecutive months, is not a member of the Legislature of the State shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister,” they said. Hence, the Minister must quit from the office if not elected within a period of six months. Mr. Prakash has been a Minister in the Bihar Cabinet for 7 months and 22 days. The court fixed the next date of hearing on August 4, 2026.

On Friday (July 31, 2026), MLC Devesh Kumar, who was nominated as a member of the Bihar Legislative Council on the Governor’s quota on March 17, 2021, tendered his resignation to the State Legislative Council chairman Awadhesh Narain Singh. This move was, apparently, to accommodate Mr. Prakash to remain as a Minister in CM Choudhary’s Cabinet.

Mr. Kumar’s tenure was to expire on March 16, 2027. He is said to have resigned from his post to “satisfy constitutional requirements for a Cabinet Minister who needed to secure his legislative membership within a period of six months”.

State BJP president Sanjay Saraogi, too, was present on the occasion. Mr. Kumar, a former journalist, refused to speak to media persons after tendering his resignation. However, party sources said he is set for a new, bigger responsibility in the party. Mr. Prakash’s nomination in the State Legislative Council is yet to be notified.

Mr. Prakash, 36, is the son of Upendra Kushwaha, NDA coalition partner Rashtriya Lok Morcha (RLM) leader and Rajya Sabha member. He has been a Minister since November 20, 2025. Mr. Prakash remained the Panchayat Raj Minister even after the Chief Minister post changed from Nitish Kumar to BJP’s Samrat Choudhary. His mother, Snehlata Kushwaha, is the party MLA of the Sasaram Assembly constituency, Rohtas district.

World.title: Man falls to death from high-rise building in Gachibowli
World.content:
A man was found dead after falling from the 17th floor of a high-rise apartment in Gachibowli on Thursday evening.

The deceased, identified as Sujeet Kumar Pandit, was residing at Vasavi GP Trends Apartments in Gachibowli along with his flatmate.

According to the police, a petition was received from his elder brother Ajit Kumar Pandit, a resident of SG Palya, Venkateshwara Layout, Bengaluru, at around 11.50 p.m. on Thursday, July 30.

In his complaint, Ajit Kumar stated that he received information about his brother’s death at around 4.30 p.m. and travelled from Bengaluru to Hyderabad on the same day.

The complainant requested the police to complete the necessary legal formalities and hand over the body so that it could be transported to his native place at Sector-II, Bokaro Steel City, Jharkhand, for the last rites. The Gachibowli police registered a case and are conducting further investigation.

World.title: Egg procurement price falls to ₹6 in Namakkal
World.content:
Egg procurement price in Namakkal, which was expected to touch an all-time high of ₹7, has fallen to ₹6 over weak demand across the country.

Popularly known as the Egg Town, Namakkal houses over 1,600 poultry farms and produces 6-7 crore eggs per day. It caters to egg demand across Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, and Puducherry and supplies eggs to the ‘Noon Meal Scheme’ in schools. The district also exports eggs to a few countries.

Egg procurement prices are fixed by the National Egg Coordination Committee (NECC-Namakkal Zone) on a daily basis based on demand and supply. On June 17, the procurement price climbed to a record ₹6.45, a first in Namakkal. Over the next one month, it rose steadily and touched ₹6.80 on July 16, staying steady until July 24. However, the price began to fall soon after and settled at ₹6 on July 30, staying unchanged on July 31 as well.

Demand crunch

NECC-Namakkal Zone treasurer Sundar Rajan said demand for eggs began to decrease after the onset of festivals in temples, especially in south Tamil Nadu, in the Tamil month of Aadi. Similarly, the Sawan month, running from July 30 to August 28, has begun in north India. Egg consumption drastically falls during this time, he said.

Egg procurement prices at various zones, including Andhra Pradesh, have come down drastically, affecting the price in the Namakkal NECC Zone, too. “If we do not reduce the price, eggs from Andhra Pradesh will enter Tamil Nadu market,” Mr. Sundar Rajan said.

Egg procurement prices may remain unchanged or even fall further over the next three months, as the Tamil month of Purattasi will begin after Sawan ends in north India, keeping egg demand tepid in the State. Around Deepavali, the prices will start to rise again, he added.

World.title: TIMS Sanathnagar renamed after former Chief Minister Marri Chenna Reddy, Narendra Kumar appointed In-charge Director
World.content:
The Telangana government has renamed the Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (TIMS), Sanathnagar, as Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences, Sanathnagar, while also appointing Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr. A. Narendra Kumar as the institute’s In-charge Director following his retirement from government service on July 31. The orders were issued by Health Secretary Christina Z. Chongthu on July 30.

The appointment of Dr. Kumar will take effect from August 1 on a temporary basis and will continue until a regular Director is appointed or until the need for the arrangement ceases, whichever is earlier.

World.title: Effective utilisation of CSR funds to boost infra in govt. hospitals: Kerala Health Minister
World.content:
Kerala Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Friday (July 31, 2026) inaugurated four major initiatives at the Kerala University of Health Sciences (KUHS) here, including the university’s first on-campus academic programme, an MSc in Medical Bioinformatics.

The Minister also dedicated a medicinal plant garden established with financial support from the National Medicinal Plants Board and technical assistance from the Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI). He also launched a YouTube channel for public health awareness and inaugurated an e-learning studio that will offer master classes to students across various academic disciplines.

Launching the university’s YouTube channel, Mr. Muraleedharan said the initiative was timely as misinformation and unscientific claims on issues such as COVID-19 and organ transplantation continued to circulate widely. Evidence-based health awareness programmes by the university would greatly benefit society, he added.

Speaking after inaugurating the medicinal plant garden, the Minister expressed confidence that the initiative would help address the shortage of medicinal plants faced by the Ayurveda sector. He also appreciated the university’s public awareness initiatives on snakebite prevention.

In his inaugural address, Mr. Muraleedharan stressed that the State government was committed to ensuring quality education and health care for the people. The government’s focus, he said, was to implement projects that would maximise public benefit while creating opportunities that could help reduce the migration of students and professionals to other States and abroad.

The Minister said the government was willing to collaborate with the private sector to strengthen infrastructure in government hospitals and medical colleges by effectively utilising corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from banks and other institutions.

KUHS Vice-Chancellor Prof. Dr. Mohanan Kunnummal, who presided over the function, said the government’s decision to consider bringing Government Medical College, Thrissur, under the university as a constituent college would significantly strengthen health research. He urged the government to expedite the process, noting that the proposal had already been included in the State Budget.

World.title: Government to question Meta global team on issues around algorithmic bias, role in public order
World.content:
Meta's global team, which has been summoned by the government after the social media company restricted Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Facebook post, will be questioned on issues around algorithmic bias and their role in public order, sources said on Friday (July 31, 2026).

Sources further said that Meta's global team is expected sometime in the middle of next week.

Sources said Meta's global team will be "categorically" asked to clarify issues around algorithmic bias, how their algorithm operates, and the company's role in public order.

The team will also appear before a parliamentary panel.

The move assumes significance as the government earlier this week summoned a top Meta executive after Mr. Modi’s recent post addressing India’s youth and promising stringent measures against paper leaks was briefly restricted on Facebook.

While the U.S.-headquartered social media giant attributed the incident to a technical glitch and apologised, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) found the explanation "inadequate".

In the aftermath of the issue, Meta informed the IT Ministry that posts by the prime minister and select prominent accounts will be subject to additional oversight on the platform, with multiple levels of checks involving senior company officials.

Meta wrote to the government outlining the specifics of enhanced and rigorous safeguards it implemented for content posted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and other prominent accounts.

It is pertinent to mention that Hyderabad Cyber Crime police has also registered cases against Meta India head Arun Srinivas and certain accounts on Facebook and Instagram over allegedly morphed and AI posts targeting PM Modi.

Sources said that when rules and laws are violated, liabilities will arise, sources said.

Government sources said that the impact of social media on society is well documented. They also cited studies indicating that excessive use of social media and digital media can adversely affect the cognitive health and mental well-being of children and adults.

"Keeping all these aspects in mind, steps that are needed will be taken," a source said, asserting that the government is serious about these issues.

World.title: Pranab Doley, activist jailed for protesting against hotel in Assam, now faces NSA
World.content:
A day after a local court granted bail to land rights activist Pranab Doley, who was arrested on July 12 in connection with protests against a proposed luxury hotel project in Kaziranga, the Assam government invoked the National Security Act (NSA) against him, stating that his activities “are prejudicial to the maintenance of public order as well as security of the state”.

Doley is a prominent indigenous and land rights activist who had been arrested on July 12 by the Golaghat police in connection with a June 28 protest by activists and locals against a proposed luxury hotel project in Inglay Pathar, adjoining the Kaziranga National Park. Four other activists were also arrested in connection with this. Doley has been leading protests against the project for years, raising concerns about the potential ecological impact of the project and the displacement of indigenous villagers.

In its FIR, police alleged that Doley and “about fifty other persons” went to the site of the project “with pre-planned manner, being armed with deadly weapons like machete, sharp sticks, etc” and “trespassed” into it, “attempted to set dire” to a cement mixer there, assaulted police personnel on duty, that Doley and others “instigated the crowd” and “threatened” further agitation, among other allegations.



Bail order

In a July 29 order granting bail to Doley, an Additional Sessions Judge in Golaghat observed that there is prima facie absence of video footage demonstrating these allegations and that no “deadly weapon” has been seized by the investigating officer during the course of the investigation.

Interestingly, after ordering bail for Doley with the conditions that he cooperate with the investigation, the judge had in his order stated, “In matters where ecological preservation intersects with indigenous survival, the standard apparatus of criminal law cannot be used to suppress local anxieties. True public order is achieved not by silencing the affected, but by listening to them.”

“Therefore, while granting bail to the accused in order to ensure his personal liberty, this Court expects that the underlying grievance be addressed through structured peaceful community dialogue involving all stakeholders, rather than adversarial confrontation. It is also germane to mention here that in cases involving marginalized groups like the Tea Tribes, structural inequalities often prevent local communities from negotiating on equal terms with corporate or state entities. In such a scenario, treating the activists or community leader as ‘external disruptive element’ will not yield any fruitful result in the long run and hence, including the social activists and community leaders in the dialogue process would ensure fairness and balance in the power dynamics for a sustainable solution,” the court observed.



Preventive detention

However, while Doley was still lodged in Golaghat district jail, the state government issued an order for his preventive detention under the NSA, citing a report by the SSP of Golaghat. The order states that the government “has considered the nature, gravity, frequency and potential consequences of the activities attributed to the detenue and is satisfied that there is a real and imminent possibility of the detenue continuing to indulge in activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and security of the State, if he is not prevented from doing so.”
