World.title: Heatwave Drives Electricity Demand Growth in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Abnormally high temperatures have contributed to rising electricity consumption and increased pressure on Kazakhstan’s power system, notably during evening peak hours, according to the Ministry of Energy.

The ministry said the national energy system is operating normally, while additional demand is mainly observed during periods of maximum consumption. Higher temperatures have increased the use of cooling systems and other equipment, adding to electricity demand, reported Kazinform on July 29.

The ministry noted that weather conditions are only one factor behind consumption growth, with rising household and economic activity also contributing to the trend.

Electricity consumption in Kazakhstan has continued to increase in recent years. According to the ministry, consumption reached 57.1 billion kilowatt-hours as of July 1, compared with 48.4 billion kWh on June 1 and 43.7 billion kWh on May 1.

To manage peak demand, Kazakhstan uses electricity imports from neighboring countries when necessary. The ministry emphasized that such supplies are used only to cover temporary local shortages.

Kazakhstan is expanding generation capacity to meet future demand. The government expects the introduction of new capacities to fully cover domestic electricity demand from 2027 and create additional reserves for economic growth.

The impact of extreme heat in Kazakhstan has also extended beyond energy demand, affecting public health and daily life.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Smart City Strategy Enters New Phase Through Global AI Partnerships
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has taken a new step in its digital transformation agenda by signing an agreement with the Global Digital Economy Cities Alliance (DEC40), an international organization promoting cooperation in smart city development and the digital economy, on July 28, to advance collaboration in smart cities, artificial intelligence and regional innovation.

The partnership between the Kazakh Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and DEC40 provides opportunities to exchange international expertise, attract technology companies and investors and introduce advanced solutions in artificial intelligence, digital governance and Smart region/Smart city development.

Its success, however, will depend on how effectively international cooperation is converted into practical projects that improve public services, urban efficiency and quality of life.

Astana as a model for AI-driven urban management

Astana is becoming the main testing ground for Kazakhstan’s smart city ambitions. The capital is developing an integrated digital ecosystem combining AI, video analytics, intelligent transport systems and data-driven public administration.

A major initiative is the city’s partnership with UAE-based Presight AI. The $190 million six-year project aims to modernize existing infrastructure, expand AI-powered monitoring systems and create a digital twin of Astana by 2030.

The initiative will connect urban data systems, improve traffic management, strengthen emergency response and support more efficient city operations. At the same time, the expansion of AI-based technologies will require strong safeguards for data protection, transparency and public trust.

Creating a national smart region ecosystem

The DEC40 agreement expands Kazakhstan’s focus beyond the capital by supporting regional smart city projects. As one of the first practical steps, Kazakhstan plans to compile a list of priority Smart region/Smart city projects and present them to the DEC40 international community to attract technological solutions, strategic partners and potential investors.

This fits into Kazakhstan’s wider digital transformation agenda, which includes AI development, GovTech modernization, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure expansion and the use of technology in sectors such as energy, agriculture and logistics.

For global technology companies, Kazakhstan’s advantages include a strategic location between Europe and Asia, growing digital infrastructure and state support for innovation.

Alatau City and future urban models

Kazakhstan is also developing Alatau City as a future-oriented innovation hub. The city’s plans include AI-driven urban management, digital twins, smart city technologies and Web3 solutions.

Projects such as K-Smart City and Alatau AI-Driven City aim to create an urban environment where artificial intelligence and big data support planning, services and investment growth. Authorities have identified 53 investment projects worth around 2 trillion tenge (US$4.2 billion), expected to create approximately 51,000 jobs.

Unlike the modernization of existing cities, Alatau represents an opportunity to design a new urban ecosystem around emerging technologies from the beginning.

Turning ambition into results

Technology alone will not determine the outcome of Kazakhstan’s smart city strategy. Skilled specialists, effective governance and investment will be essential, with results ultimately measured through safer streets, improved transport, faster government services and stronger economic opportunities.

Kazakhstan’s cooperation with DEC40 is a global shift toward AI-powered urban development. The next stage will be whether these partnerships produce measurable results and help position Kazakhstan as a regional leader in smart city innovation.

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Amy V. Diaz appointed Chargé d’Affaires at US Embassy in Georgia
World.content:
The US Embassy has announced that Amy V. Diaz has been appointed Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Georgia. The announcement was published on the embassy’s official website.

According to the embassy, Diaz is a senior career member of the US Foreign Service and has served in the role since July 2026.

Who is Amy V. Diaz?

Amy V. Diaz has held a range of diplomatic and leadership positions throughout her career. Before her current appointment, she served as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim and Deputy Chief of Mission at the US Embassy in Lilongwe, Malawi.

Earlier, she worked at the US State Department’s Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs, where she was Deputy Director of the Office of Policy and Global Issues.

Diaz also headed the consular section at the US Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, and led the counternarcotics team at the US Embassy in Afghanistan.

Her previous assignments also include serving as rule of law adviser and coordinator for the Summit of the Americas at the US Embassy in Panama, chief of the internal political unit at the US Embassy in Tbilisi, and vice consul at US diplomatic missions in Harare and Monterrey, Mexico.

US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia Amy W. Diaz

Diaz joined the US State Department in 2002 through the Presidential Management Fellows programme and has been a career member of the US Foreign Service since 2005.

She holds a bachelor’s degree from St. John’s College in Annapolis, Maryland, and a Juris Doctor degree from the University of Arizona. According to the State Department, she has received multiple Superior Honor Awards and Meritorious Honor Awards in recognition of her distinguished service.

The post of US ambassador to Georgia has remained vacant since July 2025, when Robin Dunnigan stepped down. Since then, the embassy has been headed by a series of Chargés d’Affaires ad interim. Alan Purcell initially led the mission, before Amy W. Diaz was appointed US Chargé d’Affaires ad interim to Georgia in July 2026. Washington has yet to nominate a new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to the country.

Amy W. Diaz named acting US envoy to Georgia

World.title: Foreign visitor numbers and tourism revenue decline in Georgia
World.content:
The number of foreign visitors to Georgia and the country’s tourism revenue both declined in the second quarter of 2026, although visitor satisfaction and the average length of stay increased, according to a new report by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat).

Official data show that 1.3 million foreign visitors travelled to Georgia between April and June, down 5.2% compared with the same period in 2025.

Most visitors — 81.5% — were tourists, meaning they stayed in Georgia for at least one night. Same-day visitors accounted for 14.8%, while 3.8% made both same-day and overnight visits.

According to the statistics, neighbouring countries continued to account for the largest share of international visitors to Georgia. Russia remained the biggest source market, with 328,900 visitors, or 25.1% of the total. It was followed by Turkey (16.9%) and Armenia (10.8%).

The largest age group among visitors was people aged 31 to 50, who accounted for 45.6% of the total. Men made up 57.1% of visitors, while women accounted for 42.9%.

Nearly half of all visits to Georgia (49.6%) were made for holidays, leisure and recreation. Visiting friends and relatives accounted for 25.6% of trips, while 12% were made for transit purposes.

Tbilisi and the Adjara region remained the most popular destinations. The capital accounted for 36.9% of all visits, while Adjara attracted 26.2%.

The decline in visitor numbers was reflected in tourism revenue. According to Geostat, foreign visitors spent a total of 3 billion lari (around $1.11 billion) in Georgia during the second quarter of 2026, down 13.3% compared with the same period last year.

Average spending per visit also fell by 9.2% over the same period, to 1,922.1 lari (around $711.9). Visitors spent the largest share of their budgets on food and drinks (27.3%), shopping (25.2%) and accommodation (24.3%).

Despite the decline in both visitor numbers and tourism spending, foreign visitors continued to rate their experience in Georgia highly. Some 54.4% of respondents described their trip as “very satisfying”, while 38.7% said it was “satisfying”, bringing the combined satisfaction rate to 93.1%.

The Geostat report also showed that the average length of stay increased from 5.30 to 5.48 nights. Meanwhile, 81.8% of visits were made by repeat visitors, indicating that most foreign travellers who have visited Georgia at least once return to the country.

Tourism in Georgia

World.title: Nirmal Purja among climbers missing in Pakistan as rescuers find four bodies
World.content:
Four bodies have been recovered from a mountain in Pakistan during a search for 10 international climbers missing after an avalanche, according to officials.

A major search operation is underway on Pakistan's Broad Peak, in the Karakoram mountain range, to find the six other missing climbers.

But adverse weather has been hampering rescue efforts, according to the region's Chief Minister Amjad Hussain.

Broad Peak is the world's 12th-highest mountain at 8,047 meters and attracts climbers from around the globe.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan Vice President, Karrar Haidri, said the climbers lost contact with their base camp while attempting to scale the mountain on Thursday.

"We remain hopeful for the safe recovery of the missing climbers," the club said.

" The entire team has reportedly been out of communication since the avalanche. "

A mountaineering rescue team is helping search for climbers missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak. (Supplied: Alpine Club of Pakistan)

According to the alpine club, the expedition included five Nepali climbers, Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, Omani climber Nathira, American climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang and another foreign climber.

The expedition leader was the renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, a Nepal-born former soldier in the British army. widely known as Nims Dai.

Also widely known as Nims Dai, he climbed the world's 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in a Netflix documentary.

Moving Mountains, a travel company based in Pakistan, announced late last month that the expedition team was on its way to the small town of Askole and wished them a safe journey climbing Broad Peak.

Mr Purja posted on social media earlier this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 "super peaks" twice without oxygen.

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down," he wrote on X.

"I take zero mountains for granted. Not one. The moment my foot leaves basecamp, it's 100%. Always has been. Always will be.

"It's about showing YOU that your own mountains — whatever they are — are climbable."

Moving Mountains said the expedition would be Ms Geis' first try at an 8,000-meter peak in Pakistan, while it was expected to be Mr Sakhi's final one.

Mr Sakhi is a guide for the company, as well as a geographer and high-altitude photographer, and has climbed some of the world's major peaks, according to Moving Mountains' website.

Ms Geis, who lives in San Antonio, announced on social media earlier this year that she was closing her Pilates studio to take "a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes".

"I have a sneaking suspicion there will be lots of helmets, harnesses, and crampons involved," she posted.

Pakistan's Broad Peak in the Karakoram mountain range is a popular expedition for climbers. (AP)

The Nepalese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said six of the 10 climbers missing in the avalanche were from Nepal.

Nepal had "received assurances from the Pakistani authorities that they would mobilise all available resources for timely search and rescue operations", it said in a statement.

On Friday, China's government said it was trying to verify whether any of its nationals were among the 10 missing climbers.

"We will provide assistance to Chinese citizens in need and are also willing to offer help in accordance with the needs of the Pakistani side," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said.

The four bodies found had not yet been recovered, according to Pakistani security sources, who did not give details of where they were found.

Accidents are common during climbing expeditions in northern Pakistan because of avalanches and rapidly changing weather.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Infantino's advisor quits as FIFA's World Cup plan triggers backlash
World.content:
A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup on Friday, as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the controversial proposal.

Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football".

Mr Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Mr Infantino to help shape FIFA's future, said the soccer body was "mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification".

"It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game," Mr Cordeiro said in a statement.

A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Mr Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it "unequivocally".

Senior adviser to FIFA president Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also called for Mr Infantino to resign over the plans, labelling them an "outrageous".

"The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA [president] is the wrong man to lead the organisation," Mr Burnham said.

Despite the mounting opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA said "incorrect media reports" this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but that it would press on with putting the proposal in front of its 211 national football associations.

"We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (Member Association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts," it said in a statement issued in the middle of the European night.

FIFA has proposed creating a $US 20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 per cent to be offered to external investors.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

UEFA leads opposition to FIFA World Cup plan

The European football association, UEFA, has led the widespread opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

FIFA equity plan hits strong opposition FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's controversial plan to sell 20 per cent of the organisation's commercial operations to private investors hits trouble, with European nations threatening a World Cup boycott if it goes ahead.

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned World Cup champions.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA responded in Friday's statement.

"Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world.

"Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA."

CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat.

The Asian Football Confederation, comprised of 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a boycott.

The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal following an overwhelmingly negative response.

It also raised doubts over FIFA's decision-making processes in a thinly-veiled attack on Mr Infantino.

FIFA says process is a democratic one

This week, Mr Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

On Friday, FIFA said that it would not go ahead with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations.

"These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs," FIFA said.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members.

FIFA boss reveals $US20b plan to sell World Cup FIFA president Gianni Infantino earns more criticism after unveiling a brazen plan to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup.

However, not all individual member nations would be certain to follow their federations' line.

Czech Football Association President David Trunda told Sky Sports that he could see the "positive impact of FIFA's intentions", while the Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position, despite CONCACAF's rejection.

Xabi Alonso, a World Cup winner with Spain in 2010, said on Friday that football had to prioritise the people who watch the game, not private interests.

"We have to defend the interests of all the people," the Chelsea coach told reporters in Sydney.

"I think that it's the common feeling of football people that we want something that we keep in the hands of everyone, that it's for all the people. So, hopefully it won't happen."

Reuters

World.title: Hobart deputy mayor snack matter referred to police
World.content:
Hobart's city council has voted to refer the matter concerning its deputy lord mayor and the taking home of snacks to police and the director of local government.

Deputy Lord Mayor Zelinda Sherlock took home snacks and drinks meant to be consumed in the council's Elected Members' Lounge on multiple occasions, something which she has apologised for, saying she misunderstood the policy.

Some of her fellow councillors have called for further investigations and for her to step down.

Zelinda Sherlock says she will not be leaving the council. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

In newly released minutes from Monday's closed-door meeting, councillors voted 5 to 3 in favour of writing to the director of local government and Tasmania Police, noting that the council "makes no finding concerning the conduct of any person while those independent processes remain incomplete".

Zelinda Sherlock pictured with a companion in the council car park on January 10 at 10:13pm. (Supplied)

CCTV to be provided to police

Inside Hobart council's 'snack saga' Hobart's deputy lord mayor has admitted to and apologised for taking snacks and drinks from a council lounge over several years, but some of her fellow councillors won't let the matter die.

In his letter to the Office of Local Government and Tasmania Police, City of Hobart chief executive Michael Stretton said "notwithstanding previous consideration by Tasmania Police, the Office of Local Government and independent legal advisers, differing views continue to exist regarding both the conduct itself and the adequacy of the City of Hobart's response".

"Given those differing views, the ongoing public interest in the matter, the importance of maintaining confidence in local government governance arrangements, and consistent with the Council's direction, I respectfully refer this matter for any further consideration your offices consider appropriate."

Mr Stretton said the council would "continue to make available any additional records, correspondence, file notes, CCTV material, legal advice, council reports and supporting documentation should they be requested".

Louise Elliot has led the campaign to oust Cr Sherlock over the matter. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

On Friday, Councillor Louise Elliot, who has repeatedly called for Cr Sherlock to step down, said "all I have wanted is for the proper authorities … to have every snippet of evidence and for the council to ask them to take the matter seriously with their independent eyes".

"The council's resolution is pathetic, but better than nothing. Instead of showing any respect for basic governance responsibilities and saying 'This isn't right and we need you to investigate', the council has effectively just said, 'Others have told you about it … said it was a policy misunderstanding, but whatever'."

Sherlock thanks supporters

In a post to her social media on Friday, Cr Sherlock reiterated she had misunderstood council policy and that she had already been investigated over the matter.

"In January 2026, independent legal advice also concluded that no misconduct had occurred. In March 2026, Tasmania Police also concluded that there was insufficient evidence for an offence. In June 2026, the Integrity Commission also investigated and cleared me of any misconduct," she wrote.

" While no council policy was broken, I know some people are upset about it. I have unreservedly apologised to the people of Hobart. "

Cr Sherlock said she had offered to repay council for the cost of the items but "council processes mean this is difficult to coordinate, and so I've made a meaningful donation to Hobart City Mission".

"I hope the people of Hobart feel I am sincere in my apology and regret about the matter," she said.

World.title: Politics were the focus, but Bluey stole the show at Garma
World.content:
The first day of Garma Festival began with a reminder of this year's theme, "bukmak", a Yolŋu word meaning "everyone".

"I can think of no better word to put at the very centre of education, because a future that leaves a single child behind is not a future that benefits anyone in this country," National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter said on Friday morning.

The commissioner promised that she would come back to Garma every year for as long she held her role and "tell the truth about how this nation is treating our children".

Sue-Anne Hunter told the crowd Indigenous children "learn to walk in in two worlds, yet they walk in many". (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"Our children learn in two worlds, yet they walk in many," she told those gathered in Arnhem Land for the nation's largest Indigenous meeting.

"They carry language, kinship, ceremony, country in one hand and the classroom and the curriculum and the exam in the other.

"We ask a great deal of them."

On Friday young people from local schools played AFL and took part in workshops as part of the festival's education fair.

Education was the focus on Friday. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Opposition makes the most of PM's absence

Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser said the "single best thing" to improve outcomes across the board in Indigenous affairs was to get kids to attend and complete school.

Leeser says Albanese has 'lost his direction' on Indigenous affairs Shadow Indigenous Australians Minister Julian Leeser has accused the federal government of being "adrift" on Indigenous affairs during his speech at the Garma Festival.

"In Australia an Aboriginal boy is more likely to go to jail than university," he said.

"But, as I have said before, on graduation, an Indigenous graduate will earn at least on par with a non-Indigenous graduate."

Mr Leeser took advantage of Anthony Albanese's absence from the event, telling the audience that the prime minister had "lost his direction on Indigenous affairs" since the Voice referendum failed.

"We all know where the prime minister stood on the Voice," he said.

"I stood there too. But since the defeat of the Voice he just hasn't gotten off the mat."

Albanese's absence looms large over Garma The theme of this year's Garma Festival is "bukmak", a Yolŋu word meaning "everyone", but the prime minister's decision not to attend may indicate how high on the government's priority list Indigenous affairs sit.

Mr Albanese's absence from Garma this year has not gone unnoticed.

"Mob want to hear directly from our prime minister, showing leadership and the ability to come and listen," Kerrupmara and Gunditjmara man Travis Lovett told the ABC's Tahnee Jash.

"Our people — as First Peoples, but also Australians — have expectations that when politicians say they will do something, that they deliver on that."

Lia Finocchiaro announces a major Aboriginal land tenure agreement to help save the remote town of Nhulunbuy ahead of its Rio Tinto mine winding up. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro used her first keynote address at the festival to announce a major Aboriginal land agreement to help the remote town of Nhulunbuy ahead of the winding up of the Rio Tinto mine there.

As ABC Darwin's Matt Garrick reported, the announcement comes as long-term businesses prepare to sell up and leave the region, including Woolworths.

It also coincided with the 50th anniversary of the NT Aboriginal Land Rights Act.

Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy are set to address the festival on Saturday. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy have arrived at the festival and will be giving a keynote speech on Saturday.

The most popular guest at Garma on Friday was not a politician. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Bluey steals the show

The most popular guest at Garma on Friday was not a politician, but a beloved Australian dog.

One boy brought his puppy to meet Bluey. (ABC News: Dana Morse)

Bluey was welcomed onto country with a ceremonial dog dance and posed with kids and adults, including ABC Chair Kim Williams, throughout the day.

One child even brought his puppy, Rio, to meet the cartoon blue heeler.

Later tonight people will gather to watch Bluey episodes translated into Yolŋu Matha. They were produced at Yolŋu Radio's studio in north-east Arnhem Land.

Garma attendees will gather to watch episodes of Bluey that have been translated into Yolŋu Matha. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Bluey's dad, Bandit, is voiced by Dimathaya Burarrwanga, a founding member of Yolŋu surf rock band King Stingray, and her mum, Chilli, is voiced by Yolŋu educator Rosie Mununggurr.

"It was really fun to be able to put the oldest language into an actual Bluey scene," Burarrwanga told the ABC.

"I think it's really important for the Yolŋu kids to be able to understand what Bluey means."

Loading Instagram content

ARDS Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Julia Wormer said the communities across north-east Arnhem land were thrilled about the translated episodes.

"Absolutely, the kids have been so excited to watch it," she said.

"There's been so much excitement across all of the communities in north-east Arnhem Land and it's created a real sense of pride in these children.

"I have already heard from other language groups that they would love more translations in their own languages."

World.title: Freo all but seal minor premiership with hard-fought win over Bulldogs
World.content:
Josh Treacy has broken through the Western Bulldogs' flood in his 100-game milestone as Fremantle all but sealed the minor premiership with a 37-point win at Perth Stadium.

Fremantle's perfect record in Perth this season was under threat in Friday night's blockbuster after the Bulldogs' flooding tactics ensured scores were level at half-time.

(Getty Images)

But spurred on by 53,524 fans, Fremantle kicked seven goals to one in the second half to secure the 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41) win.

While key forwards Jye Amiss (0.1 from six disposals) and Pat Voss (1.0 from eight disposals) struggled in the flooded forward line, Treacy used his big frame to take some important contested grabs on the way to 3.2 and eight marks to go with 13 disposals.

Treacy's contested mark above three opponents and subsequent goal early in the final quarter gave Fremantle a 19-point buffer, and more importantly finally broke the spirit of the flood.

It sparked a four-goal burst from the Dockers as they extended their record at Perth Stadium to 11-0 this season.

The win guaranteed a top-two berth and two home finals for Fremantle (18-2).

And if Sydney (14-5) lose to St Kilda on Saturday, the Dockers will be crowned minor premiers with three rounds still remaining.

The Bulldogs (12-8) face North Melbourne, Carlton and Melbourne in their final three rounds, and they may need to win all three in order to snare a top-six berth and avoid the wildcard round.

Ed Richards (26 disposals, nine clearances, 752m gained) and Tom Liberatore (28 disposals, six clearances) racked up big numbers for the Bulldogs, while Cooper Hynes kicked two goals from 22 disposals in the absence of Aaron Naughton and Cody Weightman.

Fremantle star Luke Jackson (26 hitouts, five clearances, 16 disposals, two goals) edged Bulldogs big man Tim English (27 hitouts, one clearance, 15 disposals) in an intriguing ruck battle.

AAP

World.title: It's easy to see why Australia brought a psychiatrist to Glasgow
World.content:
When Kiana Elliott finished fourth for the second straight Commonwealth Games, to say the Australian weightlifter was crestfallen would be an understatement.

Over the Birmingham and Glasgow Games, a combined 11 kilograms of weight on the bar kept the gymnast from back-to-back bronze medals.

After faltering on the 118-kilogram clean and jerk that could have secured her third place on the podium, Elliott sat on the Armadillo stage and dropped her head to a depth only permitted by her background as an elite gymnast.

Australian weightlifter Kiana Rose Elliott after missing her last lift at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old was distraught to have missed the medals just as she did four years ago in Birmingham, graciously speaking to the media in barely a whisper as she tried to maintain her composure.

For a woman who embodies strength and power, her vulnerability was incredibly affecting.

"It's just a moment in time, and you're just hoping that everything will be there," she said.

"Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't."

Competition weightlifting is a tricky beast, with athletes having to walk a fine line between lifting the most they can, while also ensuring they can fall into the optimum weight class.

Kiana started weightlifting after an injury. Now, she's a Comm Games athlete Kiana Elliott thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but turned to weightlifting after an injury forced her to retire.

Elliott was in the 71kg weight class in Birmingham four years ago. At last year's Commonwealth Championships, she won as a 58kg competitor. In Glasgow, she lifted as a 63kg athlete.

She said it was a "really tough decision" to go up to the higher weights where the lifts need to be bigger, but she did it for her mental health.

"In Australia we do sport and we do life, and I needed my brain and my mind for the rest of my life," she said.

"Pushing my body fat down that low was not a sustainable thing for me, so I chose the competitive option.

"Weightlifting is about lifting weights, it's about lifting more weights, it's not about being a smaller person, and I'm proud that I chose the difficult option and fought my hardest.

"This isn't the end of my story. I'm not done yet."

Kiana Elliott is a study in determination while lifting. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But for this one moment it was. As painful as the result was, she could drop her shoulders and unclench her jaw in an enormous release of emotion.

"So much has gone into this and while I was hoping for a podium result, I think it's just all a culmination of all that's gone into this starting to come out," she said of her reaction after the competition.

"There's so much to process as part of this; there's more stuff to do when I get home. I think I just need to breathe a sigh of relief and move on."

It was five minutes of wholly self-aware introspection, spoken like a woman who has done and will continue to do a lot of work on her brain.

That reflects an emphasis for the entire Australian team, so much so that, for the first time, they have an in-house psychiatrist travelling with the team.

Australian team psychiatrist Adam Deacon. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Adam Deacon is part of a varied team of experts embedded within the team, with one of the floors of the Team Aus HQ effectively transformed into a mini hospital ward.

"We'd be very surprised if any other country has matched the standards that have been established here in the headquarters," Dr Deacon told ABC Sport.

"There's an extraordinary range of talented, experienced people who are able to cater to the broad needs of the athletes.

"It's really just a pop-up sports medicine clinic where all aspects are covered as it would be in a regular clinic."

The margins are fine and tension is high at meets like the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And while massage therapists, physios, nutritionists and dietitians have been working to keep Australia's 255 Commonwealth Games athletes physically fit over 10 days of intense competition, Dr Deacon is focusing on their minds.

"I think most athletes would argue when they're in a good mental space they're more likely to perform at a high level," he said.

"And you could argue they can't compete at a high level unless their mental health is well. So I think that's a necessary focus."

The team has travelled with sports psychologists before but, after consultation with the athletes, feedback was received that many of them, with their own dedicated psychologists, would like to stick with those programs.

Dr Deacon provides a different, more clinical than therapeutic, service.

"The athletes are people before they're athletes and they can experience everyday issues and concerns and mental health challenges as we all do," he said.

"There are particular things that arise in this environment, in terms of performance or lack of performance or perceived failure, and that can be really, really challenging for the athletes and also the staff.

Failure is a part of sport, but it's still hard to swallow. (Supplied)

"Injuries, illness, these sort of interruptions are not necessarily expected or anticipated, and that can be enormously stressful, and that's where an acute level of crisis response is sometimes necessary."

Unlike footy players who get to take it "one week at a time", for many the Commonwealth Games is the culmination of four or more years of tireless, single-minded work.

Elliott's teammates Chloe Perkins, who missed her 48kg weight, did not even get a chance to compete, and Brenna Kean and Ridge Barredo, both suffered nasty injuries while on stage at the Armadillo.

Dr Deacon, of course, did not reveal any of the people he had spoken to in the team, but the weightlifters like Elliott, Perkins, Kean and Barredo perhaps best exemplify the risky prospect of this high-stakes quadrennial cycle.

Some athletes seek him out, some are referred to him, and for some he attends their competition for a little extra care.

Whatever form it takes, the Australian team is lucky to have him here.

World.title: Drug driver who killed 20yo in stolen car to have sentence reduced
World.content:
The speeding drug-driver who received the maximum penalty for killing Matthew McLuckie in a head-on crash in Canberra's south four years ago will have her sentence reduced.



Warning: This story contains a confronting image of a car crash.

Shakira Adams, 24, was sentenced to 14 years' jail, with a nine-year non-parole period after pleading guilty to culpable driving causing the death of the 20-year-old in May 2022.

The ACT Court of Appeal is set to re-sentence Adams after the Director of Public Prosecutions conceded the offending did not fall within the "worst category" of culpable driving.

While both parties agreed Adams should be re-sentenced, they disagreed over how much weight should be given to her disadvantaged background, traumatic brain injury, guilty plea and new evidence about her conditions in custody.

Shakira Adams (far right) pleaded guilty to culpable driving causing death and driving a stolen car. ( ABC News: Ethan French )

Driver was unlicensed, affected by drugs

Adams was 19 when she drove a stolen car almost 20 kilometres across Canberra before crashing head-on into Mr McLuckie's vehicle on Hindmarsh Drive as he drove home from work in 2022.

The ACT Supreme Court found she was unlicensed, affected by methamphetamine and travelling at up to 186 kilometres per hour and on the wrong side of the road immediately before the crash.

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum sentenced Adams to the rare maximum penalty for culpable driving causing death, describing the offending as "one of the utmost seriousness".

She found Adams's driving had placed other road users at risk "almost every second" during the journey.

While Adams suffered a severe traumatic brain injury in the crash she caused, the court heard she continued using methamphetamine afterwards, which the chief justice said made her a "significant danger to society" and "more dangerous" than she had been at the time of the crash.

"I cannot be confident that Ms Adams would not attempt to drive if she were at liberty in the community. That is a risk that cannot be taken, and will not be taken through me," she said.

Shakira Adams was travelling at a speed of up to 186km/h, on the wrong side of the road, when the two cars collided. (ABC News)

Sentence 'excessive': defence lawyer

Adams's barrister, Kristin Edwards SC, argued the original 14-year sentence was "manifestly excessive" and said greater weight should be given to Adams's disadvantaged upbringing, youth, traumatic brain injury and prospects of rehabilitation.

She relied on new evidence, including an ACT Corrective Services report that found Adams's placement in the Alexander Maconochie Centre's management unit breached her human rights and risked exacerbating her brain injury.

She told the court her client remained housed in segregation in the management unit because she could not safely be accommodated in the general prison population, leaving her in a "punitive environment", "lonely and isolated" from other prisoners.

Ms Edwards said the unit was not designed for female inmates or long-term accommodation and was usually used as a form of punishment or protection.

Matthew McLuckie was killed in a car crash while driving home from work on May 19, 2022. (Supplied)

She argued Adams's traumatic brain injury and complex medical needs, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychiatric care, could not be adequately managed there.

The court heard Adams had experienced panic attacks and engaged in self-harm because "she hoped she'd die".

Ms Edwards argued the risks identified at Adams's original sentencing had "now crystallised".

She said hopes Adams could be transferred to a more suitable interstate facility had not materialised, and a transfer also did not guarantee she would receive better care.

Ms Edwards also challenged Chief Justice McCallum's finding that Adams remained a danger to the community, describing it as "particularly puzzling" and urged the sentencing judges to consider her adverse childhood.





Matthew McLuckie (centre) with his brother Joe and parents Amanda and Tom. (Supplied) "She's a 19-year-old who was from a disadvantaged background. She's at a very early stage to be considered someone who is beyond hope, who is beyond redemption," she said.

Reduced sentence to be handed down

Counsel for the Director of Public Prosecutions Elizabeth Ruddle SC accepted Adams's disadvantaged background and cognitive impairment reduced her moral culpability and agreed the case did not fall within the worst category of culpable driving.

However, she argued those factors did not diminish the objective seriousness of the offending.

In the nine minutes before the crash, Adams was seen travelling at extreme speeds, ran a red light, drove on the wrong side of the road and overtook other vehicles.

"Due to the appellant's extreme recklessness, a young law-abiding citizen is dead," she said.

"The driving conducted in this case was at the extreme end of culpable driving.

"Given the nature of the driving, it's surprising it took nine minutes for a fatal collision to occur."

The prosecution did not dispute the ACT Corrective Services report that found Adams's placement in the Alexander Maconochie Centre's management unit breached her human rights, but argued it was a "technical breach" that arose from her placement.

Ms Ruddle said authorities continued to pursue a transfer to New South Wales, where specialist treatment remained available, and argued Adams's rehabilitation prospects remained uncertain because of her cognitive impairment and history of dangerous driving.

Justices David Mossop, Darryl Rangiah and Andrew Muller reserved their decision, with a new sentence to be handed down at a later date.

World.title: Live: Aussie cyclists DQed from individual pursuit, boxer to fight for gold
World.content:
Simon, given your post regarding the inequality of equipment regarding Erica Sedzro of Ghana's plight in the individual pursuit , it seems a tad incredulous anyone would be disqualified for an altered helmet or clothing that somehow changes your body shape (profile I suspect).... - Mike

Hi Mike, lovely to have you with us.

Yes, you're absolutely right, it is a wild situation.

Equipment is, obviously, such a massive factor in cycling performance that the UCI are quite strict and rigid in people trying to get an advantage, they don't seem to worry about those at a disadvantage.

There are so many reasons why this might be the case, and why the equipment section of the UCI website looks like it has enough info in it to fill a library.

Of course, money is the major issue, but linked to that is the desire - and some would say need - for companies to push the boundaries of what's possible on the bike.

That in itself raises the point why they don't all ride the same bikes: the bike manufacturers.

They are all in an arms race to develop the fastest, most aerodynamic machines possible and are willing to spend thousands upon thousands of dollars to do so.

It's a tough balance for them, in fairness.

This is what the UCI says about equipment.

Bicycles and equipment used in competition across the different disciplines are at the forefront of the latest technology. The rules governing the use of equipment aim to ensure both the safety of riders and the fairness of competition while at the same time making the most of the advantages that technological evolution can bring to cycling.

I don't know if that waffling answers any questions about why there is such a wild imbalance, but you'd love to see some better tech trickle down to some of the countries where there would be a need for it.

World.title: Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage
World.content:
InspirationAntarctica Nothing in normal life can prepare you for this surreal voyage Carolyn Beasley August 1, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s difficult to think of penguins as violent. And yet, from my position in a double sea kayak between two Antarctic islands, I’m witnessing a full-blown penguin dust-up. Above us on the rocks, two gentoo penguins are flippering, slapping and scrapping in a way that looks like it might end badly. Finally, they simmer down, and our kayak group slides forward. We’re winding through a fantasy landscape straight out of a Dr Seuss picture book; an iceberg graveyard, where powder-blue ice shapes, artfully sculpted by the elements, remain trapped until they wither. The sea is glassy, reflecting mountain tops draped in a moving shawl of cloud. We pause for a moment of silence; motionless in a place so surreal that it’s difficult to process. From your first Zodiac ride to jumping into frigid water, Antarctica provides countless pinch-me moments. It’s one of countless pinch-me moments on the 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise with HX Expeditions. The journey onboard MS Roald Amundsen had promised spectacular scenery and wildlife delights, but it is the collective mood, the enthusiastic high of the passengers, that fills this trip with joy. Turns out, there’s science in this phenomenon. Psychologists have long known that when people are pushed beyond their comfort zone, physically or mentally, and they succeed, the experience delivers a strong emotional pay-off. There’s the relief of having conquered something difficult, but when the experience exceeds expectations, there is a dopamine-triggered uplift.



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zones, with every aspect of this trip being unfamiliar. Take the crossing of the Drake Passage, the 1000-kilometre-stretch of tumultuous ocean between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula. Many passengers dread it, but after surviving the two-day crossing, there’s a sense of elation. 



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zone. The feeling of awe is ever present, that mind-stretching sense of appreciating something so much bigger than yourself. The shared wonder is the ultimate icebreaker, with strangers frequently turning to each other to talk it through, processing their adventures. Most passengers view their Antarctica expedition as a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and as their bravery grows, they’re bagging as many dopamine-filled additional activities as the expedition team can offer. Choose your vessel: the Roald Amundsen, or a sea kayak? Kayaking is a popular option, and HX Expeditions offers two separate formats, both available to beginners. The first is adventure kayaking, the 1½-half-hour guided format I had experienced with the penguin brawl. This option requires moderate fitness, and the need to wear a rubber-sealed survival dry suit.



New for the 2025/26 season is discovery kayaking, a gentler format using stable, inflatable kayaks. These are easy to climb into, and guests paddle unguided within a delineated zone, watched over by four guides in Zodiacs. As I tootled around with my partner, I relished the chance to slow right down, listening to the sounds of penguins and in the distance, the cracking of glaciers. Kayak guide Lise Drejstel says if guests are concerned about their fitness or confidence on the water, then discovery kayaking is a great option. Gentoo penguins get ready for their close-up. “It’s only one hour, but you can go back after 15 minutes; it’s up to you,” Drejstel says. “You can sit out in the kayak and just look around. Don’t paddle at all, if you like.” Drejstel, in her fifth season guiding in Antarctica, says her favourite part of the job is helping expeditioners unlock awe.



“Guests come in, they start paddling, and then the first penguins come jumping,” she says. “The guests are almost screaming. I can just remember my first time down here, and I was just the same, tears in my eyes.” Those wishing to sleep outside their comfort zone are catered for, too. Conditions permitting, HX offers camping onshore in two-person tents, and in the 2025/26 season introduced the more adventurous “bivvy bag” option, a glorified swag in the snow for one. My trip takes place in late March and due to insufficient snow, neither camping activity was operating. But earlier in the season, I’m told bivvy bag campers had revelled in the solitude of staring at the southern sky, serenaded by the unfamiliar sounds of penguins. A passenger takes the plunge. Another foreign concept for many is the complete lack of a published itinerary. World.title: Treacy the key as Dockers finally beat Bulldogs flood
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Treacy the key as Dockers finally beat Bulldogs flood Justin Chadwick July 31, 2026 — 11:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Josh Treacy has broken through the Western Bulldogs’ flood in his 100-game milestone as Fremantle all but sealed the minor premiership with a 37-point win at Optus Stadium. Josh Treacy kicked three goals as Fremantle defeated the Bulldogs at Optus Stadium. Getty Images Fremantle’s perfect record in Perth this season was under threat in Friday night’s blockbuster after the Bulldogs’ flooding tactics ensured scores were level at half-time. But spurred on by 53,524 fans, Fremantle kicked seven goals to one in the second half to secure the 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41) win. While key forwards Jye Amiss (0.1 from six disposals) and Pat Voss (1.0 from eight disposals) struggled in the flooded forward line, Treacy used his big frame to take some important contested grabs on the way to 3.2 and eight marks to go with 13 disposals.



View post on X Treacy’s contested mark above three opponents and subsequent goal early in the final quarter gave Fremantle a 19-point buffer, and more importantly finally broke the spirit of the flood. It sparked a four-goal burst from the Dockers as they extended their record at Optus Stadium to 11-0 this season. The win guaranteed a top-two berth and two home finals for Fremantle (18-2). And if Sydney (14-5) lose to St Kilda on Saturday, the Dockers will be crowned minor premiers with three rounds still remaining.



The Bulldogs (12-8) face North Melbourne, Carlton and Melbourne in their final three rounds, and they may need to win all three in order to snare a top-six berth and avoid the wildcard round. Ed Richards (26 disposals, nine clearances, 752m gained) and Tom Liberatore (28 disposals, six clearances) racked up big numbers for the Bulldogs, while Cooper Hynes kicked two goals from 22 disposals in the absence of Aaron Naughton and Cody Weightman. Fremantle star Luke Jackson (26 hitouts, five clearances, 16 disposals, two goals) edged Bulldogs big man Tim English (27 hitouts, one clearance, 15 disposals) in an intriguing ruck battle. Fremantle won the inside 50m count 15-6 in the opening quarter, but their only reward for effort was a late Jackson goal as the Dockers went into the first break with a one-point lead. There was plenty of push and shove late in the second quarter when Voss gave Richards a bit of extra treatment after the Bulldogs star had been caught holding the ball by Caleb Serong.



View post on X Serong kicked the goal while Voss was in the thick of a mini melee, but Fremantle’s 12-point lead vanished in an instant as Rhylee West and Rory Lobb kicked late goals to level things up by half-time. Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce needed running repairs in the second quarter after dislocating a finger on his left hand while bravely flying into a pack for a mark. Only two goals were scored in the third quarter - both to Fremantle - and Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge cut a frustrated figure due to his team’s costly mistakes. First, Rory Lobb’s attempt to square the ball to a teammate in attack went horribly wrong, with the ball flying over Richards’ head before Laitham Vandermeer fumbled the bouncing ball.



It allowed Fremantle to swing it all the way into attack for Treacy to take a strong mark and kick a goal. Then late in the third quarter, Sam Davidson’s attempted square kick across the Bulldogs’ defence instead landed in the lap of Serong for another easy goal. It meant Fremantle’s lead was 14 points at the final change, and a powerful mark in attack to Treacy early in the last quarter proved to be the moment that broke the Bulldogs’ spirits. AAP

World.title: Bulldogs burst into top eight despite gutsy display from injury-hit Storm
World.content:
Bulldogs captain Stephen Crichton has scored two late tries to seal a 36-22 win over a brave and seriously undermanned Melbourne in an entertaining clash at AAMI Park.

The Storm threatened a famous victory for almost an hour before the surging Bulldogs stamped their authority on Friday night’s game, moving into the top eight for the first time since round six with a sixth win in their last seven games.

Loading

While the Bulldogs scored seven tries to four, the Storm were valiant in defeat.

Already without Harry Grant, Cameron Munster and Jack Howarth, they suffered another crushing blow pre-game with Jahrome Hughes a late withdrawal due to hamstring soreness.

That pushed 19-year-old star-in-waiting Hayden Watson into his NRL debut after just seven NSW Cup appearances.

Watson showed flashes of his undoubted potential in attack, kicked well and was solid in defence, despite the constant threat of Viliame Kikau, Crichton and Matt Burton on his edge.

Storm fullback Sua Fa’alogo was at his dangerous best too, scoring a try, setting up another and lighting up the game with his kick return threat. He also saved what looked like a certain Jacob Kiraz try in the first half with a last-ditch tackle.

For the Dogs, big names Kikau, Crichton, Burton and Jacob Preston all stood up at various stages, while Jaeman Salmon nabbed a double and Enari Tuala threatened constantly.

Moses Leo opened the scoring on five minutes, leaping high over Jacob Kiraz to pull in a Trent Toelau bomb.

Loading

Ten minutes later Kikau split the defence on halfway with Salmon the beneficiary, touching down under the posts to square things up.

Another deft kick from Toelau, this time a grubber for Fa’alogo, put the Storm back in the lead at the game’s quarter way mark.

The scoreboard was ticking again four minutes later when Crichton was rocked in a late tackle that landed Oryn Keeley on report, and from the resulting set of six Jethro Rinakama crossed for the Dogs.

Salmon had the Bulldogs’ third on the half hour mark, but Melbourne kept fighting, Leo crossing out wide on the stroke of half-time for a 16-all scoreline at the break.

Just a minute earlier Dogs’ hooker Bailey Hayward was sin-binned for a professional foul on Toelau.

The Storm struck seven minutes into in the second period, Angus Hinchey scoring off a Tyran Wishart break, only for Burton to toe a loose pass ahead and touchdown for the Dogs three minutes later.

When Josh Curran scored just past the hour mark the Bulldogs were back in front and after a pair of tries followed for Crichton the win was sealed.

Despite the loss, the Storm will finish the weekend still in 12th, but they are now in genuine danger of posting their worst ladder finish since their inception in 1998 – 10th, excluding the 2010 season when they were stripped of their competition points.

The name Orazio is synonymous with blistered Neapolitan-style pizza in Sydney. So it’s a surprise to find chef-restaurateur Orazio d’Elia’s new trattoria in Rushcutters Bay doesn’t serve a single slice.

Instead, the menu draws on regional specialities from across Italy, from tortelli Milanese bundled with braised osso buco ragu to cannelloncini alla Fiorentina, pasta tubes filled with spinach and ricotta and baked in bechamel. It’s also the only place in town serving ’ndujella, a custom-made mortadella infused with Calabrian chilli paste.

Given d’Elia also runs a pasticceria in Alexandria, it makes sense that you can finish with a platter of mini pastries, little lobster tails, mini maritozzo and baby baba al rum included.

World.title: Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again
World.content:
St George Illawarra 22 Dolphins 28 SportNRLNRL 2026 Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again Christian Nicolussi Updated July 31, 2026 — 8:54pm ,first published 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

You have to give St George Illawarra a bit of credit for refusing to throw in the towel, despite knowing they have already won the wooden spoon this season. The Dragons lost 28-22 against the Dolphins on Friday evening, but they were pushing for a try inside the final two minutes in the hope of sending the game in Wollongong to golden point. Loading Kyle Flanagan put up the kick at the end of an ordinary set, the Dragons kept the ball alive, then lodged a captain’s challenge when they thought the Dolphins had got a hand to the ball during the frantic play. But the bunker spotted Hamish Stewart in an offside position as he chased through Flanagan’s kick, and the Dolphins received the ball.



The Dragons have not had much luck for a lot of the year when it comes to close calls, which was pointed out by the club’s own CEO Tim Watsford last week after the club officially announced Dean Young would be the head coach. There was a moment late in the game when Isaiya Katoa knocked down a Valentine Holmes pass, and there was a suggestion the ball went forward. Katoa himself laid there and looked at debutant referee Kieren Irons to make a call. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins. Getty Images But Katoa played on, and the Dolphins scored a minute later through Tom Flegler to give them a decent lead. Dragons coach Dean Young was not too bothered by the call, especially given Irons was overseeing his first game, and was disappointed his side squandered their chances.



“There are moments we’re not icing,” Young said. “We’ll make a couple of line breaks, but not turn them into points, while the Dolphins made a few line breaks, score tries and nail them – we need to nail our opportunities when we get them.” Lyhkan King-Togia was brought into the starting halves at the expense of Daniel Atkinson, grew in confidence the longer the game went – and Young confirmed he would retain the starting role next Sunday when they host Cronulla. The Dragons celebrate Tyrell Sloan’s try. Getty Images King-Togia started to ask plenty of questions down the left edge, and came up with a ripper of a cutout ball for Tyrell Sloan that sent him down field before the play finished with Clint Gutherson getting across the line. King-Togia was also the one who went down the short side before Holmes’ pass was touched by Katoa.



“I thought he was great, I thought he defended great, he saved a tackle down on the tryline against Kuli [Finefeuiaki] who is a handful,” Young said. “He’ll only get better from here on in. Lyhkan will be five-eighth next week because of tonight’s performance.” Young added Atkinson would feature in reserve grade on Saturday, while another playmaker, Kade Reed, was a chance to return from a broken hand via NSW Cup next weekend. The Dragons trailed at half-time, but three of the Dolphins tries had come from nowhere, and inside their own half. Connelly Lemuelu’s flick pass hit the chest of Kodi Nikorima who stormed down field before he threw the final pass back in for Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to score the opening try.



Related Article Melbourne 22 Canterbury 36

NRL 2026 Bulldogs burst into top eight despite gutsy display from injury-hit Storm Jack Bostock’s pass for Selwyn Cobbo was even better, while Kurt Kurt Donoghoe brushed past some soft defence to gallop down field before the Dolphins scored the next play through Ray Stone. When young referred to his side not cashing in on their chances, there were none bigger than just after half-time when Holmes intercepted a Katoa pass, sprinted 40m, then threw a bludger of a ball for Setu Tu that dribbled another 10m forward. Tu scored a try in the first half and came up with the shot of the night on future Dragons’ teammate and Dolphins’ playmaker Kodi Nikorima. The Dragons, who have already collected the unwanted wooden gong, host the Sharks, while the Dolphins try to keep their top-four hopes alive when they host the Broncos next Saturday.
