It’s difficult to think of penguins as violent. And yet, from my position in a double sea kayak between two Antarctic islands, I’m witnessing a full-blown penguin dust-up. Above us on the rocks, two gentoo penguins are flippering, slapping and scrapping in a way that looks like it might end badly. Finally, they simmer down, and our kayak group slides forward. We’re winding through a fantasy landscape straight out of a Dr Seuss picture book; an iceberg graveyard, where powder-blue ice shapes, artfully sculpted by the elements, remain trapped until they wither. The sea is glassy, reflecting mountain tops draped in a moving shawl of cloud. We pause for a moment of silence; motionless in a place so surreal that it’s difficult to process. From your first Zodiac ride to jumping into frigid water, Antarctica provides countless pinch-me moments. It’s one of countless pinch-me moments on the 12-day Highlights of Antarctica cruise with HX Expeditions. The journey onboard MS Roald Amundsen had promised spectacular scenery and wildlife delights, but it is the collective mood, the enthusiastic high of the passengers, that fills this trip with joy. Turns out, there’s science in this phenomenon. Psychologists have long known that when people are pushed beyond their comfort zone, physically or mentally, and they succeed, the experience delivers a strong emotional pay-off. There’s the relief of having conquered something difficult, but when the experience exceeds expectations, there is a dopamine-triggered uplift.



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zones, with every aspect of this trip being unfamiliar. Take the crossing of the Drake Passage, the 1000-kilometre-stretch of tumultuous ocean between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula. Many passengers dread it, but after surviving the two-day crossing, there’s a sense of elation. 



Simply being in Antarctica places guests out of their comfort zone. The feeling of awe is ever present, that mind-stretching sense of appreciating something so much bigger than yourself. The shared wonder is the ultimate icebreaker, with strangers frequently turning to each other to talk it through, processing their adventures. Most passengers view their Antarctica expedition as a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and as their bravery grows, they’re bagging as many dopamine-filled additional activities as the expedition team can offer. Choose your vessel: the Roald Amundsen, or a sea kayak? Kayaking is a popular option, and HX Expeditions offers two separate formats, both available to beginners. The first is adventure kayaking, the 1½-half-hour guided format I had experienced with the penguin brawl. This option requires moderate fitness, and the need to wear a rubber-sealed survival dry suit.



New for the 2025/26 season is discovery kayaking, a gentler format using stable, inflatable kayaks. These are easy to climb into, and guests paddle unguided within a delineated zone, watched over by four guides in Zodiacs. As I tootled around with my partner, I relished the chance to slow right down, listening to the sounds of penguins and in the distance, the cracking of glaciers. Kayak guide Lise Drejstel says if guests are concerned about their fitness or confidence on the water, then discovery kayaking is a great option. Gentoo penguins get ready for their close-up. “It’s only one hour, but you can go back after 15 minutes; it’s up to you,” Drejstel says. “You can sit out in the kayak and just look around. Don’t paddle at all, if you like.” Drejstel, in her fifth season guiding in Antarctica, says her favourite part of the job is helping expeditioners unlock awe.



“Guests come in, they start paddling, and then the first penguins come jumping,” she says. “The guests are almost screaming. I can just remember my first time down here, and I was just the same, tears in my eyes.” Those wishing to sleep outside their comfort zone are catered for, too. Conditions permitting, HX offers camping onshore in two-person tents, and in the 2025/26 season introduced the more adventurous “bivvy bag” option, a glorified swag in the snow for one. My trip takes place in late March and due to insufficient snow, neither camping activity was operating. But earlier in the season, I’m told bivvy bag campers had revelled in the solitude of staring at the southern sky, serenaded by the unfamiliar sounds of penguins. A passenger takes the plunge. The cold compresses the air from my lungs and I surface, blurting out expletives. But then I’m climbing the ladder, accepting a towel, and I’ve done it. Instead, the menu draws on regional specialities from across Italy, from tortelli Milanese bundled with braised osso buco ragu to cannelloncini alla Fiorentina, pasta tubes filled with spinach and ricotta and baked in bechamel. It’s also the only place in town serving ’ndujella, a custom-made mortadella infused with Calabrian chilli paste.

Given d’Elia also runs a pasticceria in Alexandria, it makes sense that you can finish with a platter of mini pastries, little lobster tails, mini maritozzo and baby baba al rum included.

World.title: Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again
World.content:
St George Illawarra 22 Dolphins 28 SportNRLNRL 2026 Spoon-bound Dragons push Dolphins all the way but beaten again Christian Nicolussi Updated July 31, 2026 — 8:54pm ,first published 8:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Loading

You have to give St George Illawarra a bit of credit for refusing to throw in the towel, despite knowing they have already won the wooden spoon this season. The Dragons lost 28-22 against the Dolphins on Friday evening, but they were pushing for a try inside the final two minutes in the hope of sending the game in Wollongong to golden point. Loading Kyle Flanagan put up the kick at the end of an ordinary set, the Dragons kept the ball alive, then lodged a captain’s challenge when they thought the Dolphins had got a hand to the ball during the frantic play. But the bunker spotted Hamish Stewart in an offside position as he chased through Flanagan’s kick, and the Dolphins received the ball.



The Dragons have not had much luck for a lot of the year when it comes to close calls, which was pointed out by the club’s own CEO Tim Watsford last week after the club officially announced Dean Young would be the head coach. There was a moment late in the game when Isaiya Katoa knocked down a Valentine Holmes pass, and there was a suggestion the ball went forward. Katoa himself laid there and looked at debutant referee Kieren Irons to make a call. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins. Getty Images But Katoa played on, and the Dolphins scored a minute later through Tom Flegler to give them a decent lead. Dragons coach Dean Young was not too bothered by the call, especially given Irons was overseeing his first game, and was disappointed his side squandered their chances.



“There are moments we’re not icing,” Young said. “We’ll make a couple of line breaks, but not turn them into points, while the Dolphins made a few line breaks, score tries and nail them – we need to nail our opportunities when we get them.” Lyhkan King-Togia was brought into the starting halves at the expense of Daniel Atkinson, grew in confidence the longer the game went – and Young confirmed he would retain the starting role next Sunday when they host Cronulla. The Dragons celebrate Tyrell Sloan’s try. Getty Images King-Togia started to ask plenty of questions down the left edge, and came up with a ripper of a cutout ball for Tyrell Sloan that sent him down field before the play finished with Clint Gutherson getting across the line. King-Togia was also the one who went down the short side before Holmes’ pass was touched by Katoa.



“I thought he was great, I thought he defended great, he saved a tackle down on the tryline against Kuli [Finefeuiaki] who is a handful,” Young said. “He’ll only get better from here on in. Lyhkan will be five-eighth next week because of tonight’s performance.” Young added Atkinson would feature in reserve grade on Saturday, while another playmaker, Kade Reed, was a chance to return from a broken hand via NSW Cup next weekend. The Dragons trailed at half-time, but three of the Dolphins tries had come from nowhere, and inside their own half. Connelly Lemuelu’s flick pass hit the chest of Kodi Nikorima who stormed down field before he threw the final pass back in for Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to score the opening try.



Related Article Melbourne 22 Canterbury 36

NRL 2026 Bulldogs burst into top eight despite gutsy display from injury-hit Storm Jack Bostock’s pass for Selwyn Cobbo was even better, while Kurt Kurt Donoghoe brushed past some soft defence to gallop down field before the Dolphins scored the next play through Ray Stone. When young referred to his side not cashing in on their chances, there were none bigger than just after half-time when Holmes intercepted a Katoa pass, sprinted 40m, then threw a bludger of a ball for Setu Tu that dribbled another 10m forward. Tu scored a try in the first half and came up with the shot of the night on future Dragons’ teammate and Dolphins’ playmaker Kodi Nikorima. The Dragons, who have already collected the unwanted wooden gong, host the Sharks, while the Dolphins try to keep their top-four hopes alive when they host the Broncos next Saturday.

Ellese Andrews' disappointing Commonwealth Games campaign has continued, with the cyclist out of the medal race in the individual sprint in Glasgow.

The Olympic champion was beaten in consecutive races in a best-of-three quarter final against Welsh rider Emma Finucane.

Andrews was also part of the New Zealand sprint team that was bundled out during qualifying on Friday.

Rebecca Petch and Olivia King both were unable to get past the round-of-16 stage in their respective sprints.

On the endurance side, Bryony Botha has been given a second life in the 4000m individual pursuit following the disqualification of two Australian riders, and will now line up for bronze later Saturday morning.

Botha initially failed to qualify, placing fifth, as did team-mate Emily Shearman, who finished eighth.

However, officials said Australian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who originally finished fourth, broke protocols due to strapping on her shoulder that "altered her morphology".

Fellow Australian rider Sophie Edwards was also disqualified due to a non-compliant helmet.

Botha will face Scotland's Erin Boothman for bronze from 3.30am NZT.

Police say a seal pup that was spotted making its way through the South Auckland suburb of Papakura has been taken back to its natural environment.

Police consulted DOC about how to help the seal pup. Supplied / Counties Manukau Police

World.title: Police officer shot by Tom Phillips returns to work
World.content:
The officer who was shot in the head by Tom Phillips is returning to work.

The officer, who has not been named, was critically injured when Phillips shot him several times last September.

Phillips died shortly after a shootout with another officer, when police were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025, after 1358 days in the bush with his children.

It is understood the officer who was shot underwent numerous surgeries at Waikato Hospital, after being hit in his skull and his right shoulder.

Waikato District Commander Scott Gemmell said he had made positive progress in his recovery and was continuing rehabilitation.

World.title: Weekend weather: Snow warnings and strong wind watches as chilly days ahead
World.content:
The country is set to face a chilly weekend as subantarctic winds move up the country, MetService says.

In the South Island, temperatures will start to drop in the south on Friday morning as the southerly pushes through Otago, and then into Canterbury this afternoon, with colder temperatures expected overnight Friday and Saturday.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island mountain passes on Friday and the Desert Road on Saturday, with motorists told to avoid travel.

The mountain passes include Crown Range Road, Lindis Pass, Milford Road, Arthur's, Porters and Lewis Pass.

The Civil Defence said just a few centimetres of snow would make driving dangerous on Desert Road, and said to only do so if necessary.

MetService forecasted snow showers lowering to 800 metres and 1 to 2cm of snow could accumulate about the summit.

Meanwhile, the northern Cook Strait and the North Taranaki Bight have experienced thunderstorms.

Strong wind watches are also in place for parts of the South Island.

Coastal Otago's watch is in place from noon to 10pm on Friday, where southwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

A watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains kicks off from 5pm Friday until 1am Saturday.

The watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland kicked in late Thursday and continues until 5pm Friday.

All watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

MetService said subantarctic air was being dragged north by southerly winds - resulting in "bitterly cold conditions".

It would make temperatures feel close to -2C in Invercargill on Friday afternoon "and even colder for higher elevations".

The cold weather would move up to the North Island during Saturday, it said, "with the wind chill cooling things to a feels-like temperature of just 1C in Wellington".

For those running or on the sidelines at the Taupō marathon, meteorologist Braydon While suggested dressing warm.

"Those preparing for the marathon, whether competing or cheering on the sidelines, will want to wrap up warm and bring a cosy jacket in case a few showers manage to sneak over the hills."

Sunday would bring clear skies for most of the country, MetService said, and "widespread frosts".

World.title: Silver Ferns to meet England in Commonwealth Games semi-finals
World.content:
The Silver Ferns will have to beat England in the semi-finals in Glasgow if they are to make their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014.

England will have their tails up after putting up their best performance in Glasgow by far with a 58-54 win over the fifth-ranked South Africa on Friday morning.

Anticipation was high that South Africa would pull off an upset over the third ranked England Roses in the last pool match of the tournament.

Earlier in the week, the Diamonds posted a 19-goal win over England, before beating South Africa by a 10-goal margin.

With South Africa beating England 2-1 in a series earlier in the year, Pool A was always considered the 'Pool of Death'.

The Silver Ferns topped Pool B earlier in the day after demolishing Trinidad and Tobago 83-23 to make it five straight wins.

Australia went through Pool A unbeaten, and will meet Jamaica in the second semi-final at midnight Saturday evening. The Silver Ferns and England will meet at 8pm Saturday New Zealand time.

The New Zealanders were reduced to 10 players for their final pool match with young defender Catherine Hall awaiting a MRI scan to determine the extent of a knee injury suffered in the previous match against Wales.

Shooter Georgia Heffernan was also left off the team sheet after suffering an ankle knock in the same match but coach Dame Noeline Taurua said Heffernan would be available for selection for the semi-final.

At the 2023 Netball World Cup, the Silver Ferns suffered a massive blow when strike shooter Grace Nweke suffered a tournament ending injury in pool play. The Ferns finished outside of the medals in fourth.

Taurua said selectors picked a versatile squad.

"We're always looking at the depth and making sure that if an injury happens or people can't take the court, we've already got the depth and we knew that in each position we've got three deep," Taurua said.

"The positive is that we're in towards the business end. We're not at the beginning, so we've got fresh legs and that's why those combinations and the changes that we've made earlier in the tournament, we've got something in our back pocket."

The 10 players were rotated throughout the match as New Zealand went on to post their highest score and biggest winning margin in 24 outings against a poor Trinidad & Tobago.

The Silver Ferns went through pool play unbeaten, with earlier wins over Scotland, Jamaica, Uganda, and Wales.

The Proteas boast one of the best shooters in the world in Elmeré van der Berg, who scored the most goals in her debut season in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition this year.

South Africa came out strong to win the first quarter 17-11 but a defensive change for England saw them mount a fight-back in the second spell.

Coming on at goal keep Halimat Adio applied all kinds of pressure on van der Berg and put doubt into the feeders minds.

At half-time, South Africa held a slim 29-28 goal lead.

South Africa lost their starting wing attack to a head knock in the third quarter, which disrupted the Proteas attacking end.

England ramped up their efforts in the third quarter, to lead by four going into the final turn.

Liv Tchine and Lois Pearson combined brilliantly in the England shooting end.

Pearson has stepped up brilliantly into the goal attack position, with the England Roses missing the experienced Helen Housby through injury.

The Roses also lost impressive defender Jaz Brown in the lead-up to the event to injury but Adio's efforts against South Africa show what she is capable of.

The Silver Ferns and England have played out some tight matches in recent years.

England beat New Zealand on their way to finishing runners up at the 2023 World Cup to Australia.

World.title: El Niño could bring a 'highly unusual warm' spring
World.content:
A scientist says El Niño could bring an 'highly unusual warm' spring to New Zealand.

El Niño was officially declared at the start of July and could strongly influence the upcoming seasons.

Earth Sciences New Zealand's chief scientist Chris Brandolino said they expect more profound and more noticeable weather conditions beyond 1 September.

"We're expecting to see more westerly pipe winds, so that could be maybe northwest or southwest or somewhere in between," he told RNZ.

"We're expecting it to become more persistent, more regular, and more intense with time."

Rainfall for lower South Islands, dry spells for North

He said that did favour increased rainfall for the western and lower part of the South Island.

Meanwhile, Brandolino said the upper North Island and many other parts of the country were at risk of dryness.

He said areas such as Northland, the Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Waikato, Auckland would most likely receive below normal rainfall.

"In terms of temperatures over the next three months, we think in spite of a pretty cold start to the August month, there will be some pretty chilly mornings over the next, probably four to nine days, the first week of August roughly," Brandolino said.

"But that won't be a theme, we think, when we look at the three-month period as a collective, as in its totality. We think temperatures are probably going to end up being somewhere between the average or even above average category for the next three months."

Brandolino said the hottest temperature recorded in New Zealand was 42.4 degrees in 1973.

He said that was during a "super El Niño", which is what we are experiencing now.

"El Niño is expected to become very strong, or so-called super El Niño in intensity. So, I'm not predicting a new national record, don't get me wrong, that's not my prediction," Brandolino said.

"But I'm just sort of making the linkage that when we have these westerly winds and we have El Niño, because of these westerly winds, that does cause Australia to go through these hum spells, or at least increased risk of these hot spells of weather or heat waves.

"When our air or our wind does come from Australia, that will bring it into New Zealand, that will happen."

Weather events harder to predict

Brandolino said there would be an increase in spiky temperatures.

He said that could see periods of one to three days of "highly unusually warm" temperatures for September, October and beyond.

"That's followed up by perhaps a big sharp downturn in temperature. So, big variability, roller coaster type weather.

"But when our winds align, so that it's kind of plugging air from Australia, and if their air is warm, we're going to get that warm air."

Brandolino said the odds particularly favoured spells of unusually warm temperatures for eastern areas of both islands.

Whether or not that translates into a record or not, we'll have to wait and see, but it certainly loads the dice for those outcomes, he said.

He said climate change was making it harder to use historical weather events to predict the future.

"Ordinarily we'd like to say we know the average outcome of El Niño, but no El Niño is average," Brandolino said.

"So, we know the average outcome and when you throw in climate change, that does tend to underscore that statement.

World.title: Almost 1000 medals reunited with families yet Ian's own search continues
World.content:
Returning medals to the relatives of New Zealand servicemen First Up Download MP3 4m

Ian Martyn has returned almost a thousand military medals to the relatives of New Zealand servicemen, but the medals that started his quest continue to elude him.

Despite his own extensive military record that stretches from 1970 to 2007, Martyn didn't get involved in returning medals until after he retired.

His initial interest was sparked in 2010, when he discovered the identity of his great-grandfather, Private Jack Sullivan.

Sullivan served in the Australian Army during the First World War. He survived the Gallipoli campaign but was killed at the Battle of the Somme in 1916.

"I was pretty keen to know whether or not any medals or any of his paraphernalia or memorial bits and pieces still existed because all the family were dead, bar me."

Martyn's search resulted in him founding Medals Reunited New Zealand, after encountering a massive volume of medals belonging to Australian and NZ servicemen.

"There was probably a hell of a lot of people like me out there that would dearly love to have their own family's medals return, and so I thought I could link both projects together," he said.

"If I was in the business of returning medals, that might spawn somebody offering up medals that perhaps were my great-grandfather's."

However, while Martyn has now successfully returned almost a thousand medals to the families of former service personnel, Private Sullivan's have remained out of reach.

"Nothing has turned up to date in 15 odd years, but I remain ever hopeful."

Medals come to Martyn in a variety of ways, and some he even uses his own money to secure.

"I'm of the opinion you can't take it with you," he said.

"If I spent it all and it meant the medals went back to families, and that they cherish having them, that to me is a total win."

Some are sent in to Martyn, people finding them anywhere from op shops to auction sites or even old cars.

Martyn said a World War II Memorial Cross had just been sent to him by a person who had came into its possession when they bought a car via Trade Me.

He said the medal had been awarded to an airman who was killed in a bomber aged 22. "So that is now off on its way back into the hands of his nephew, who's about 92 at this point."

One of his highlights had been returning another Memorial Cross, awarded to an airman who died in the same action that saw the Victoria Cross awarded to Flying Officer Lloyd Trigg.

Only nine New Zealanders had been awarded Victoria Crosses - the military's highest award for valour - during World War II.

Trigg's was awarded for sinking a German submarine despite his Liberator bomber aircraft being heavily damaged and on fire. Trigg and his crew died when they crashed into the sea.

"It was as a result of the submarine commander's after-action report, that actually secured the VC posthumously for Trigg," Martyn said.

The Memorial Cross was returned to a relative, who still had the paperwork that had been issued with it.

"When I took the Memorial Cross down to meet him and he produced the certificate, I was absolutely blown away."

Martyn doesn't just return medals and paraphernalia either. He's also helped expose people for wearing military medals they're not entitled to - a deception known as "stolen valour".

"It's kind of grown out of my own distaste for these people, and the fact that I was a disciplinarian in the military myself and had a significant background in the knowledge of that.

"I certainly don't pull any punches when I 'out' somebody, and we had a particularly successful one down at the Rolleston RSA. But that sort of thing, really irks me."

Fortunately, Martyn believes the practice is declining, despite New Zealand having lighter penalties than elsewhere.

As for his commitment to returning medals to their rightful owners, Martyn says won't stop when he reaches a thousand.

"That would be a nice milestone to reach" he said. "I think the last post I put on was 982. Well, it's 988 now. I'm closing in.

World.title: 'We're not going to the finals': Storm set for 16-year first after loss
World.content:
Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy has conceded his side will not be playing finals in 2026, with the club set to miss out for just the fourth time in its history.

The Storm entered the round 22 clash needing to win all five of their remaining games to finish the season on 32 points, which has been needed to make two of the past three finals series.

Missing captain Harry Grant, five-eighth Cameron Munster, and halfback Jahrome Hughes ruled out 90 minutes before kick-off, the Storm threatened a famous upset win when they led 22-16 early in the second half.

But the Bulldogs rallied with the final four tries of the match to record a sixth win in their last seven matches, and leapfrog North Queensland into the NRL top-eight.

The loss ends Melbourne's realistic chance of making the top eight, but Bellamy said he will not be accepting a drop in standards during the final month of the home and away season.

Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy (left) says his side will not be playing finals in 2026. (NRL)

"If anyone wants to go through the motions, if I see that at training and feel that at training, they won't be playing first grade," he said on Friday.

"At the end of the day, every game is important. It's not quite as important as it has been the last few years because we're not going to the finals now.

"But we're out there to play for each other and play for our fans."

The Storm have only missed finals three times since their inaugural season in 1998. The Victorian club missed finals in 2001 and 2002, the two seasons prior to Craig Bellamy becoming head coach.

Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years The Roosters have scored the third-most points ever seen in Australian rugby league first grade match and beaten the clock against a hapless North Queensland side.

The only time the Storm have not made finals under Bellamy was in 2010, when the club was not allowed to earn premiership points as punishment for salary cap breaches which led to the stripping of the 2007 and 2009 premierships.

The Storm, who have lost the previous two grand finals, have been one of the league's most injury-affected teams in 2026.

Several players have made their NRL debuts this year for the Storm, including playmakers Hayden Watson and Jai Bowden on Friday night.

Bellamy, who is contracted until the end of the 2028 season, said the tough results the club is going through now will hopefully be worth it in coming seasons.

"We haven't got a lot of that experience playing at the moment, with these guys making their debuts or it's their third or fourth game," Bellamy said.

"But next year and the year after, that experience will be really handy for us.

"It's just hard to see past the results at the moment of our games."

Earlier, the Dolphins consolidated fifth place on the NRL ladder with a nervous 28-22 win over the last-placed St George Illawarra Dragons.

World.title: Magpies coach throws support behind Bobby Hill as star exits
World.content:
Collingwood's Bobby Hill has exited the club amid support from coach Craig McRae after the premiership hero was racially abused on social media.

Meanwhile Geelong has confirmed its own mutually arranged split with 2022 flag forward Tyson Stengle.

The Magpies have formally split with Hill, cutting short the 26-year-old's bumper contract, which was due to expire at the end of 2030.

"I'm going to take a break from football to keep working on myself and regain my passion for the game," Hill said in a statement released by the Magpies today.

Hill was the star of Collingwood's 2023 premiership under coach Craig McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal for a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But having taken stretches of personal leave, he hasn't played at AFL level for almost a year — making just three VFL appearances in 2026.

On Thursday, before the Pies lost to Geelong at the MCG, Hill shared on Instagram a vile direct message from a Collingwood supporter that included a racist slur among other insults.

"You have disappointed this whole club and it's (sic) 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months," the account also posted.

"… I hope nothing but the worst for you."

Hill posted a screenshot of the message and captioned it "anyone know this tough guy?"

The Magpies have publicly supported Hill throughout his turbulent period, and McRae again expressed his care for the forward's wellbeing — and disgust at those posting abusive comments on social media.

"Bobby, our thoughts are with you," McRae said after the MCG defeat on Thursday night.

"Not just for Bobby — what's going on? It's a crazy place at times, isn't it?

"I don't do social media, so bear with me, but I did look on a website which had feedback, and the feedback is unbelievable.

"It's just a cesspool for people just to vent. I find it fascinating that's actually something that people would be interested in.

"If Bobby's listening there, I'm sorry to hear that's the case. We'll always love him. It's sad to hear that."

This morning, the Pies' football manager Charlie Gardiner confirmed the end of Hill's contract.

"The club has been working with Bobby over the past 12 months to put support structures in place to help him work through some personal matters," Gardiner said in a statement.

"Despite this, Bobby has unfortunately struggled to meet his commitments to the club consistently this year and agreed that taking a break from football is the best decision for him and his family."

Meanwhile, the Magpies are counting the cost of Thursday night's loss with veteran defender Jeremy Howe suffering a fractured arm.

It is the same arm that he broke horrifically after a nasty landing from an aerial contest, also against Geelong, in 2023.

"The likelihood is he'll probably need an operation," McRae said post-game.

Utility Harry Perryman suffered a left hamstring injury — having strained his right hamstring earlier in the season.

And Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos has a bruised right foot, but he played out the game.

Stengle agrees Cats departure

Geelong meanwhile formally cut ties with Stengle, who said he has chosen to step away from AFL football and return home to South Australia after a difficult year.

Stengle, 27, still had three years left on a bumper five-year extension signed in 2024.

Tyson Stengle's last AFL game for Geelong was the 2025 grand final defeat to Brisbane. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But the Cats confirmed on Friday they had reached a mutual agreement with Stengle and finalised it with his management and the AFL Players' Association.

The forward played only one VFL game this season amid off-field issues, and last played at the top level in Geelong's 2025 AFL grand final loss.

"Geelong Football Club gave me another chance to play at the highest level and achieve a lot of highs and lows and to win a premiership and All Australian in 2022 will forever be my greatest achievements I would have never thought I would have done," Stengle said in a post on Instagram.

"But after a tough year or so I have made the decision to step away from AFL football and move home and be with family where I feel more comfortable. It was a tough decision but it was the best decision for me mentally.

"I will always be grateful for playing at the top level and playing in the biggest games of them all, it was always fun and exciting.

"Thank you to everyone who has supported along the way."

World.title: How a classification change ended Korey's Commonwealth Games hopes
World.content:
As the track cycling competition at the 2026 Commonwealth Games gets underway, Australians expecting to see Paralympic champion Korey Boddington in action will be left disappointed.

The popular para cyclist, who won the kilometre C4-5 time trial in Paris, has joined swimmer Alexa Leary as another high-profile para athlete removed from the Glasgow Games after a reclassification of his disability.

Leary, the reigning S9 100m world record holder, was to make her Commonwealth Games debut in Scotland but was reclassified as an S10 athlete earlier this year.

Partly due to the stripped-down nature of these Games, there are no sprint freestyle events for S10 swimmers at the Tollcross pool, with the only event in that category being the 200-metre individual medley, which Leary does not compete in.

Boddington, the reigning Sir Hubert Opperman Trophy winner and 2025 Australian cyclist of the year, was also reclassified, twice in the space of a year, first becoming eligible to compete, and then ineligible.

Boddington's year as a C3 athlete

Korey Boddington is the world record holder in the kilo at C3 and C4 classifications. (Supplied: Cycling New Zealand)

Classification for para athletes has long been a contentious and complicated issue.

The process exists in para sport to enable athletes with different impairment types — not necessarily the same disabilities — the chance to compete on a relatively level playing field.

"International classification is conducted by a panel comprising medical classifiers and technical classifiers before a competition, after which they will be informed which class they are in and why," AusCycling told ABC Sport in a statement.

"Their role is to assess whether an athlete has an eligible impairment that meets the minimum impairment criteria for Para cycling, assess the extent to which the athlete is able to execute the specific tasks and activities fundamental to Para cycling, and, where required, undertake observation in competition assessment."

Within the classification framework imposed by the sport's governing body, the UCI, Boddington — who won two Paralympic medals as a C4 athlete — was, briefly, reclassified as a C3 athlete in 2025.

This indicates a higher level of impairment than under which he competed in Paris. In cycling, the scale is from 1-5, where 1 is the most severe impairment and 5 the least.

This is not uncommon.

Boddington only made his first national team appearance in the Paralympic year of 2024.

He endeared himself to the Australian public with his love of burritos, enjoying up to four of them a day: "You know how many carbs are in the wrap, and you can specifically portion out all your protein that are on them," he told AusCycling in 2025 by way of explanation.

It earned him the affectionate nickname the Flying Burrito.

Korey Boddington was a breakout star of the Paris Paralympics. (Getty Images: PA Images/Andrew Matthews)

For an athlete like Boddington, who lives with an acquired brain injury and had not spent all that long in the sport, it is understandable that his classification level was still being sorted out.

But having been reclassified, Boddington promptly won four world championship gold medals as a C3 athlete at the 2025 world championships in Rio, winning the men's sprint, 1,000-metre (kilo) time trial and elimination race before helping Australia clinch victory in the mixed C1-5 team sprint.

The 30-year-old Queenslander, the world record holder for the C4 flying 200m sprint time trial, also broke world records in the C3 flying 200m sprint and the C3 kilo at the Oceania Championships in Cambridge, New Zealand in February this year.

He won four gold medals in total at those championships: the kilo, sprint, individual pursuit and mixed C1-5 team sprint, as well as winning silver medals in the elimination and scratch races.

All signs were pointing towards Boddington competing in the C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events at the Games in Glasgow.

However, upon his return from New Zealand, Boddington was reclassified a C4 athlete and competed in that category at the TrackNats in Brisbane in late March.

Boddington still won gold in the sprint, elimination, scratch, kilo and C1-C5 team sprint at the Anna Meares Velodrome.

However, there are only four men's para cycling events set to be contested on the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow; none of which C4 athletes are eligible for — the sprint and 1,000m time trial in the tandem B category, and the 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events in the C1-3 classification.

Classification can be 'tough'

Korey Boddington won gold in the men's C4 1,000m time trial at the 2024 Paralympic Games in Paris. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Being rubbed out of a major competition like the Commonwealth Games, the only multi-sport event where able-bodied and para athletes compete on the same program, through no fault of their own, is a bitter pill for the athletes to swallow.

And classification can be a very sensitive and personal process.

A Four Corners investigation in 2023 found that some Paralympic athletes were deliberately exaggerating their impairments in a bid to win medals and that the system itself was ripe for manipulation.

Australians embroiled in Paralympics scandal Former athletes and officials tell Four Corners the system of Paralympic classification is flawed and easily manipulated.

AusCycling said it took care to ensure that its athletes are educated about classification throughout their time in the sport.

That takes the form of education about the classification system itself, guidance from classification experts, discussion of possible classification outcomes, and planning for different scenarios.

"The focus is on ensuring athletes understand the UCI Classification Rules, including eligible impairments, sport class profiles and assessment methods, while continuing to focus on their development and performance goals," the statement read.

The statement also noted that "not all classification outcomes can be anticipated, particularly for more complex impairment profiles".

Classification for para athletes can take place over the course of an athlete's career to ensure they are in their correct category for competition.

They may also have to be tested if the criteria for their classification change or if the governing body changes its tests. In cycling, that falls under the UCI's jurisdiction.

When a classification panel allocates a sport class to an athlete, it also assigns a status to that status: confirmed, review at the next available opportunity, review with a fixed review date or expired.

Needless to say, most athletes have to go through the process multiple times during their career.

Double world champion Tara Neyland detailed the process of classification. (Supplied: AusCycling)

Two-time world champion on the road and three-time track world champion Tara Neyland, who is also competing in the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome at these Games, said in a detailed Instagram video in May that classification days can be incredibly tough.

Neyland lives with facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness, which means her level of impairment is likely to change over time.

"Being a progressive degenerative condition, they need to keep reassessing as my body will keep changing," Neyland said in her Instagram video.

AusCycling noted that in instances such as Neyland's, athletes can request a medical review, but it is not imposed by AusCycling out of competition if it is against the athlete's wishes.

Regardless, the process is clearly incredibly emotionally draining for the athletes involved.

"Classification day is a tough one," Neyland said.

"Essentially you're being assessed, being graded, for your level of impairment of your condition, disability, injury, whatever it may be, however you define it.

"It can bring up a lot of emotions.

"It's a necessary part of para sport so that we can be as fairly graded as possible, but it's still quite challenging.

"For me, until coming into para sport, I've tried to view myself as someone who's incredibly capable, and then to flip the mindset and have to prove your level of impairment and speak to all your challenges and struggles and areas that, for me, weaken, struggle to do the same things that an able body can do is hard."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

AusCycling said it was committed to helping athletes with any issues that arose from classification changes.

"Ultimately, classification exists to protect the integrity and fairness of Para sport," AusCycling's statement read.

"While the prospect of reclassification can be challenging, particularly given its potential impact on competitive opportunities and performance goals, AusCycling remains committed to prioritising athlete wellbeing and supporting athletes' continued performance throughout the entire process.

"Athlete wellbeing remains a key priority throughout any classification review process, whether anticipated or unexpected.

"Appropriate support is identified both on the ground and remotely to ensure athletes are well supported throughout the process."

World.title: 'It was weird': De Minaur beats Hewitt in Aussie tussle
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has cast aside sentiment to end Cruz Hewitt's breakout run and storm into the Washington Open quarter-finals.

The top seed and defending champion produced a clinical display to defeat the 17-year-old Hewitt, son of former world number one Lleyton, 6-2, 6-3 in just 61 minutes.

De Minaur shared a warm embrace with Hewitt at the net as Lleyton looked on from the stands at Stadium Court.

"It was definitely weird," de Minaur said.

"I knew I was going to play him on the tour some day, but I didn't actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling."

Cruz Hewitt has breakthrough Tour win Cruz Hewitt wins for the first time at ATP Tour level, his Washington upset of former world number 37 Marcus Giron set to rocket him up the tennis rankings.

A Wimbledon boys' finalist this month, Hewitt idolised de Minaur while growing up around the Davis Cup team captained by his father.

"Even [with] all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together and how we've grown up, I'm glad I managed to get through," de Minaur said.

"But I'm sure we're going to have many battles in the years to come."

Australia's world number six charged to the net with authority and displayed great hands en route to improving his win-loss record to 29-14 this season.

Despite his defeat, Hewitt is set to soar some 252 spots in the rankings to a fresh career high of about world number 360 after qualifying in Washington and then winning his maiden ATP match.

Competing for the first time since marrying British WTA star Katie Boulter this month, de Minaur next faces American Brandon Nakashima, who ousted seventh-seed Jakub Mensik 7-6 (5), 3-6, 6-4 to reach his second consecutive Washington quarter-final.

Nakashima holds a 2-1 edge over the Australian, with de Minaur's lone win against the American also coming in last year's quarter-finals before he went on to lift the title.

AAP

World.title: England hires NZ's Fleming to coach men's Test side, Root as captain
World.content:
English cricket has turned to another New Zealander to coach the men's Test team, hiring former Kiwi star Stephen Fleming, while batting great Joe Root has been reappointed as captain.

Fleming replaced his former teammate Brendon McCullum, who was fired after losing the Ashes series in Australia 4-1 over the winter and, last month, losing at home to New Zealand 2-1.

England now has an all-New Zealand coaching set-up, with McCullum remaining in charge of the one-day and Twenty20 teams.

Fleming will not take charge until after Pakistan's three-Test tour, which begins on August 19 in Leeds. McCullum's former assistant, Marcus Trescothick, will be the interim England coach for that series.

Root was previously the permanent Test captain from 2017-22 in a national record 65 Tests. He won a record 27 of those matches but has won only one of his past 18 in charge.

The 35-year-old Root formally replaces Ben Stokes, who retired suddenly from international cricket after the New Zealand series in June. Stokes had endorsed his vice-captain, Harry Brook, as the next captain.

McCullum sacked as Test coach The architect of England's controversial Bazball approach to Test cricket is given his marching orders after a disappointing string of results.

Fleming said he was excited to work with Root and Brook, adding: "I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll."

Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving captain across 80 Tests and he won 28 of them. He played for three English county teams and won a league title with Nottinghamshire in 2005.

"English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back," he said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said it was allowing Fleming to spend time with family as he stepped down from his role at the Chennai Super Kings only this month.

Fleming led Chennai to a record five titles and 10 finals in the Indian Premier League. He also coached sister franchises in South Africa and the United States.

He will prepare England for three Tests in South Africa in December-January.

Fleming has only seven Tests in charge to ready England for the home Ashes series next year.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Tongan dance moves bring joy, David Beckham hits the velodrome
World.content:
A para athletics race will be run again amid much drama, a Tongan weightlifter thrills the crowd with his dancing, and Nigeria wins the fashion stakes at the velodrome.

Here are the quick hits from day seven of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Para athletics race to be re-run

Eliza Ault-Connell's crash in the first running of the women's 1500m T54 final prompted the re-run. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

After a dramatic crash that took out two athletes, a disqualification that reordered the medal spots, and a subsequent protest, para athletics officials ordered a re-race of the women's 1,500m T54 final.

The race was thrown into chaos early on when Australian Eliza Ault-Connell went down heavily in a nasty crash, with Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse also knocked out of contention.

Canadian Nandini Sharma, who went on to finish second across the line, was disqualified for causing the crash.

After having that medal taken off her, Australia's Mikaela Dingley was promoted into the bronze medal position.

However, Australia and Mauritius protested the decision and, after Athletics Canada's appeal was dismissed, authorities decided to re-run the race, with some commentators saying it should have been stopped at the time of the crash.

Sharma will not be able to take to the start, with Canada saying it was "disappointed" in the decision.

"Having considered the multiple appeals that were submitted, the Jury has decided that the disqualification will stand," the statement read.

"While Athletics Canada is disappointed with this decision, we accept the process and look forward to Nandini competing again in the T53/54 400m race."

The re-race will be held on Friday 7:24pm AEST.

2. World record falls

Tara Neyland broke her own C4 4,000m Individual Pursuit world record. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australian para cyclist Tara Neyland laid down a stunning time to top qualifying in the women's C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit qualifying, setting a world record.

Her factored time was 4:45.796, achieved at an average speed of 49.716km/h.

Neyland later returned to the track to win gold in the final.

The 32-year-old is already a three-time world champion on the track and a two-time world champion on the road.

The women's individual pursuit distance officially moved from 3,000m to 4,000m on January 1, 2025, so competing at this distance is still relatively new.

Which perhaps accounts for England's Morgan Newbury breaking the world record in the C5 classification qualification period.

3. Tonga's dancing weightlifter

Josh Uikilifi treated spectators to his best dance moves. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

If weightlifting medals were handed out for post-lift moves, Tonga's Joshua Uikilifi would have topped the podium.

Uikilifi had the SEC Armadillo crowd eating out of the palm of his hand as he competed in the men's 110kg classification.

He treated spectators to some spectacular dance moves after each successful lift.

Uikilifi produced a total of 331kg to finish fourth behind Fiji's Taniela Rainibogi, who won gold with a Games record of 378kg.

4. Nigerian para cyclists turn heads

The Nigerians were the best dressed at the velodrome on day seven. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australia dominated the medals on the opening day at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, but it was Nigeria which turned heads.

The Nigerian para cyclists hit the track in eye-catching uniforms, reportedly inspired by the kit worn by the national men's football team at the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Oyindamola Abdullahi Tijani and pilot Okeyah Bethel looked magnificent as they contested the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

They deservedly got the seal of approval across social media platforms.

For the record, Tijani and Bethel finished fifth in the final.

Scotland's Neil Fachie (pilot: Aaron Pope) won gold ahead of James Ball (Matthew Rotherham) of Wales.

Australia's Kane Perris (Luke Zaccaria) took bronze.

5. Ronaldo and Beckham in the velodrome

If you thought the only sightings of David Beckham and Ronaldo at a major global sporting event were going to be in North America this year, then we have news for you.

Yes, that's right, David Beckham and Ronaldo were at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow, a stone's throw away from the footballing theatre of Celtic Park.

Well, David Beckham Elkatohchoongo and Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam were there, joining Rojit Singh Yanglem in India's team sprint squad.

"My father was a footballer in the national team, and he was a huge fan of David Beckham," Elkatohchoongo told AFP in 2023 at the Asian Games.

"When I was born in the hospital, they told my mum: if it's a boy, then it's David Beckham."

Laitonjam was also named after a footballer, not actually Ronaldo but Ronaldinho.

His father had, according to AFP, made a bet with his work colleagues that the Brazilian would score against England in the 2002 World Cup match they were watching.

The Barcelona legend promptly did, and minutes later Laitonjam senior received a phone call telling him that his wife was in labour.

"Just as the ball went in the goal, I must have started making an appearance," Laitonjam told The Hindu newspaper.

"I think my dad won some money that day. That's probably why I got that name. He felt I was very lucky for him."

David and Ronaldo could not add the necessary star power to the Indian team their namesakes may have demanded, though, finishing seventh and last in qualifying.

World.title: 'Never for sale': European nations vow World Cup boycott over FIFA plan
World.content:
European nations have agreed to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions in protest over president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in soccer's biggest tournament to private equity investors.

"UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 member nations.

On a seismic day in soccer politics, support in Asia and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) for FIFA and Infantino was also shaken.

The next scheduled FIFA tournament is in weeks in Europe — the Women's Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 — and the four British federations comprise FIFA's only bidder to host the 2035 Women's World Cup. That decision is due on November 23.

"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

The strategy meeting was called to counter Infantino's offer of $US20 million ($28.45 million) to each of FIFA's 211 global members, which has to be accepted by mid-September.

Infantino's secret project to spin off its commercial operations in a new $US20 billion ($28.45 billion) subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), 20 per cent owned by private investors was revealed on Tuesday.

The core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Infantino wrote to the 211 members — already the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law — that if they approved FFE, their promised $US10 million basic funding for the next four years would double to $US20 million. He projected their FIFA funding through 2038 would be $US86 million ($122 million) each, instead of about $US36 million ($51 million).

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football," said UEFA, where Infantino was a staffer and its CEO-like general secretary when he was first elected to lead FIFA in 2016.

Infantino's high-stakes gambit now could threaten his previously secure 11-year presidency of FIFA as anger and frustration with him rise among soccer stakeholders, including three of the six continental bodies.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in a presidential vote of the 211 members scheduled next March in Rabat, Morocco.

Infantino had seemed after the World Cup to have a clear path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office until 2031, despite a furore over letting United States forward Folarin Balogun play against Belgium after a red card in his previous game.

"Game over, Gianni #InfantinOUT," the Football Supporters Europe group, which advises UEFA on fan issues such as ticket prices, posted after the boycott threat.

UEFA detailed why soccer officials fear external investors owning a stake in the global game's biggest events, including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever," UEFA said. "Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure."

Infantino has presented the private equity offer as a chance to "turbocharge" funding development of soccer across the world, where a majority of the 211 FIFA members rely on its funding.

Officials from about 40 UEFA members spoke at the urgent meeting, with anger expressed that FIFA is not using some of its multi-billion-dollar reserves to fund extra development programs.

"As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive," the European soccer body said, "unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership."

CONCACAF also released a statement saying its organisation was built on service, "transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football".

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," it said.

Deep concerns were raised about the lack of due process, the short deadline imposed, the lack of review or approval by relevant bodies, and the need for private investment to fund programs.

"For these reasons, CONCACAF and its 41 Member Associations have rejected the proposal," it said.

The associations called on their FIFA Council Members to engage FIFA to determine how existing reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across the region, and urged that all matters follow proper governance processes.

CONCACAF did not threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions. However, Europe's 55 associations and CONCACAF's 41 would make nearly half of the 211 total votes available.

"FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football," the Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said in a letter to its 46 members of FIFA, warning of risks to their own competitions.

Sheikh Salman, an ally of Infantino since losing the FIFA presidential election to him in 2016, wrote: "Such an initiative will not succeed without the support of all the confederations, which is not the case now."

In a video message published Wednesday by FIFA, Infantino insisted spinning off its money-making operations was "an offer, not an obligation."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

A FIFA presentation for its members, co-written with its banking advisors from J.P. Morgan and seen by the AP, set a goal for FFE as "commercial rigour and expertise to better capitalise on broadcast rights, sponsorships and a growing tournament portfolio."

That growing portfolio would likely include adding more teams to FIFA competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup for men and women, and potentially staging them more often than every four years, including in the US.

FIFA adding teams, games and competitions would squeeze the value, status and space in the congested global fixture calendar for those that fund and are organised by the six continental soccer bodies like UEFA and the AFC.

A threatened World Cup boycott from Europe helped derail Infantino's 2021 plan to stage World Cups every two years instead of four.

AP/ABC

World.title: Australia's old friend wasn't at the Glasgow velodrome, but the old enemy was
World.content:
The crowds at the 2026 Commonwealth Games have varied in size and spirit.

Particularly at the Scottish Event Campus, not far from the city centre, casual fans will wander down and get a taste of the action if they've got time on their weekend.

It's school holiday time in Glasgow too, so plenty of families looking for a way to occupy the kids have made their way into the various arenas.

You may never get the chance to watch again, so a spot of 3x3 basketball or bowls, accompanied by some frankly excellent tunes and an overpriced carton of chips, is a decent way to spend four hours.

Aussie sprint stars through to 200m finals, gold rush at the velodrome Australia's track cycling squad claims three golds on the first day of competition at the velodrome, as Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis fly into their second finals of the week.

That's especially true when the weather has been so dreary to start the Games.

But on a day when it dried out at last, thousands made a decidedly purposeful pilgrimage to the velodrome at the Glasgow International Arena, just next to the home ground of Celtic Football Club.

This was not something you happen upon. This was something you go to. This was the moment Scotland had been waiting for at the arena named for one of their favourite sons, Sir Chris Hoy.

Ironically, before every race it was a pre-recorded Sir Chris (the real thing might have caused a riot) and fellow Scottish icon Duncan Scott telling the crowd to quiet down — or "haud yer wheesht", as Scott said — for the starter's buzzer.

But even Sir Chris — the six-time Olympic, 11-time world and two-time Commonwealth cycling champion — couldn't have contained his house when it was Scotland's Neil Fache (along with pilot Aaron Pope) who won the first gold of the track cycling program for these Games in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

Scots Neil Fachie MBE (left) and pilot Aaron Pope won the first gold medal of the cycling program in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Australian Kane Perris won Australia's first medal in that event alongside pilot Luke Zaccaria, and earlier in the day, Tara Neyland had picked up Australia's first world record in any event at these Games when she clocked 4:49.648 in qualifying for the C4-5 4,000m individual pursuit.

She later went on to win gold, but only after the women's team pursuit squad started what the cycling team hopes will be a gold rush in Glasgow.

Trailing New Zealand at the halfway mark of the gold medal race against New Zealand, the team of Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden put away their schedule and just started racing.

"That's my happy place. When we start racing, that's when I'm happiest. When the board goes away, and the hand signals come out, that's when I come into my own," 21-year-old gun Wilson-Haffenden said.

Women's team pursuit gold marked the start of what promises to be a big Games for Australian cycling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Just pedal. I was riding 50-cent coins by the end; the pedals weren't going around smooth but giving as much power as I had, grit the teeth, and get to the finish line."

England pipped their men's counterparts, and Jessica Gallagher was unable to defend her Birmingham gold in the tandem B sprint final after a tyre failure caused a nasty crash with the New Zealanders in the second race.

But, as pilot Jacqui Mengler-Mohr put it: "It's not how many times you fall, it's how many times you get back up."

Silver medallists Jessica Gallagher (right) and Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr had a nasty fall as they won tandem B sprint silver. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

And getting back up was exactly what the men's team sprinters did, going one better than the women's team and taking down their English rivals in the final.

They never looked like getting caught over the 1,000m race as Leigh Hoffman won a title as the leader of a new-look team with 23-year-old Danny Barber and 22-year-old Ryan Elliott.

The revamp came after the defection of Olympic gold medallist and sprint superstar Matthew Richardson, whose name Elliott wouldn't even utter when talking about the rivalry with Team England.

"I think it's definitely grown a lot since the swap and defection," he said.

"Between the GB guys maybe a bit less so but definitely between the defector himself."

Australian defector Richardson out of Games after fall Matt Richardson, a three-time Olympic medallist in Paris for Australia before he sensationally defected to the land of his birth, has been ruled out of the Commonwealth Games.

He wasn't the only departure after the team's gold medal at the Paris Olympics, with Matthew Glaetzer retiring and Tom Cornish pivoting to endurance events, making way for Elliott and Barber.

"There's a big change in the roster after Paris, and everyone's question then is: how well can our system back up? What's their depth?" he said.

"Us as the younger guys coming through wanted to prove we have depth in Australia and we're here because we're hungry."

Hoffman said he enjoyed riding with teammates who were 100 per cent in it for Australia.

Ryan Elliott (left), Danny Barber and Leigh Hoffman won team sprint gold in their new formation. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"It would've been great if he stayed with Australia but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance," he said.

Richardson is no longer coming to Glasgow after an ugly fall during a keirin race in Japan just days ago, and Hoffman is disappointed he and Barber won't get a crack at him in the individual event.

"I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how I and Danny stack up against him," Hoffman said.

"I'm upset he's not here, but that is what it is. … I've got plenty of other fish to worry about."

England, Wales, Scotland, Australia and New Zealand are some of the world's strongest track cycling nations, with Malaysia's Azizul Awang and Nicholas Paul from Trinidad and Tobago threats for Hoffman and Barber.

But the good news is Hoffman isn't going anywhere.

"We checked his passport and his lineage," Elliott said.

"So he's good."

Tech.title: Anthropic says Claude accidentally hacked real companies too
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic just realized several of its Claude AI models hacked into the systems of three different organizations during testing, acting on their own and without the company noticing. The revelation comes days after rival OpenAI said one of its own models had breached developer platform Hugging Face, adding to growing unease over whether frontier AI labs are doing enough to control the increasingly capable systems they are building.

In a blog post describing the incidents, Anthropic said Claude gained unauthorized access to the systems during cybersecurity evaluations. All of the attacks happened during “capture-the-flag” exercises, a common way of testing hacking ability, where models are asked to find and obtain hidden information inside of a simulated network.

The disclosure adds to mounting pressure on frontier AI labs in the wake of the Hugging Face incident and the release of powerful open-weight Chinese models. Employees at the major labs are now calling for coordinated global governance, and US lawmakers have begun weighing tighter oversight of powerful models and who can access them.

Anthropic says the environment for its cybersecurity tests was supposed to be isolated. However, a “misconfiguration” left the machines Claude accessed “with live internet access,” the company said, and because all models had been “explicitly told” they had no internet access, they “assumed” the real networks it encountered were part of the simulated environment.

The earliest incidents date back to April and involved three different Claude models: Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and “an internal research test model,” according to the blog post. As the models were being tested on their cyber abilities, Anthropic said they lacked the standard safeguards usually put in place to curtail riskier behavior.

The company said it discovered incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 cybersecurity test runs, something it only did after OpenAI disclosed its rogue AI agent was behind the attack on Hugging Face.

The three models behaved very differently when they encountered information suggesting that the systems they were encountering were, in fact, real. By Anthropic’s account, the oldest model, Opus 4.7, recognized it had reached a real system, “but continued its attack.” Its flagship Mythos 5 figured out it was using the internet but somehow reasoned this was all still part of the simulation, so continued. The internal test model, which Anthropic describes as “our latest model,” stopped the exercise when evidence emerged that its targets were real.

Anthropic did not identify the affected organizations and said it will continue to investigate the incident and provide updates when it can. The company said it is also speaking with AI research nonprofit METR about conducting a third-party review of what happened. OpenAI has also hired METR to conduct an independent review.

Throughout the post, Anthropic repeatedly contrasts both the nature and its handling of the incidents with OpenAI’s, ending with a bulleted, four-point list outlining the differences — and why it believes its own response was better. Anthropic emphasizes that it “proactively” reviewed its tests, and did so before a company detected any activity. It also said its models accessed the internet “via an open path,” rather than using a novel exploit like OpenAI’s agent, adding that its most recent model also stopped when it realized it was working in a real environment.

Anthropic also said its models failed in a different way from OpenAI’s agent, indicating that this was a safer form of failure. “While there is not a perfectly sharp distinction between the two, we believe these incidents to be closer to a harness and operational failure than a model alignment failure,” the company said. In plain English: The Claude models were doing what they were told, while OpenAI’s agent pursued its goal in a way its creators did not intend, described as misalignment in the AI safety world.

Anthropic called on other AI labs to conduct similar proactive reviews of its cyber testing, adding that the discovery underscores the need for stronger controls and safety measures when testing AI systems.

Tech.title: D&D is getting World of Warcraft and Star Wars crossovers
Tech.content:
Dungeons & Dragons is no stranger to franchise crossovers, and now it’s kicking off its biggest multiverse initiative to date, starting with a World of Warcraft expansion. Wizards of the Coast (WotC) has announced that D&D: World of Warcraft — a new sourcebook that brings Blizzard’s Azeroth setting to the popular tabletop roleplaying game — will be launching on November 17th.

A D&D / Star Wars collaboration has also been announced, which will be set during the Rebellion era of the Star Wars franchise. Details on that are sparse, but it’s expected to arrive sometime in 2027. Both of these projects are part of what D&D publisher WotC is calling its “D&D Universes Beyond” initiative, which aims to build on the highly profitable success of the Universes Beyond series it launched for Magic: The Gathering in 2021. While wading into other IPs has been met with mixed reactions from MtG fans, the collectible card game is one of the few franchises that isn’t hemorrhaging money for WotC owner Hasbro.

D&D: World of Warcraft, uses the revised 5th edition Player’s Handbook as a foundation, and includes rules for how to play all 13 World of Warcraft classes using the TTRPG system, featuring a bunch of new spells, magic items, and professions. It also adds 11 new WoW-themed player species, and six additional subclasses, including the Oath of the Ebon Blade and Oath of the Holy for Paladins, Demon Hunter Ranger, Shadow Domain and Discipline Domain for Clerics, and the Path of the Elements Barbarian.

Tech.title: This tattoo is permanent, pain-free, and might soon come in the mail
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The refurbished railway station in London I entered last week had none of the usual signs of being a tattoo studio. The walls were devoid of any art, and there were no reclining chairs or massage tables in the room. The only tattoo gun on the premises sat in a display case instead of buzzing in someone’s gloved hand. I felt like I was getting inked in a half-assembled biolab with some interesting benefits.

I’m not trying to put on a show of bravado when I say my latest tattoo didn’t hurt. Getting the small sparkle lineart permanently marked on my skin was a genuinely painless experience. It was over in seconds, and didn’t involve any grisly needles — at least, not in the traditional sense.

It was applied by CipherX, a London-based biotech company that’s developed disposable “Microdot” patches that provide an alternative form of permanent tattooing. Each patch is roughly the size of a US quarter and uses microscopic, biodegradable needles to deposit pigment into the upper layers of the skin. The process is designed to be “quiet, fast, and pain-free,” all of which I found to be true, opening the door for even more people to rock some permanent ink.

CipherX set up this rotating display, and I had to really squint to see the microneedles on the tattoo patches. Here’s a closer look at the microneedles, viewed using a live microscope video feed.

Some cosmetic products already use a similar technology, and microneedle tattoo patches have been explored since at least 2022, but CipherX appears to be the first to turn that latter concept into a consumer-ready product. My Verge colleagues have previously put their bodies on the line in the name of testing technology, and I was more than happy to offer up my flesh.

The application itself was actually faster than I expected. After choosing my design — a “Bold Sparkle,” now widely associated with AI iconography — CipherX CEO Ferdinand Kohle placed an ink-coated transparent guide disc on my arm to indicate where it would be applied. He then lined up the seemingly 3D-printed applicator with the ink guidelines, pressed a button, and removed it to reveal the Microdot patch affixed to my arm, embedding 112 microneedles into my skin.

Applying the Microdot patch took a few seconds, and I barely felt anything.

A flexible tattoo bandage was applied to prevent it from moving around, and a branded plastic sticker was placed over that — presumably for marketing as Kohle admitted that part wasn’t necessary. The final step involved waiting 15 minutes for it to process, and I was free to move around during that time.

I was warned that I might feel a slight “flicking” sensation as the applicator was pressed, but I barely noticed a thing. It felt more like someone had lightly touched my arm with their finger. I wouldn’t even describe the sensation as uncomfortable, let alone painful. It’s also worth mentioning that I have sensitive skin and bleed very easily, but I didn’t experience any bleeding or irritation from the microneedles. There was no scabbing or healing time at all, unlike my other tattoos.

Step 1) pick your design and position it using the ink-coated guide lens. I obviously didn’t opt for the smiley face. Step 2) the applicator is lined up with the ink guidelines, and snaps the patch against your skin. (This photo was taken between steps (3) and (4) — note the skin irritation caused by the sticker.) Step 3) cover the patch to prevent it from moving and chill for 15 minutes while the pigment is deposited. Step 4) remove the covering and patch to reveal your new tattoo. This is what it looked like immediately after application.

The tattoo is revealed after the patch is removed, and becomes visibly darker over the course of two days. Initially, the tattoo consisted of lots of teeny dots rather than a smooth, connected line. The ink is supposed to “bleed” together as it develops, like a regular tattoo does over the years, but that hasn’t occurred in the five days since I had it done. I now have to look very closely to see the dots, but they’re definitely still there.

This macro shot was taken five days later. The dots remain visible but you’d have to be creepily close to actually see them.

The superfluous branded sticker they applied over the tattoo bandage was actually the most annoying part of the entire experience because it pinched my skin when I moved my arm. I had the tattoo applied near the inside of my elbow as that’s one of the more painful areas for traditional tattooing — I have my ankles done already (another notable pain zone) and wanted to compare.

This isn’t a viable solution for tattooing most of the more painful body areas like your ankle joint or fingers though. The applicator requires enough of a flat surface area to accommodate the patch and skin that can be lightly stretched, so bony areas aren’t ideal if you want every bit of the tattoo to come out cleanly. CipherX also isn’t applying these on people’s face, neck, hands, or groin area, but that’s more because the company isn’t comfortable doing so, and some tattoo artists reject those areas over similar personal boundaries.

Previous Next



1 / 3 This is the applicator used to apply the Microdot patches against your skin.

Right now, the tattoo selection only includes about 15 designs, they can’t be customized or measure larger than 15mm in diameter, and black is the only color option. CipherX is working on expanding beyond those limitations: It’s developing additional colors, including an invisible UV-reactive ink, and is working on a larger size option, both of which were previewed at the event. The company is also increasing its range of designs and plans to collaborate with established artists for future releases.

The bigger size option that’s in development can be seen here, compared to the current patch size on the right. These are some of the available designs. The UV-reactive ink option CipherX is testing is pretty neat! The patches are disposable and come in this silver packaging, with clear warnings that this is going to be permanent.

As someone who prefers larger, colorful custom ink, I can confidently say that I’m not the target demographic for Microdot tattoos, but I’m also not entirely sure who is. The tats could be a good space filler for people with existing tattoos, but those folks clearly don’t have any issues with going the more painful traditional route. It’s a good option for needlephobes, but they would have to really want a tattoo while simultaneously not caring about hosting a generic design on their skin, forever.

CipherX showed me another interesting perk in development: It’s planning to sell kits that let you apply the tattoo yourself at home. At the launch event I attended, the company showed off a mockup of a palm-sized metal tin that could be shipped to a customer’s doorstep in the future. I asked CipherX for a launch timeline, but it hasn’t responded at the time of writing. CipherX is currently only offering tattoos through approved pop-ups in London, using trained practitioners to manage age verification requirements.

This is the current prototype for the DIY home kit that CipherX is planning to launch. It doesn’t include a tiny applicator, which might mean customers have to purchase it separately or 3D print their own.

I don’t think Microdot patches will revolutionize tattooing, but it might make them more accessible for a wider audience of needle-fearing folk. At £50 (about $66), I feel it’s a fair price for a more comfortable tattooing experience, and comparable to the price of similarly sized tattoos, though this obviously varies by area and artist rates. My only remaining test will be to see how “permanent” these tattoos really are. While it did darken, it’s now settled to a shade of black that looks fairly washed out, as if I’d had it for years, not days.
